title: Cache Memory — concept notes
text: Cache memory GATE ka sabse zyada baar poocha gaya single topic hai (is corpus me 69 PYQs — sabse highest). Har saal kam se kam ek question guaranteed hai. Isliye ye topic P1 hai aur ismein deep numerical practice zaroori hai. Cache ek chhota, fast memory hai jo CPU aur main memory ke beech baithta hai. Idea simple hai: 'Principle of Locality' — agar CPU ne abhi kisi address X ko access kiya hai, to (a) wo address phir se jaldi access hoga (temporal locality), aur (b) uske paas-paas ke addresses bhi jaldi access honge (spatial locality). Isliye jab CPU X maangta hai, cache sirf X nahi, X ka pura 'block' la ke rakh leta hai. Socho cache ek chhota sa drawer hai tumhari table par, aur main memory poore ghar ki almirah. Har baar almirah tak jaana slow hai. Jo cheez tum baar baar use karte ho (ya jo cheez ek saath use hoti hai, jaise ek hi shelf ki cheezein), wo tum apne table ke drawer me rakh lete ho. Cache memory yahi karta hai — recently/nearby accessed data ko fast memory me copy rakh leta hai taaki agli baar almirah tak na jaana pade. Cache is divided into 'lines' or 'blocks'; main memory is divided into blocks of the same size. Mapping function decides WHERE a main-memory block can go in the cache: Direct-Mapped (exactly 1 place), Fully Associative (anywhere), k-way Set-Associative (any of k places within one set). Every cache line carries a Valid bit (is the line holding real data?) and, for writable caches, a Dirty/Modified bit (has this line been written to since it was loaded?). Write policy: Write-Through (write goes to cache AND main memory immediately — simple, more memory traffic) vs Write-Back (write only to cache, marked dirty, flushed to memory only on eviction — faster, needs dirty bit). Replacement policy (needed only when Fully/Set-Associative, since Direct-Mapped has no choice): LRU, FIFO, Random, Optimal. Inclusion property (multi-level cache): if L2 is inclusive of L1, everything in L1 must also be in L2. Address = [ TAG | LINE/SET index | WORD/BLOCK offset ]. #offset bits = log2(block size in words/bytes). #index bits = log2(number of lines). #tag bits = total address bits − index bits − offset bits. Address = [ TAG | SET index | WORD offset ]. #set bits = log2(number of sets) = log2(number of lines / associativity k). Everything else same as direct-mapped, just index now selects a SET not a single line. Address = [ TAG | WORD offset ] — no set/index field at all, since a block can go anywhere; the entire remaining address (after offset) is the tag, compared against every line in parallel. Average Memory Access Time = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty. For multi-level: AMAT = HitTime_L1 + MissRate_L1 × (HitTime_L2 + MissRate_L2 × (... × MissPenalty_MainMemory)) Effective CPI = Base CPI + (memory accesses per instruction) × (miss rate) × (miss penalty in cycles) — used in speedup/CPI-impact numericals. Cache size = number of lines × block size (data only; tag/valid/dirty bits are usually NOT counted in 'cache size' unless question explicitly says 'tag memory size' or 'total bits including tag'). Confusing 'number of lines' with 'number of sets' — in a k-way set-associative cache, #sets = #lines / k, and the SET index field is computed from #sets, not #lines directly. Forgetting byte-addressability: if block size is given in WORDS but address is byte-addressable, offset bits must account for both word offset AND byte-within-word offset. Mixing up which quantity is 'given' vs 'asked' in AMAT chains — always write the formula first, then substitute. In LRU-trace questions, forgetting that a HIT also updates recency order (not just misses). Assuming direct-mapped cache needs a replacement policy — it doesn't, there's only one possible line per block. For ANY address-split question: first find block size → offset bits, then #sets → set/index bits, then tag bits = total − offset − index. Draw the 3-field box every time, don't do it in your head. For AMAT/hierarchy questions: draw the tree of hit/miss paths level by level before writing one formula. For LRU-trace questions: maintain a simple table, one row per access, and cross out the least-recently-used entry on every miss with a full set.

title: Address Field Decomposition (Tag / Set-Index / Offset)
text: Agar question me diya hai: cache size, block size, associativity (direct-mapped / k-way / fully-associative), aur total address width (ya main memory size) — aur poocha hai TAG/SET/INDEX/WORD/OFFSET field me kitne bits hain — to ye is pattern ka sabse classic question hai. Yehi single sabse-zyada-repeat-hone-wala GATE cache pattern hai. Step 1: Offset bits = log2(block size) Step 2: #lines = cache size / block size; #sets = #lines / associativity Step 3: Set/index bits = log2(#sets) (0 if fully associative, since there's only 1 'set') Step 4: Tag bits = total address bits − offset bits − index bits Sanity check: tag + index + offset MUST equal total address width. 1. Note down: total address bits (A), cache size (C), block size (B), associativity (k) — convert everything to consistent units (bytes or words) first, this is where most silly mistakes happen. 2. offset = log2(B) 3. number of lines = C / B 4. number of sets = (number of lines) / k [k=1 for direct-mapped, k=∞/1-set for fully-associative] 5. index/set bits = log2(number of sets) 6. tag bits = A − offset − index 7. Double-check with the identity tag+index+offset = A. Not converting KB/MB consistently (1K = 2^10, not 1000, in this context). Treating 'number of lines' as 'number of sets' directly for a set-associative cache. Forgetting the extra bits needed for byte-offset within a word when block size is given in words but memory is byte-addressable. Given main memory size instead of address width directly (need log2(memory size) first). Byte-addressable vs word-addressable memory — changes what the 'offset' actually measures. Question gives TAG bits and asks you to back-solve for associativity or cache size (reverse direction of the same formula). 2D array traversal wrapped around this (see pattern 04) where the array's memory layout feeds into the address split.

title: AMAT / Multi-Level Cache Hierarchy Access Time
text: Agar question me L1/L2 (ya cache + main memory) ke hit rates aur access times diye hain aur 'average access time' ya 'effective access time' poocha hai — ye AMAT pattern hai. Do-level se teen-level tak ho sakta hai. AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty Miss penalty at level i = AMAT of level (i+1) — recursion chalti hai neeche tak Draw the hit/miss tree before plugging into the formula. 1. Identify the number of levels (L1, L2, ..., main memory). 2. Start from the LAST level (main memory access time is just its own access time — no 'miss' beyond it). 3. Compute AMAT of the second-to-last level using: hit_time + miss_rate × (AMAT of next level). 4. Work backward level by level until you reach L1's AMAT — that's the final answer. 5. If the question instead gives 'local miss rate' vs 'global miss rate', clarify which one is used in the formula — local miss rate is what plugs directly into this recursive formula. Using GLOBAL miss rate at an inner level when the formula needs LOCAL miss rate (or vice versa) — always check which one the question defines. Forgetting to add hit_time even when miss_rate is being processed — hit time is paid on EVERY access, hit or miss. Unit mismatch: mixing ns and clock cycles without converting via clock frequency. Asked as 'effective CPI impact' instead of raw time (multiply the miss-penalty-in-time term by clock frequency to convert to cycles, then fold into CPI). Given bandwidth + latency instead of a flat access time (compute time = latency + size/bandwidth first). Speedup-style framing: 'by what factor does adding this cache improve performance' — same AMAT machinery, just take the ratio of before/after.

title: Replacement-Policy Trace (LRU/FIFO block-reference simulation)
text: Agar question me memory-block references ki ek sequence di hai (jaise '0,1,2,3,0,4,...') aur poocha hai ki kaunsa block cache me RAHEGA ya kitne MISSES honge, given a replacement policy (mostly LRU) — ye simulation/trace pattern hai. Isme formula nahi, step-by-step haath se trace karna padta hai. Draw a table: one row per reference, columns = cache lines/sets. On every reference: is the block already present? HIT (update recency) else MISS (evict per policy, insert new block). For set-associative, only worry about the ONE set that block maps to — reduce the problem to a smaller direct/fully-associative trace within that set. 1. If set-associative, first compute which SET each referenced block maps to (block number mod number-of-sets). 2. Group the reference sequence by set — only references to the SAME set interact with each other. 3. Within one set, simulate LRU: maintain an ordered list (most-recent to least-recent); on hit, move block to front; on miss with full set, evict the back (least-recent) and insert new block at front. 4. Count misses / read off final cache contents as asked. Mixing FIFO and LRU behavior — FIFO ignores hits for eviction order, LRU doesn't. Forgetting that different sets are INDEPENDENT — a reference to set 2 does not affect set 0's LRU order. FIFO instead of LRU (evict oldest-INSERTED, not oldest-USED — different from LRU when there are repeated hits). Question asks 'which block will NOT be in the cache' instead of the miss count — same trace, different final read-off.

title: Loop/Array Traversal Cache-Performance Analysis (row-major vs column-major, code-segment comparison)
text: Agar question me C code diya hai jisme nested for-loop se 2D array traverse ho raha hai (do versions P1 aur P2, jaise i-then-j vs j-then-i order), aur poocha hai kaunsa version zyada cache-friendly hai ya kitne hits/misses honge — ye locality-of-reference application hai, address-split pattern ke sath combine hota hai. C arrays are stored ROW-MAJOR — traversing row-by-row (i outer, j inner) accesses consecutive memory addresses → good spatial locality. Traversing column-by-column (j outer, i inner) jumps by (row-size) addresses each step → poor spatial locality → more misses. Combine with Pattern 01: figure out how many array elements fit in one cache block, that tells you how many consecutive accesses are 'free' (hits) before the next miss. 1. Determine array storage order (row-major, given as default for C unless stated otherwise) and element size. 2. Compute how many array elements fit per cache block = block size / element size. 3. For the GOOD traversal order (matches storage order): every (elements-per-block)-th access is a miss, rest are hits. 4. For the BAD traversal order (against storage order): almost every access is a miss (each element lands in a different block). Assuming row-major traversal is ALWAYS all-hits-after-first — if the array is large enough that consecutive rows alias to the same cache set/line, you get conflict misses even in the 'good' order. Forgetting array indexing starts at 0 when computing addresses. Two-loop comparison (P1 vs P2) asking which has fewer misses, vs a single-loop version asking for the exact miss count. Combined with direct-mapped index-conflict: even the 'good' row-major order can thrash if the row length causes different rows to map to the SAME cache line.

title: Write Policy / Inclusion Property / Coherence — Conceptual (True-False / MSQ style)
text: Agar question me numerical calculation nahi hai, balki statements diye hain about write-through/write-back, dirty bit, inclusion property, ya cache coherence, aur poocha hai kaunse statements TRUE hain — ye conceptual/MSQ pattern hai, GATE 2020 ke baad ye zyada common ho gaya hai. Write-through: every write goes to memory immediately → simpler, more bus traffic, no dirty bit needed. Write-back: write stays in cache, dirty bit set, flushed to memory only on eviction → less bus traffic, needs dirty bit + write-back on evict. Inclusion property: L2 ⊇ L1 (everything in L1 also in L2) is needed for cache-coherence protocols to only need to snoop L2. 1. For each statement, mentally classify it under one of: write-policy behavior, replacement-policy behavior, or inclusion/coherence behavior. 2. Check it against the definitions above — most traps are simple reversals (swapping write-through and write-back behavior). 3. For MSQ, evaluate each option independently — don't assume the count of correct options. Swapping write-through/write-back properties. Assuming inclusion is automatic — it must be actively maintained by the replacement policy. Combined with TLB/MMU (virtual vs physical addressed cache) — cross-links to Virtual Memory topic. Combined with multiprocessor cache-coherence framing.

title: Basic Definition / Principle of Locality (rare now, mostly pre-2000 descriptive)
text: 'What is cache memory', 'principle of locality justifies use of ___' jaise seedhe definitional questions — GATE ke bahut purane papers (1987-1995) me the, ab MCQ/NAT era me lagbhag nahi aate directly, lekin concept clarity ke liye zaroori hai. Cache = small fast memory exploiting locality of reference to reduce AMAT. Direct recall — no calculation needed.

title: Pipelining
text: CO & Architecture pipelining

title: Pipelining — concept notes
text: Pipelining GATE ka bahut high-value CO&A topic hai (39 PYQs). 4 skills: pipeline TIMING/cycle-time compute karna (biggest cluster), pipelined-vs-non-pipelined SPEEDUP comparison, HAZARDS (data/structural, forwarding, register renaming), aur BRANCH/control hazards (delayed branching). Pipelining = multiple instructions ko OVERLAP karke execute karna (jaise ek assembly line) — jab instruction 1 stage 2 me hai, instruction 2 stage 1 me shuru ho sakta hai. CLOCK CYCLE TIME = MAXIMUM stage delay + inter-stage LATCH delay (sabse SLOW stage bottleneck hai, sab stages ko uska wait karna padta hai). Total time for n instructions = (k + n - 1) × cycle_time, jahan k = number of stages. Pipelining ko ek 'car wash assembly line' socho — 4 stations hain (wash, rinse, dry, wax), aur jab ek car station 2 me hai, agli car station 1 me shuru ho sakti hai (wait nahi karni padti pehli car ke poora hone tak). Lekin PURI line ki speed SABSE SLOW station se decide hoti hai — agar 'wash' 10 min leta hai aur baaki sab 2 min, to HAR station effectively 10 min ka slot lega (fastest station bhi slowest ka wait karega). Speedup = (Non-pipelined time) / (Pipelined time) = [n × Σstage_delays] / [(k+n-1) × cycle_time] — approaches k (number of stages) as n→∞ (asymptotic/ideal speedup = k). Clock cycle time is ALWAYS bottlenecked by the SLOWEST stage (+ latch delay) — even if other stages are much faster, the pipeline clock must accommodate the slowest one. If a stage is SPLIT into two sub-stages, the new bottleneck is the max of ALL stage delays (including the two new sub-stage halves) — splitting the SLOWEST stage typically reduces cycle time and speeds up the pipeline; splitting an already-fast stage does nothing for cycle time. DATA HAZARDS occur when an instruction needs a result that a PRIOR instruction hasn't yet computed/written back (RAW — Read After Write) — resolved via FORWARDING (bypass the result directly from EX/MEM stage to the next instruction needing it, skipping the register-file round trip) or STALLING (insert bubbles/NOPs until the value is ready). STRUCTURAL HAZARDS occur when two instructions need the SAME hardware resource (like a single ALU or single memory port) at the same cycle — resolved via resource duplication or stalling. CONTROL HAZARDS occur from branch instructions (don't know the next instruction to fetch until the branch is resolved) — resolved via branch prediction, delayed branching (execute a fixed number of 'delay slot' instructions regardless of branch outcome), or stalling. Delayed branching: the instruction(s) immediately following a branch (in the 'delay slot') execute REGARDLESS of whether the branch is taken or not — compiler tries to fill this slot with useful, order-independent work. Register renaming resolves WAR (Write After Read) and WAW (Write After Write) hazards (name dependencies, not true data dependencies) by giving each write operation a fresh physical register — NOT used for RAW hazards (those are handled by forwarding/stalling). Clock cycle time = max(all stage delays) + inter-stage latch delay Time for n instructions, k-stage pipeline = (k + n - 1) × cycle_time Time for n instructions, non-pipelined = n × Σ(all stage delays) Speedup = NonPipelinedTime / PipelinedTime; asymptotic (n→∞) speedup → k (number of stages) Extra cycles per taken branch (no prediction/delay slot) = (stage number where branch resolves) − 1, roughly — depends on exact pipeline design Forgetting to include the inter-stage LATCH delay when computing cycle time — often given as a small extra constant added to the max stage delay. Applying the ideal (k+n-1)×cycle_time formula even when the question specifies hazards/stalls/branch penalties are present — must add the extra stall cycles explicitly in those cases. Confusing WHICH hazard type (data/structural/control) a given scenario represents — RAW dependency = data hazard, resource conflict = structural, branch = control. Assuming register renaming helps with RAW hazards — it specifically addresses WAR/WAW, not RAW. For cycle-time questions: identify the maximum stage delay, add the latch delay, that's your clock cycle time. For total-execution-time questions: apply (k+n-1)×cycle_time for the ideal case; ADD extra cycles explicitly for each stall/hazard/branch-penalty the question specifies. For speedup questions: compute non-pipelined time and pipelined time separately, take the ratio; recall the asymptotic speedup approaches k (stage count) for large n. For hazard-classification questions: check if it's about DATA dependency (RAW/WAR/WAW), shared HARDWARE resource (structural), or BRANCH/jump uncertainty (control) — match to the resolution technique (forwarding/stalling, renaming, or branch prediction/delay slots respectively).

title: Pipeline Timing / Cycle-Time Computation
text: Stage delays (aur shayad latch delay) diye hain, aur poocha hai clock cycle time kya hai, ya n instructions execute karne me total time kya lagega — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (39 me se 18 PYQs). Cycle time = max(stage delays) + latch delay. Total time for n instructions through k stages = (k+n-1) × cycle_time (ideal, no hazards). Splitting the SLOWEST stage into two typically reduces cycle time; splitting a fast stage doesn't help. 1. Find the maximum stage delay among all stages, add the latch delay (if given) — that's the cycle time. 2. For total execution time of n instructions: apply (k+n-1)×cycle_time. 3. For stage-splitting questions: recompute the new maximum stage delay after the split, apply the same formulas with the updated cycle time and stage count. Forgetting to add the inter-stage latch delay when it's given. Applying (k+n-1) blindly even with branch penalties or stalls explicitly present in the question — must add those extra cycles on top. Loop execution timing (instruction sequence repeated multiple times) — multiply per-iteration pipelined time by iteration count, watching for pipeline-fill/drain effects only happening once (at loop start/end) vs per-iteration. One stage has an EXCEPTION/longer delay for specific instructions (like branches) — handle that instruction's extra cycles separately from the general formula.

title: Speedup / Pipelined vs Non-Pipelined Comparison
text: Poocha hai pipelined vs non-pipelined processor ke execution time/speedup compare karo, ya do DIFFERENT pipeline DESIGNS compare karne hain — ye comparative pattern hai (39 me se 8 PYQs). Speedup = NonPipelinedTime / PipelinedTime. Asymptotic speedup (very large n) approaches k (number of pipeline stages) — a useful sanity-check limit. 1. Compute non-pipelined time (n × sum of all stage delays, or CPI×clock-period×n for a given CPI model). 2. Compute pipelined time ((k+n-1)×cycle_time). 3. Take the ratio for speedup; for comparing two DIFFERENT pipeline designs, compute total times for both and compare directly. Forgetting that pipelining often REDUCES clock frequency slightly (due to added latch overhead) even while improving overall throughput — must account for BOTH effects, not just stage count. Non-pipelined CPU with given CPI, converted to a pipelined design with different (usually slower per-cycle but more overlapped) clock — reconcile clock RATE change with CPI/stage-count change together.

title: Hazards (data/structural), Forwarding, Register Renaming
text: Poocha hai kaunse hazards present hain (data/structural), forwarding se kya solve hota hai, ya register renaming kis purpose ke liye hai — ye hazard-classification pattern hai (39 me se 11 PYQs). RAW (true dependency, needs a not-yet-computed value) → DATA hazard → forwarding/stalling. Shared hardware resource conflict → STRUCTURAL hazard → resource duplication/stalling. WAR/WAW (false/name dependencies) → resolved by REGISTER RENAMING (not forwarding). 1. For a given instruction sequence, check register overlaps between consecutive/nearby instructions — identify if it's RAW (data), WAR/WAW (name), or a resource conflict (structural). 2. Match the hazard type to its appropriate resolution technique (forwarding for RAW, renaming for WAR/WAW, duplication/stalling for structural). 3. For 'does forwarding solve this' questions, verify forwarding specifically addresses RAW — not WAR/WAW or structural conflicts. Assuming register renaming helps with RAW hazards — it specifically targets WAR/WAW, RAW still needs forwarding/stalling. Reservation-table-based Minimum Average Latency (MAL) computation — a structural-hazard-avoidance scheduling technique, find the shortest safe interval between issuing identical instructions. Multi-statement TRUE/FALSE about forwarding correctness across various hazard scenarios.

title: Branch/Control Hazard (delayed branching)
text: Poocha hai delayed branching kaise kaam karta hai, ya branch delay slot me kaunsi instruction safely rakhi ja sakti hai — ye control-hazard-specific pattern hai. Instruction(s) in the delay slot execute UNCONDITIONALLY (regardless of branch outcome) — must be chosen carefully by the compiler to be safe in EITHER case. An instruction can go in the delay slot only if it doesn't depend on the branch's outcome and doesn't get incorrectly affected whether the branch is taken or not. 1. Identify the instruction(s) immediately after the branch (the delay slot). 2. Check if that instruction's effect is SAFE regardless of whether the branch is taken or not (doesn't depend on / interfere with the branch condition or target). 3. Confirm it executes unconditionally in the given code trace. Assuming the delay-slot instruction only executes when the branch is NOT taken (or only when taken) — it always executes, that's the defining feature of delayed branching.

title: Machine Instruction
text: CO & Architecture machine-instruction

title: Machine Instruction — concept notes
text: Machine Instruction topic 4 skills test karta hai: assembly program TRACE karna (registers/memory final values), instruction ENCODING (bit-field sizing for opcode/operands), CLOCK CYCLE/timing analysis, aur conceptual properties (privileged instructions, addressing modes, stack). Assembly instructions register/memory pe directly operate karte hain (LOAD, STORE, ADD, MOV, CMP, etc.). Instruction ENCODING me fixed-width instruction word ko OPCODE + OPERANDS me divide karna hota hai — agar r registers hain to log2(r) bits per register-operand chahiye, agar i instruction types hain to log2(i) bits opcode ke liye. Assembly program ko trace karna bilkul waisa hai jaise C code trace karna (Programming In C topic) — bas ab 'variables' registers/memory-locations hain, aur 'statements' specific instructions (LOAD/STORE/ADD/etc.) hain. Instruction ENCODING ko socho ek 'fixed-size form' jisme alag-alag boxes hain — kitne boxes (bits) OPCODE ke liye chahiye (kitne alag instructions hain, unka log2), kitne REGISTER-naam ke liye (kitne registers hain, unka log2), baaki bache bits IMMEDIATE VALUE ke liye available hain. Bits for opcode = ⌈log2(number of distinct instruction types)⌉. Bits per register operand = ⌈log2(number of registers)⌉. Remaining bits for immediate operand = total instruction width − opcode bits − (register bits × number of register operands). Privileged instructions (like RFE — Return From Exception) can only execute in KERNEL/SUPERVISOR mode, not user mode — attempting in user mode triggers a fault/trap. Effective Address modes: (X)+ (auto-increment AFTER use, for sequential forward access like array traversal), -(X) (auto-decrement BEFORE use, for stack push/pop or reverse traversal) — recognize these as classic addressing-mode notations from PDP-11-style architectures. Data forwarding/internal forwarding: bypass the register file by directly routing a computed result to where it's needed next, SKIPPING an intermediate store-then-load round trip — reduces instruction count/latency. ⌈log2(number of distinct instructions)⌉ ⌈log2(number of registers)⌉ per register operand total instruction width − opcode bits − (register bits × number of register operands) Σ (clock cycles per instruction × number of times that instruction executes, accounting for loops) Miscounting bits available for the immediate operand — forgetting to subtract for ALL register operand fields (not just one) when an instruction has multiple register operands. For program-counter legality questions, forgetting that PC values must be ALIGNED to instruction boundaries (e.g., every instruction is k bytes, so PC must be a multiple of k from the start address) — not every arbitrary address is a valid instruction start. Losing track of loop iteration counts when computing total clock cycles for a program with branches/loops. For program-trace questions: maintain an explicit table of register/memory values, updating after each instruction exactly as specified. For instruction-encoding bit-sizing: apply the direct formula (opcode bits + register-field bits × operand count, subtract from total width for immediate bits). For clock-cycle/timing questions: sum (cycles per instruction type × execution count), being careful to account for loop repetitions. For conceptual addressing-mode/privileged-instruction questions: recall the standard definitions directly rather than deriving from first principles.

title: Trace Assembly Program Execution
text: Ek assembly language program diya hai aur poocha hai final register/memory VALUE kya hoga, ya program kya COMPUTE karta hai — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (21 me se 14 PYQs). Maintain an explicit table of register and relevant memory values, update after EVERY instruction. Read each instruction's semantics carefully (given as comments/documentation in the question) before tracing — don't assume standard meaning without checking. 1. List all registers/memory locations involved with their initial values. 2. Process each instruction in order, updating the table exactly per its documented semantics. 3. Report the requested final value(s). Misreading a hypothetical processor's custom instruction semantics (they often differ from standard x86/ARM conventions) — always use the EXACT semantics given in the question, never assume. Data-forwarding optimization questions — identify which instruction sequence can be shortened by bypassing memory round-trips. Latency-table-based dependency questions — track WHEN a value becomes available (not just what it becomes) for pipelined/dependent instruction sequences.

title: Instruction Encoding / Bit-Field Sizing
text: Poocha hai ek fixed-width instruction word me OPCODE, REGISTER operands, aur IMMEDIATE operand ke liye kitne bits allocate honge, ya kaunsa PC value legal hai — ye bit-arithmetic pattern hai. opcode bits = ⌈log2(#instructions)⌉. register field bits = ⌈log2(#registers)⌉ per operand. Immediate bits = total width − opcode bits − (register bits × number of register operands). PC legality: must be aligned to instruction-size boundaries from the program's start address. 1. Compute opcode bits and register-field bits using the ceiling-log2 formulas. 2. Subtract from total instruction width to find remaining bits for the immediate operand. 3. For PC legality, check the candidate address is start_address + k×(instruction size in bytes) for some integer k≥0. Forgetting to account for MULTIPLE register-operand fields (subtracting only once when an instruction has 2 or 3 register operands).

title: Clock Cycles / Timing Analysis
text: Poocha hai program execute karne me KITNE clock cycles lagenge, given per-instruction cycle costs (aur shayad loops/latencies) — ye timing-summation pattern hai. Sum (cycles per instruction type × execution count) — carefully account for LOOP repetitions, not just static instruction count. For latency-dependency questions, track when a value becomes AVAILABLE for the next dependent instruction, not just when the producing instruction issues. 1. Identify each instruction's cycle cost from the given table. 2. Determine how many times each instruction actually executes (accounting for loop bodies running multiple times). 3. Sum up total cycles = Σ(cost × execution count). Counting loop-body instructions only ONCE instead of accounting for all iterations.

title: Conceptual Properties (privileged instructions, addressing modes, stack behavior)
text: Poocha hai ek instruction (jaise RFE) PRIVILEGED hai ya nahi, ya specific addressing-mode notation ((X)+, -(X)) ka matlab kya hai, ya stack pointer behavior — ye definitional/conceptual pattern hai. Instructions that affect processor MODE or handle exceptions (like RFE) are typically PRIVILEGED (kernel-mode only). (X)+ = auto-increment AFTER use (forward traversal); -(X) = auto-decrement BEFORE use (stack push style, or reverse traversal). 1. For privilege questions, reason about whether the instruction could compromise system integrity if available to user programs — exception-handling and mode-switching instructions are privileged. 2. For addressing-mode notation questions, apply the standard convention directly (+ after = increment-after-use; - before = decrement-before-use). Confusing which addressing mode increments/decrements BEFORE vs AFTER the memory access.

title: Addressing Modes — concept notes
text: Operand kaise specify hota hai: immediate, direct, indirect, register, indexed, based, relative, auto-increment. Position-independent code aur high-level construct ke saath matching. Effective address (EA) = operand ka address, mode ke rule se banta hai. Relative mode (PC + offset) position-independent code ke liye best hai kyunki code ke saath hi move ho jaata hai. Indexed/base modes arrays aur structs ke liye. Immediate constants ke liye. Indirect pointers ke liye. Immediate: operand instruction me. Direct/absolute: address instruction me. Indirect: address ka address. Register: operand register me. Indexed: EA = base + index register (arrays). Based: base register + displacement (relocation, structs). Relative: EA = PC + offset (position independent, branches). Auto-increment/decrement: stack, array traversal. Relocation without change: relative/base-register modes. EA = A + Xi EA = PC + offset PC ki value (next instruction) use karna bhoolna. Indirect me extra memory access ignore. EA formula likho phir memory se value uthao.

title: Grammar
text: Compiler Design grammar

title: Grammar — concept notes
text: Compiler Design ka Grammar topic CFG ko PARSING lens se dekhta hai. 5 skills: ambiguity detect/prove karna, grammar transform karna (left-recursion removal, ε-production removal), parser-class determine karna (LL/LR/SLR/LALR), grammar se language identify karna, aur structural properties (operator grammar, cycles) check karna. Grammar ambiguous hai agar KISI string ke DO alag parse trees (ya do alag leftmost derivations) hain. Left recursion (A→Aα) predictive/top-down (LL) parsing ke liye PROBLEMATIC hai (infinite loop) — isliye remove karna padta hai. LL(1) = top-down, 1 lookahead se deterministic parse. LR(1)/SLR/LALR = bottom-up, shift-reduce parsing. Ambiguous grammar ko socho ek 'confusing sentence' jaisa — jaise English me 'I saw the man with the telescope' do alag matlab de sakta hai (maine telescope se dekha, YA us aadmi ke paas telescope tha). Grammar me bhi, agar EK hi string ko DO tareeke se build (parse) kar sakte ho, to grammar ambiguous hai — compiler confuse ho jaayega ki kaunsa matlab lena hai. Left recursion ek 'infinite mirror' jaisa hai — agar A apne aapko IMMEDIATELY (bina kuch consume kiye) reference karta hai, top-down parser hamesha usi rule ko try karta rahega, kabhi aage nahi badhega. LL(1) requires: NO left recursion, NO ambiguity, and for each non-terminal, its alternative productions' FIRST sets (and FOLLOW, if nullable) must be disjoint. Every LL(1) grammar is unambiguous, but NOT every unambiguous grammar is LL(1) (LL(1) is a strict subset — some unambiguous grammars still need more lookahead or are inherently non-LL). Ambiguous grammars can NEVER be LR(k) for any k — LR parsing fundamentally requires unambiguous grammars. SLR(1) ⊊ LALR(1) ⊊ LR(1) — every SLR(1) grammar is LALR(1), every LALR(1) is LR(1), but not conversely (LALR/LR are strictly more powerful, can handle more grammars). Left recursion removal: A→Aα|β becomes A→βA', A'→αA'|ε (standard transformation, doesn't change the generated language). A grammar with both left AND right recursion for the same non-terminal — CANNOT determine ambiguity from this fact alone (insufficient information; some such grammars are ambiguous, some aren't). 'Cycles' in a grammar (A⇒+A, deriving itself with no terminals consumed) make it IMPOSSIBLE to be unambiguous in a useful sense — actually cycles specifically break the grammar's usability for deterministic parsing entirely. Chomsky Normal Form (CNF): every production is A→BC or A→a (B,C non-terminals, a terminal). A derivation of a string of length n in CNF takes EXACTLY 2n-1 steps (for n≥1). String of length n (n≥1) in CNF grammar: exactly 2n-1 derivation steps A→Aα|β becomes A→βA', A'→αA'|ε SLR(1) ⊊ LALR(1) ⊊ LR(1); LL(1) ⟹ unambiguous (but not all unambiguous grammars are LL(1)) Ambiguous grammar ⟹ NOT LR(k) for any k Confusing 'grammar is ambiguous' with 'language is inherently ambiguous' — the SAME language might have both an ambiguous AND an unambiguous grammar (disambiguation is often possible); only some languages are INHERENTLY ambiguous (every grammar for them is ambiguous). Assuming left+right recursion together automatically means ambiguous — insufficient information without further analysis. Forgetting operator-grammar restrictions: NO ε-productions, and NO two adjacent non-terminals on any RHS (must have a terminal between any two non-terminals) — both violate operator-grammar rules. Miscounting CNF derivation steps — it's 2n-1, not n or 2n. For ambiguity detection: try to find TWO different leftmost derivations (or parse trees) for the SAME specific string — the classic dangling-else example is the canonical template to recognize. For grammar transformation: apply the standard left-recursion-removal formula mechanically; for ε-production removal, first find all NULLABLE non-terminals, then add alternative productions skipping each nullable occurrence. For parser-class determination: compute FIRST/FOLLOW sets, check LL(1) table for conflicts (multiple entries in one cell = not LL(1)); for LR-family, construct the item sets and check for shift-reduce/reduce-reduce conflicts. For 'what language does this grammar generate': derive a few short strings, look for the pattern, match against given options by testing each option's example strings for derivability.

title: Ambiguity Detection / Proof
text: Poocha hai grammar AMBIGUOUS hai ya nahi, prove karo via parse trees — classic 'dangling-else' style questions is pattern ka signature hain. Find ONE specific string, construct TWO different parse trees (or leftmost derivations) for it — if both succeed differently, ambiguous. The dangling-else problem (if-then-else nesting) is THE canonical ambiguity example — recognize this shape immediately. 1. Pick a specific string likely to expose ambiguity (often nested/repeated structure). 2. Attempt TWO different derivation orders/choices that both successfully derive the SAME string. 3. If both succeed with DIFFERENT tree structures, the grammar is ambiguous — exhibit both trees as the proof. Assuming left+right recursion automatically implies ambiguous — need direct verification. Testing only ONE derivation attempt and concluding 'unambiguous' — must actively SEARCH for a second differing derivation before concluding unambiguous. Comparing an ambiguous grammar to its DISAMBIGUATED version — verify both generate the SAME language despite different ambiguity status. 'Grammar has left AND right recursion' framing — NOT enough info alone to conclude ambiguity, must check directly.

title: Parser-Class Determination (LL(1)/LR(1)/SLR/LALR/conflicts)
text: Poocha hai grammar LL(1) hai ya nahi, ya SLR/LALR/LR(1) classify karna hai, ya parsing table me conflicts (shift-reduce/reduce-reduce) find karne hain — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (47 me se 12 PYQs). LL(1): compute FIRST/FOLLOW, check no cell in predictive table has multiple entries. LR-family: construct LR(0)/LR(1) item sets, check for shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflicts in the resulting automaton. Left recursion / ambiguity immediately DISQUALIFIES LL(1); ambiguity disqualifies ANY LR(k). 1. Check for obvious disqualifiers first: left recursion (kills LL(1)), ambiguity (kills BOTH LL(1) and all LR(k)). 2. For LL(1): compute FIRST sets of each production's RHS, FOLLOW sets of relevant non-terminals, check overlap in the predictive table. 3. For LR-family: build the canonical LR(0)/LR(1) item collection (via closure and goto operations), check each state for conflicts. 4. Remember the hierarchy: SLR(1)⊊LALR(1)⊊LR(1) — a grammar failing SLR(1) might still pass LALR(1) or LR(1). Applying SLR's simpler FOLLOW-based conflict resolution when the question actually requires full LR(1) lookahead-based analysis (these can give different conflict verdicts). Partially-filled parsing table given, asked to complete specific cells — apply the table-construction rules to just the missing entries. 'Number of items in a specific item-set I_k' — construct that specific set via closure/goto from the augmented grammar.

title: Grammar Transformation (remove left recursion, ε-productions, CNF conversion)
text: Poocha hai grammar se LEFT RECURSION hatao, ya ε-PRODUCTIONS remove karo, ya CNF me convert karo — ye mechanical transformation pattern hai. Left recursion removal: A→Aα|β becomes A→βA', A'→αA'|ε (standard formula). ε-production removal: find all NULLABLE non-terminals first, then for every production containing a nullable non-terminal, add a version WITHOUT it. 1. For left recursion: identify A→Aα|β pattern, apply the standard rewrite formula directly. 2. For ε-removal: first find ALL nullable non-terminals (those that can derive ε, directly or transitively), then systematically add alternative productions omitting each nullable symbol. 3. For CNF: eliminate ε-productions and unit productions first, then break down long RHS strings into binary (A→BC) chains, and isolate terminals in mixed productions. Missing INDIRECT left recursion (A→Bα, B→Aβ — recursion through another non-terminal, not immediately visible) — must resolve this to direct form first before applying the standard removal formula. 'Minimum number of production rules' after transformation — verify the transformed grammar isn't just correct but also MINIMAL (no redundant rules).

title: Identify the Language Generated by a Grammar
text: Ek grammar di hai aur poocha hai L(G) kya hai, ya ek specific string generate hoti hai ya nahi, ya derivation length kya hogi — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (47 me se 12 PYQs), CFL topic ke Grammar-Language-Identification pattern ka direct overlap. Derive a few short strings by hand from S, look for the emerging pattern. For 'how many derivation trees for string X' — count DISTINCT valid derivation sequences, watch for ambiguity implications. 1. Start deriving from S, generate 2-3 short strings. 2. Identify the pattern (matched counts? specific structure?). 3. For derivation-length/count questions, systematically enumerate the specific derivation(s) for the target string. Not checking enough short strings before generalizing the pattern — verify against at least one non-trivial case. Programming-language-style declarations (array dimensions like int a[10][3]) — translate the real-world syntax requirement into grammar rules and verify against given options. CNF-specific derivation-step counting (2n-1 formula application).

title: Grammar Structural Properties (operator grammar, cycles, CFG expressiveness limits, SDT value computation)
text: Poocha hai grammar OPERATOR GRAMMAR rules violate karta hai ya nahi, ya grammar me CYCLES hain ya nahi, ya CFG kis cheez ko express NAHI kar sakta, ya translation-scheme se VALUE compute karni hai — ye broader structural/semantic pattern hai. Operator grammar rule: NO ε-productions, and NO two adjacent non-terminals (must have a terminal between any two consecutive non-terminals on RHS). CFG CANNOT express context-sensitive requirements like 'declare before use' (needs tracking across arbitrary distance, beyond single-stack power) — a classic 'what CFG can't do' fact. For SDT value computation: evaluate semantic actions bottom-up (or per the scheme's attribute-flow direction) as the parse proceeds. 1. For operator-grammar checks: scan each production for ε-RHS or adjacent-non-terminal patterns. 2. For 'what can't CFG express' questions: recall that CFG can't enforce SEMANTIC/context-sensitive constraints (variable declared before use, type matching) — only pure syntactic nesting. 3. For SDT/translation-scheme value questions: trace the parse and apply semantic actions in the specified order (usually bottom-up for LR-style, matching each rule's semantic action to its point in the derivation). Forgetting BOTH operator-grammar restrictions (no ε AND no adjacent non-terminals) — missing one of the two conditions. Non-associative operator grammar allowing/disallowing redundant parentheses — check if the grammar's structure permits extra bracketing around already-grouped expressions.

title: LR Parser — concept notes
text: LR Parser topic 3 skills me deep-dive karta hai: SLR/LALR/LR(1) power aur state-count COMPARISON theory, actual ITEM-SET construction aur conflict detection, aur bottom-up parsing TRACE (reduction steps, derivation order). LR parsing = bottom-up, builds RIGHTMOST derivation in REVERSE. Har step: SHIFT (input symbol stack pe push karo) ya REDUCE (stack ke top ko ek production ke RHS se match karke LHS se replace karo). Power hierarchy: SLR(1) ⊊ LALR(1) ⊊ LR(1) (canonical) — LR(1) SABSE powerful hai (sabse zyada grammars handle kar sakta hai), SLR sabse SIMPLE hai implement karna (lekin sabse kam grammars handle karta hai). LR parser ko ek 'bottom-up puzzle solver' socho — ye INPUT string ke pieces ko dekh dekh kar, jab bhi koi piece kisi grammar rule ke RHS se match kare, use LHS se REPLACE karta hai (reduce), aur jab match nahi milta, agla input symbol le leta hai (shift). LR(1) sabse powerful isliye hai kyunki har 'state' me ye PRECISE lookahead symbol yaad rakhta hai (per-item lookahead) — LALR SAME states (LR(0) jaisी) use karta hai but lookaheads MERGE kar deta hai (jo kabhi-kabhi naya conflict create kar sakta hai jo LR(1) me nahi tha). Power/generality hierarchy: SLR(1) ⊊ LALR(1) ⊊ Canonical LR(1) — every grammar parseable by SLR is also parseable by LALR and LR(1), but not conversely. State-count hierarchy: LALR(1) has the SAME number of states as LR(0)/SLR(1) (LALR MERGES LR(1) states with identical cores) — LALR states ≤ Canonical LR(1) states, often MUCH fewer, while SLR and LALR states are typically EQUAL in number (built on the same LR(0) automaton). LALR is constructed by taking the canonical LR(1) collection and MERGING states with the same 'core' (same LR(0) items, ignoring lookaheads) — this merging can occasionally INTRODUCE a new reduce-reduce conflict that wasn't present in the canonical LR(1) parser (merging is the source of LALR's slight power loss vs LR(1)). LALR(1) has a shift-reduce conflict IFF the canonical LR(1) parser ALSO has a shift-reduce conflict — merging states never introduces NEW shift-reduce conflicts (only possibly new reduce-reduce conflicts). LR parsers construct the RIGHTMOST derivation in REVERSE (i.e., trace a rightmost derivation backward) — this is a frequently tested direct-recall fact (contrast with LL parsers, which do leftmost derivation forward). Maximum reduce moves for a bottom-up parser on a string with n tokens (grammar has no ε or unit productions): exactly n-1 reduces reduce the entire string down to the start symbol IF every production is binary-branching in the worst structural sense — more precisely, for a grammar with no unit/ε productions, the number of reduces is bounded by n-1 (at most one reduce 'absorbs' one token's worth of tree structure in the sparsest case). SLR(1) ⊊ LALR(1) ⊊ Canonical LR(1) LALR(1) states = LR(0)/SLR(1) states (via merging) ≤ Canonical LR(1) states LALR(1) has shift-reduce conflict ⟺ Canonical LR(1) has shift-reduce conflict (merging never CREATES new S-R conflicts, only possibly new R-R conflicts) For grammar with no ε/unit productions, parsing a string of n tokens: at most n-1 reduce moves Getting the power-hierarchy direction backward (claiming SLR is more powerful than LALR, or LALR more powerful than canonical LR) — memorize the CORRECT direction: LR(1) is the most powerful. Assuming LALR merging can introduce shift-reduce conflicts — it specifically only risks NEW reduce-reduce conflicts. Confusing LR parsers' RIGHTMOST-derivation-in-reverse with LL parsers' LEFTMOST-derivation-forward. Miscounting item-set sizes — closure() must be applied exhaustively (add items for EVERY non-terminal immediately after a dot, recursively) before the set is complete. For item-set construction: start with the augmented grammar's initial item [S'→·S, $], apply closure() (add items for the non-terminal right after each dot), then goto() on each grammar symbol to find successor states — repeat until the canonical collection stabilizes. For conflict detection: within each state, check if a SHIFT action and REDUCE action are both valid on the same lookahead symbol (shift-reduce conflict), or if TWO different reduce actions are both valid on the same lookahead (reduce-reduce conflict). For power/hierarchy questions: recall the fixed ordering SLR(1)⊊LALR(1)⊊LR(1) directly rather than re-deriving. For bottom-up parsing trace questions: simulate shift/reduce explicitly using a stack, one input symbol at a time, counting whatever's asked (reduce steps, final derivation).

title: SLR/LALR/LR(1) Power & State-Count Comparison Theory
text: Poocha hai SLR/LALR/Canonical-LR ke beech POWER comparison (kaunsa zyada grammars handle karta hai), ya state-count relationship, ya conflict-equivalence claims — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (20 me se 9 PYQs). Power: SLR(1) ⊊ LALR(1) ⊊ LR(1) — canonical LR(1) is MOST powerful, SLR is LEAST (but simplest to implement). State count: LALR = same as SLR/LR(0) (via merging) ≤ Canonical LR(1) (often far fewer). LALR S-R conflict ⟺ Canonical LR(1) S-R conflict (merging only risks NEW R-R conflicts, never new S-R). 1. Identify exactly what's being compared: power (which grammars are parseable) or state count or conflict existence. 2. Apply the FIXED hierarchy directly: LR(1) most powerful, SLR least (but same/fewer states than LR(1)). 3. For conflict-equivalence claims, remember the S-R vs R-R asymmetry (S-R conflicts transfer exactly; R-R conflicts can be NEW in LALR). Reversing the power-hierarchy direction (a very common wrong-answer trap in MCQ options designed to catch this). 'Every LR(1) grammar is unambiguous but not every unambiguous grammar is LR(1)' style nested TRUE/FALSE claims — verify each sub-claim independently against the hierarchy facts.

title: LR Item-Set Construction & Conflict Detection
text: Ek augmented grammar di hai aur poocha hai specific item-set (jaise I_k) me kitne items hain, ya us set me shift-reduce/reduce-reduce conflict hai ya nahi — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (20 me se 8 PYQs), aur 2019 ke baad almost har saal NAT-type me poocha ja raha hai. Apply closure() exhaustively: for every item with a dot before a non-terminal, add items for ALL of that non-terminal's productions (with dot at start). Apply goto() by advancing the dot past a specific symbol across all items in a state, then closure() the result. Check for conflicts: shift-reduce (both a shift action AND reduce action valid on same lookahead), reduce-reduce (two different reduces both valid on same lookahead). 1. Start from the augmented grammar's initial item. 2. Apply closure() completely (don't stop early — every newly added non-terminal-starting item may itself need further closure). 3. Apply goto() on the relevant symbol to reach the target state (repeat closure() on the result). 4. Count items or check for conflicts as asked. Stopping closure() too early (missing a transitively-required item) — always iterate until no more items can be added. Confusing which two items belong in the SAME set (they must be reachable via the same goto() path from the start). Comparing TWO item sets for MERGE-ABILITY (do they have the same LR(0) core, differing only in lookaheads?) — check core equality first, then reason about merge-induced conflicts. Directly counting total shift-reduce conflicts across an entire canonical collection (sum across all states).

title: Bottom-Up Parser Derivation Trace
text: Ek specific string di hai aur poocha hai bottom-up parser (LR) kitne REDUCE steps lega ise parse karne me, ya LR parser kis derivation TYPE use karta hai — direct tracing/recall pattern. LR parsers build the RIGHTMOST derivation in REVERSE — memorize this direction directly. For counting reduce moves: simulate the shift-reduce process explicitly on the given string with the given grammar. 1. For derivation-type questions: directly recall 'rightmost derivation in reverse'. 2. For reduce-count questions: simulate the parse (shift symbols onto a stack, reduce whenever the top matches a production RHS) explicitly, counting each reduce action. Confusing LR's rightmost-derivation-in-reverse with LL's leftmost-derivation-forward when asked directly.

title: Syntax Directed Translation

title: Syntax Directed Translation — concept notes
text: SDT grammar productions ke saath 'semantic actions'/attributes attach karta hai — parsing ke saath-saath COMPUTATION bhi hoti hai (jaise expression VALUE, ya type-checking, ya code generation). 3 skills: given SDT se attribute VALUE compute karna, S-attributed/L-attributed classify karna, aur naya SDT design karna. SYNTHESIZED attribute: value bottom-up flow karta hai (child se parent, jaise E.val computed from E1.val + E2.val) — LR (bottom-up) parsing ke saath naturally fit hota hai. INHERITED attribute: value TOP-DOWN ya SIDEWAYS flow karta hai (parent se child, ya left-sibling se right-sibling, jaise type declaration propagate karna). S-ATTRIBUTED SDT = sirf synthesized attributes (evaluate at REDUCE time in bottom-up parsing, easy). L-ATTRIBUTED SDT = synthesized + RESTRICTED inherited (sirf LEFT-to-right dependency allowed, no right-to-left) — thoda zyada flexible but still evaluable in a single left-to-right pass. Synthesized attribute ko socho 'bachon se maa-baap tak information collect karna' — jaise 2 numbers add karke result upar bhejna. Inherited attribute 'maa-baap se bachon tak information pass karna' hai — jaise 'tum INT type ho' batana niche ke sab identifiers ko. S-attributed sirf PEHLI tarah ka flow allow karta hai (simple, bottom-up-friendly). L-attributed dono allow karta hai, but inherited attribute SIRF LEFT se aa sakta hai (apne se pehle wale sibling ya parent se), right se NAHI — isliye ek hi LEFT-TO-RIGHT pass me evaluate ho sakta hai. S-attributed SDDs are a STRICT SUBSET of L-attributed SDDs (every S-attributed is also L-attributed, since having ONLY synthesized attributes trivially satisfies the 'no right-dependency' restriction). In BOTTOM-UP (LR) parsing, inherited attributes can be evaluated ONLY IF the SDD is L-attributed (bottom-up evaluation naturally computes things left-to-right, matching L-attributed's restriction) — NOT for arbitrary inherited attributes with right-dependencies. S-attributed SDDs can ALWAYS be evaluated during bottom-up (LR) parsing, attaching the semantic action right after each REDUCE step — this is the simplest, most common case. For arbitrary (non-L-attributed) inherited attributes needing right-to-left information flow, a bottom-up parser CANNOT evaluate them in one pass — would need multiple passes or a different evaluation strategy (like building the full parse tree first, then evaluating). Annotated parse tree: draw the parse tree, compute each node's attributes bottom-up (synthesized) or top-down (inherited) following the dependency graph, respecting evaluation order constraints. S-attributed ⊊ L-attributed (every S-attributed SDD is also L-attributed) Inherited attributes evaluable during bottom-up parsing IFF the SDD is L-attributed S-attributed SDDs are ALWAYS evaluable during bottom-up (LR) parsing, at reduce time Assuming ALL inherited attributes can be evaluated during bottom-up parsing — only L-attributed ones (restricted, left-to-right-only dependency) can be. Confusing 'synthesized' (child→parent) with 'inherited' (parent/left-sibling→current) attribute flow direction. Missing the exact TIMING of semantic actions (some attached mid-production via embedded actions, not just at the very end) — track precisely when each action fires during the parse. Computing attributes in the wrong order — always respect the actual DEPENDENCY graph (which attribute needs which other attribute's value first), not just a fixed bottom-up-then-top-down assumption. For value-computation questions: build the parse tree for the given input first, then evaluate attributes following the dependency order given by the semantic rules (usually bottom-up for synthesized, but check for any inherited attributes that need to flow down/across first). For S-attributed/L-attributed classification: check EVERY inherited attribute's dependency — does it EVER depend on something to its RIGHT (later sibling, or the parent's attribute that itself depends on something right)? If yes, NOT L-attributed. If all attributes are synthesized, it's S-attributed (hence also L-attributed). For SDT-design questions: identify what information needs to flow UP (results/values — synthesized) vs DOWN/ACROSS (context like type/scope — inherited), design attributes and rules accordingly.

title: Compute Attribute Value / Output via Given SDT
text: Ek SDT/translation scheme di hai aur poocha hai specific input ke liye final attribute VALUE (ya printed output sequence) kya hoga — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (19 me se 10 PYQs). Build the parse tree for the given input first. Evaluate attributes following the dependency order (synthesized bottom-up typically, unless inherited attributes are involved needing top-down/left-to-right flow). For bottom-up (LR) parsing with embedded actions: actions fire exactly at the corresponding REDUCE step, in the order reduces happen. 1. Parse the given input string with the grammar, building the parse tree (or simulating the shift-reduce sequence if bottom-up). 2. Evaluate each node's attribute(s) following the semantic rules, respecting dependency order (a rule needs its RHS attributes computed first). 3. Report the requested final value (usually the start symbol's synthesized attribute, or the sequence of printed actions in order). Evaluating attributes in an arbitrary order instead of the actual DEPENDENCY-respecting order — always check what each rule needs before computing it. Missing embedded semantic actions that fire MID-production, not just at the end. Print-action-sequence questions (postfix/prefix-style output) — track the ORDER actions fire relative to shift/reduce steps, not just the final numeric value. Multiple SDT variants (SDD1 vs SDD2) for the SAME grammar, compared for correctness/output difference.

title: S-Attributed vs L-Attributed Classification
text: Poocha hai ek SDD S-ATTRIBUTED hai ya L-ATTRIBUTED (ya neither), ya bottom-up parsing me inherited attributes evaluate ho sakte hain ya nahi — ye classification pattern hai. S-attributed = ONLY synthesized attributes. L-attributed = synthesized + inherited attributes that depend ONLY on the LEFT (earlier siblings or the parent) — never on something to the right. Bottom-up (LR) parsing can evaluate inherited attributes ONLY if the SDD is L-attributed. 1. Check if ANY attribute is inherited — if none, it's S-attributed (and automatically also L-attributed). 2. For each inherited attribute, trace its dependency: does it EVER need a value from something to its RIGHT (a later sibling, or a parent attribute that itself needs a later value)? If yes, NOT L-attributed. 3. Determine bottom-up-evaluability directly from the L-attributed classification result. Assuming ANY inherited attribute automatically disqualifies L-attributed status — only RIGHT-dependent inherited attributes do; LEFT-dependent inherited attributes are fine for L-attributed. Multiple rules given for comparison, asked to classify EACH one independently as S-attributed/L-attributed/neither.

title: Design/Write SDT Rules for a Given Task
text: Poocha hai ek specific task (symbol table me type add karna, type-checking, code generation) ke liye semantic rules likho — design pattern hai. Identify what needs to flow UP (results — synthesized) vs DOWN/ACROSS (context like declared type — inherited). For symbol-table/type-declaration tasks: type info usually flows DOWN from a type-keyword node to each identifier (inherited attribute). 1. Identify the grammar's structure and what information each part of the task needs. 2. Design attributes: synthesized for bottom-up-computed results (expression values, generated code fragments), inherited for top-down/across context (type declarations, scope info). 3. Write semantic rules attached to each relevant production, ensuring the dependency order is well-defined (no circular dependencies). Not permitted to REWRITE the grammar (a common constraint) — must design semantic rules that work with the EXISTING production structure, not a modified one. Repeat-until loop code-generation SDT (attaching 'code' attributes representing generated instruction sequences) — think of 'code' as a synthesized string-concatenation attribute built up from sub-statements.

title: First and Follow — concept notes
text: Grammar ke FIRST/FOLLOW sets nikalna; LL(1) table ke liye. FIRST(A) = A se shuru hone wale strings ke pehle terminals; FOLLOW(A) = A ke turant baad aane wale terminals. title: Subnetting — concept notes
text: IP address = network part + host part. Subnet mask/CIDR prefix batata hai kitne bits network ke hain. GATE me 4 kaam: same network check, hosts/subnets count, CIDR block allocation/aggregation, aur routing table me longest prefix match. Network address = IP AND mask. Do addresses same network me hain agar dono ka (IP AND mask) barabar ho. Forwarding me longest matching prefix jeetta hai. Mask me jitne 1 bits hain wo network hain, baaki 0 bits host hain. Host bits h ho to total addresses 2^h, usable hosts 2^h - 2 (all-0 = network address, all-1 = broadcast). Subnet banane par host bits me se kuch bits network me chale jaate hain. Network id = IP AND mask; broadcast = network id OR (NOT mask). Usable hosts = 2^h - 2 (network + broadcast address chhodkar). Subnets = 2^s jahan s = borrowed bits (GATE me kabhi all-0/all-1 subnet bhi allowed maani jaati hai; question ke hisaab se). Class A /8, Class B /16, Class C /24. CIDR block ka size power of 2 hona chahiye aur start address block-size ke multiple par align hona chahiye. Longest prefix match: routing table me sabse bada matching prefix wali entry chuni jaati hai; default route 0.0.0.0/0. Aggregation: kai prefix ko ek chhote prefix (bada block) me jod sakte ho jab wo contiguous aur aligned hon. Variable-length subnets: bade requirement wale ko pehle allocate karo. Same subnet ke hosts ko router ki zaroorat nahi; alag subnet me default gateway chahiye. Mask 255.255.255.192 = /26, .224 = /27, .240 = /28, .248 = /29. IP AND mask networkId OR (NOT mask) 2^(32-n) - 2 2^(borrowed bits) 256 - (last non-255 mask octet) -2 lagana bhool jaana (ya galat jagah lagana). Longest prefix ki jagah pehli matching entry le lena. Binary conversion me galti. Broadcast ko host address maan lena. Interesting octet lo: block size = 256 - mask octet; address kis block me hai nikaalo. Routing: har prefix ke saath destination AND karo, matching ko compare karo, longest prefix chuno. Variable subnet allocation: size ko next power of 2 par round up karo.

title: TCP — concept notes
text: TCP reliable, connection-oriented, byte-stream transport protocol hai. GATE me: 3-way handshake (seq/ack numbers), connection termination (FIN), sequence-number wraparound/window scale calculations, timeout/RTT, aur conceptual statements. TCP har BYTE ko sequence number deta hai. Connection 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK) se khulta hai; ACK number = next expected byte. Client SYN(seq=x) bhejta hai, server SYN+ACK(seq=y, ack=x+1) deta hai, client ACK(ack=y+1) bhejta hai. SYN aur FIN ek sequence number consume karte hain. Data me ACK = last received byte + 1. Sequence number ka wrap-around tab tak safe hona chahiye jab tak purana segment network me jinda ho (MSL). TCP full duplex, byte-stream, in-order, reliable; guaranteed minimum rate NAHI deta. Sequence number bytes ko assign hota hai, segments ko nahi. 3-way handshake: SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK; SYN ek seq number khaata hai. Termination: FIN se (4-way); FIN bhi ek seq number khaata hai; half-close possible. TCP selective acknowledgement (SACK) option support karta hai. Server crash ke baad naya connection se aane wale segments par RST milta hai. Wraparound: 2^n sequence numbers >= rate x (MSL etc.) se n nikalo. Window scale ki zaroorat: bandwidth x RTT (BDP) > 2^16 bytes. Timeout RTT ke estimate se adapt hota hai (fixed nahi). Initial sequence number ToD clock se: same seq reuse rokne ke liye. SYN(x) -> SYN+ACK(y, ack=x+1) -> ACK(ack=y+1) BDP = bandwidth x RTT 2^n / rate >= MSL ack = next expected byte = last received + 1 ACK number me +1 bhoolna. Segment count ko seq number ki jagah lena. Bits/bytes/sec unit galat. TCP ko message-oriented samajhna. Handshake diagram banao, har packet ka seq/ack likho. Wraparound: time = 2^n bytes / (rate in bytes/sec) > MSL. BDP nikaalke window scale ki need check karo.

title: Database Normalization — concept notes
text: Normalization me 5 skills: FD inference/attribute closure, candidate key/superkey nikaalna, highest normal form determine karna, decomposition (lossless + dependency preserving) check karna, aur conceptual statements. Functional Dependency X -> Y ka matlab: agar do tuples ki X value same hai to Y value bhi same hogi. Attribute closure X+ = un sabhi attributes ka set jo X se determine hote hain. Candidate key = minimal set jiska closure poori relation ho. Normal forms redundancy hatane ke liye hain: 1NF (atomic), 2NF (no partial dependency), 3NF, BCNF. FD ko 'roll number se naam pata chal jaata hai' jaise socho. Closure ka trick: ek set se shuru karo, jab tak koi FD lag sake (LHS closure ke andar ho) uska RHS jodte jao. Jab kuch naya na jude, ruk jao. Isi closure se key, superkey, aur FD implied hai ya nahi — sab nikal jaata hai. Armstrong axioms: Reflexivity (Y subset of X => X->Y), Augmentation (X->Y => XZ->YZ), Transitivity (X->Y, Y->Z => X->Z). Derived: Union, Decomposition, Pseudo-transitivity. 2NF: koi non-prime attribute kisi candidate key ke PROPER subset par depend na kare (no partial dependency). 3NF: har non-trivial X->A me ya X superkey ho ya A prime attribute ho. BCNF: har non-trivial X->A me X superkey ho. BCNF is stricter than 3NF: BCNF => 3NF => 2NF => 1NF. Do attributes wali koi bhi relation hamesha BCNF me hoti hai. Agar relation ke saare attributes prime hain to relation 3NF me hoti hai (par BCNF me nahi bhi ho sakti). Agar har candidate key single attribute hai to relation 2NF me hoti hai (partial dependency possible hi nahi). Lossless + dependency-preserving decomposition 3NF me hamesha possible hai; BCNF me hamesha possible NAHI hai. Binary decomposition R -> R1, R2 lossless hai iff R1 intersect R2 -> R1 ya R1 intersect R2 -> R2 (common attributes kisi ek relation ki key hon). Dependency preserving: F ke saare FDs decomposed relations ke FDs (projection) se derive ho jaayein. Number of superkeys: agar candidate key ke bahar m attributes hain to superkeys 2^m (single key case). X+ : repeat { for each FD A->B in F: if A subset of X+ then X+ = X+ union B } until no change X superkey iff X+ = all attributes of R R1 intersect R2 -> R1 or R1 intersect R2 -> R2 If K is the only candidate key with |K|=k and R has n attributes: 2^(n-k) superkeys BCNF => 3NF => 2NF => 1NF Sirf ek candidate key nikaal ke ruk jaana; kai keys ho sakti hain. 3NF aur BCNF ko same maan lena. Decomposition me sirf lossless check karna aur dependency preservation bhool jaana. FD ko instance se 'prove' karna: instance sirf FD ko violate kar sakta hai, sabit nahi kar sakta. Closure me FD apply karte waqt LHS ka poora subset closure me hona check na karna. Key nikaalne ke liye: jo attributes kisi FD ke RHS me kabhi nahi aate wo key me zaroor honge; unse closure nikaalo. Normal form: pehle saari candidate keys, phir har FD ko BCNF -> 3NF -> 2NF ke order me test karo. Lossless: chase table ya binary common-attribute test. Minimal cover: RHS single karo, extra LHS attributes hatao, redundant FDs hatao.

title: Determine Highest Normal Form
text: Relation aur FDs diye hain; poocha hai relation kis normal form me hai ya kaunsi form me nahi hai (55 me se 11). Pehle candidate keys, phir har FD ko BCNF, 3NF, 2NF ke liye check. Prime/non-prime pehchano. 1. Candidate keys nikaalo (closure se). 2. Prime aur non-prime attributes list karo. 3. Har FD X->A: X superkey hai? to BCNF ok. Nahi to A prime? to 3NF ok. 4. Partial dependency (key ke proper subset -> non-prime) ho to 2NF fail. 5. Sabse upar wali form jo sabhi FDs satisfy kare wahi answer. Sirf ek key se test karna. BCNF violation ko 3NF violation samajhna. Multiple schemas diye hain, har ek ki form alag alag. Decomposed relations ki normal form (projection ke FDs se).

title: Candidate Keys / Superkeys / Counting
text: Kaunsi key hai, kaunsa superkey nahi hai, ya superkeys/keys ki count poochhi hai. Closure = all attributes => superkey. Minimal superkey = candidate key. 1. Jo attributes kisi RHS me nahi aate unhe pakdo. 2. Closure nikaalo; poora R mile to superkey. 3. Minimality check: koi attribute hata ke bhi closure poora rahe to key nahi. 4. Count: single key K ho to 2^(n-|K|) superkeys; multiple keys me inclusion-exclusion. Superkey ke liye minimality ki zaroorat nahi — candidate key ke liye hai. Real-world schema (empcode, pincode, street) se FDs khud likhna aur normal form/keys nikaalna. Kitni candidate keys hain.

title: Attribute Closure, FD Inference, Armstrong, Minimal Cover
text: Poocha hai kaunsi FD implied hai / kaunsi implied nahi hai, ya Armstrong axioms se rule derive karo, ya minimal (irreducible) cover. FD implied hai iff X+ me Y aaye. Minimal cover me single-attribute RHS, no extra LHS attribute, no redundant FD. 1. Given FD ke LHS ka closure nikaalo (dusre FDs ke saath). 2. RHS closure me hai to implied. 3. Minimal cover: RHS split, extraneous LHS hatao, redundant FD hatao. Instance se FD sabit kar dena. Trivial FD ki definition (RHS subset of LHS) bhoolna. Relation instance diya hai, kaunsi FD satisfy hoti hai — har FD ke liye tuples ki pair check karo. 'Useful FD' jaisi custom definition (non-empty, non-trivial, etc.).

title: Decomposition: Lossless Join & Dependency Preservation
text: Relation ko R1,R2 me todha gaya hai; poocha hai lossless hai, dependency-preserving hai, ya dono. Lossless: common attributes kisi ek part ki key hon. Dependency preserving: har FD kisi ek relation me ya derivable ho. 1. R1 intersect R2 nikaalo, uska closure dekho: R1 ya R2 ko determine kare to lossless. 2. Har FD check karo ki kisi decomposed relation me poori aati hai ya closure se recover hoti hai. 3. BCNF/3NF decomposition me pehle violating FD dhundo. Lossless ko dependency-preserving samajhna (alag properties). Decomposition ke baad redundancy compare karna. 'Kaunsi decomposition hamesha lossless dependency-preserving nahi ho sakti'.

title: Conceptual Normal-Form Statements
text: True/false: kaunsa normal form kis se strict hai, 2 attributes wali relation, all-prime attributes, 1NF properties. Do attributes => BCNF. All prime => 3NF. Single-attribute keys => 2NF. 1. Har statement ko chhote counterexample ya definition se test karo. Ulta implication (3NF => BCNF) likhna. BCNF me lossless+dependency-preserving decomposition ki guarantee nahi (3NF me hai).

title: SQL

title: SQL — concept notes
text: SQL me 4 skills: diye gaye query ka OUTPUT/tuple count nikaalna (sabse bada), query ki SEMANTICS samajhna (kya compute karta hai / equivalent kaunsi), queries LIKHNA, aur NULL/constraints/clauses ki conceptual baatein. SQL evaluation order (logical): FROM (joins) -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY. Isi order me instance par query chalao to output milta hai. Query ko ek pipeline socho: pehle tables jodo (FROM/JOIN), phir rows filter karo (WHERE), phir groups banao (GROUP BY), phir groups filter karo (HAVING), tab jaake columns chuno (SELECT). Aggregate (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX) hamesha groups par lagte hain. NULL ka matlab 'pata nahi' hai, isliye NULL ke saath comparison ka result unknown hota hai, true/false nahi. SQL duplicates ko automatically nahi hatata; sirf SELECT DISTINCT hatata hai. HAVING group-level condition ke liye hai; WHERE group banne se pehle rows filter karta hai. HAVING bina GROUP BY ke pura table ek group maanta hai. COUNT(*) NULL rows bhi ginta hai; COUNT(col), SUM, AVG NULL values ko ignore karte hain. NULL comparison (=, <, >) ka result UNKNOWN; WHERE sirf TRUE rows rakhta hai. NULL ke liye IS NULL use hota hai. x NOT IN (subquery) me subquery me ek bhi NULL ho to result kabhi TRUE nahi hota (koi row nahi milti). A.x > ALL (subquery): subquery khali ho to TRUE; > ANY/SOME: khali ho to FALSE. Cross product (FROM r, s bina condition) tuples = |r| x |s|. Natural join common columns par equality lagata hai. Outer joins me unmatched rows NULL ke saath aati hain (LEFT/RIGHT/FULL). Correlated subquery: inner query outer row ke har row par dobara evaluate hoti hai. Second-highest jaisi queries: MAX ke against subquery, ya x > ALL / NOT IN pattern. FROM/JOIN -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY |r x s| = |r| x |s| Any comparison with NULL = UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE x > ALL(empty) = TRUE; x > ANY(empty) = FALSE COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col)/SUM/AVG skip NULLs NOT IN me NULL ka asar bhoolna. AVG/SUM me NULL rows ko count karna. Join multiplicity (duplicate rows) ignore karna. WHERE me aggregate function likhna (allowed nahi, HAVING chahiye). GROUP BY me select kiya gaya non-aggregated column group-by list me hona chahiye. Instance par chhote steps me chalao: join table likho, filter lagao, group banao, aggregate nikaalo. Subquery ko pehle akele evaluate karo (uncorrelated) ya har outer row ke liye (correlated). Equivalent queries me duplicates/NULL ka counter-example khojo.

title: Query Output / Tuple Count on a Given Instance
text: Tables ka instance aur ek SQL query di hai; output values ya number of tuples poochhe hain (55 me se 21). Logical evaluation order follow karo. NULL, duplicates, join multiplicity par nazar rakho. 1. FROM/JOIN se rows ki table banao. 2. WHERE se filter. 3. GROUP BY/HAVING lagao. 4. SELECT aggregate compute karo. 5. DISTINCT/ORDER BY aakhir me. NULL rows ko count/avg me galat treat karna. Join se duplicates bane, uska aggregate par asar bhoolna. WITH (CTE) ke saath multi-step queries. NATURAL JOIN + subquery (derived table) ka count. Range of tuples: maximum/minimum possible output size given constraints.

title: What Does the Query Compute / Which Query is Equivalent
text: Query di hai aur poocha hai wo kya list karti hai (second highest, rank, students who...), ya kaunsi query same answer degi. Query ko English me translate karo. Correlated subquery / NOT IN / ALL ke patterns pehchano. 1. Subquery akele padho. 2. Outer condition ka matlab likho. 3. Chhoti sample table par test karo. Queries ko 'similar' dikhne par equivalent maan lena (duplicates/NULL me farak). Rank customers by balance (count of higher balances). Division-style 'all courses / all parts' queries via NOT EXISTS / NOT IN. Inner vs outer join equivalence.

title: Write SQL / Relational Algebra Query
text: Schema diya hai; SQL ya algebra me query likhni hai (descriptive, mostly pre-2003). Requirement ko FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING me todo. 1. Kaunsi tables chahiye. 2. Join conditions. 3. Filter/aggregate/grouping. 4. Division ho to NOT EXISTS. Join condition bhool jaana (accidental cross product). View define karna (bank transactions ka balance).

title: SQL Concepts (NULL, clauses, constraints, foreign keys)
text: True/false: duplicates, HAVING bina GROUP BY, NULL comparison, foreign key vs check, indexes ki zaroorat, disk-based query cost. Yeh facts direct yaad hone chahiye: SQL duplicates rakhta hai, HAVING bina GROUP BY chalti hai, NULL comparisons unknown. 1. Har statement ko definition ya chhote example se test karo. Aisa maan lena ki SQL result set hota hai (multiset hota hai). Foreign key ko check assertion se replace karna possible hai ya nahi.

title: Relational Algebra
