title: Relations — concept notes
text: Relations is is subject ka sabse zyada-poocha-gaya topic hai (38 PYQs). Core skill ek hi hai baar baar: ek relation di gayi hai, uske properties (reflexive/symmetric/antisymmetric/transitive) check karo. Ye skill itni baar repeat hoti hai ki isko cold master karna non-negotiable hai. Relation R on set A = subset of A×A, i.e. collection of ordered pairs (a,b) where a,b ∈ A. Har pair 'a is related to b' represent karta hai. GATE 4 properties baar-baar check karwata hai: Reflexive, Symmetric, Antisymmetric, Transitive — aur inka combination special naam paata hai (Equivalence Relation, Partial Order). Relation ko ek 'kaun kis se juda hai' graph socho (directed graph, jisme har pair (a,b) ek arrow a→b hai). Reflexive = har node ka khud pe self-loop hai. Symmetric = agar a→b hai to b→a bhi hai (arrows hamesha do-tarfa). Antisymmetric = agar a→b aur b→a dono hain to a=b hi hoga (do-tarfa arrow sirf khud pe). Transitive = agar a→b aur b→c hai to a→c bhi hona chahiye (shortcut arrow already present). Equivalence Relation = Reflexive + Symmetric + Transitive. Partial Order = Reflexive + Antisymmetric + Transitive. Total number of binary relations on an n-element set = 2^(n²) (since A×A has n² pairs, each independently in/out of R). Number of REFLEXIVE relations on an n-element set = 2^(n²−n) (the n diagonal pairs are forced 'in', the rest free). Largest equivalence relation on A = A×A itself (one giant equivalence class); smallest = the identity relation {(a,a) : a∈A} (n classes of size 1). An equivalence relation partitions A into disjoint equivalence classes — this is the deep reason equivalence relations matter. Symmetric ∩ Antisymmetric relations can only contain pairs (a,a) — i.e., subsets of the identity relation. 2^(n²) 2^(n²−n) 2^(n(n+1)/2) n² (i.e., A×A) n (the identity relation) O(n³) via Warshall's algorithm (or matrix multiplication approach) Assuming 'symmetric and transitive' implies 'reflexive' — false in general (the classic 'proof' that seems to show this has a hidden flaw: it needs SOME pair (x,y) to exist for element x, which may not hold for every x — see the proof-reasoning pattern below). Confusing symmetric with antisymmetric — they are NOT opposites; a relation can be neither, or (rarely) both. Forgetting the identity/diagonal pairs when counting reflexive relations. Assuming union of equivalence relations is automatically an equivalence relation. For property-checking: test with 2-3 concrete elements first, don't just stare at the formula abstractly. For counting questions: always start from 'total pairs possible = n²' and figure out how many of those are FORCED vs FREE given the constraint. For combination-of-relations questions (R∪S, R∩S): check each of the 3-4 properties SEPARATELY for the combined relation — don't assume properties carry over.

title: Property-Checking of a Given Relation (reflexive/symmetric/antisymmetric/transitive/order-type)
text: Sabse common pattern: relation R ek formula ya condition se define hai (jaise 'aRb iff a-b is even' ya 'aRb iff a divides b'), aur poocha hai kaunse properties satisfy hoti hain, ya R Partial Order/Total Order/Equivalence Relation hai ya nahi. Ye is topic ka #1 pattern hai (38 me se 16 PYQs). Test with 2-3 CONCRETE small elements first — don't reason purely abstractly under time pressure. Reflexive: does (a,a) hold for every a? Check the SAME element against itself. Symmetric: if (a,b) holds, does (b,a) also always hold? Antisymmetric: if (a,b) and (b,a) both hold, MUST a=b? Transitive: if (a,b) and (b,c) hold, does (a,c) also hold — try to find a 3-element counterexample chain. 1. Write down the relation's defining condition precisely. 2. Reflexivity: substitute a=b, check if condition holds for all a — if the domain has an element where it fails (e.g., a=0 for division-based relations), reflexivity fails. 3. Symmetry: assume (a,b) holds, algebraically check if (b,a) must also hold. 4. Antisymmetry: assume (a,b) and (b,a) both hold, derive whether a=b is forced. 5. Transitivity: assume (a,b),(b,c) hold, check if (a,c) follows — actively TRY to construct a counterexample (this is faster than proving transitivity holds). 6. Combine: Reflexive+Symmetric+Transitive = Equivalence; Reflexive+Antisymmetric+Transitive = Partial Order; Partial Order + every pair comparable = Total Order. Checking reflexivity/symmetry only for the example pairs GIVEN in the relation's listing, instead of the general defining rule. Assuming antisymmetric is the 'opposite' of symmetric — a relation can be neither. For divisibility-style relations, forgetting to check behavior at 0 or negative numbers if the domain includes them. Relation defined by a divisibility/GCD/product-is-perfect-square condition on integers. Relation defined on ordered pairs (a,b) with a compound condition (e.g., a+d = b+c style). 'Circular' relation definition (aRb and bRc ⟹ cRa) — a less common 5th property, test the same way as transitivity.

title: Counting Relations (binary / reflexive / equivalence relation counts)
text: Agar poocha hai 'how many binary relations', 'how many reflexive relations', 'number of equivalence relations', ya 'largest/smallest equivalence relation size' on an n-element set — ye pure counting pattern hai, formula-driven. Total pairs possible in A×A = n². Total binary relations = 2^(n²) (each pair independently in/out). Reflexive relations: n diagonal pairs are FORCED in, remaining n²−n pairs are free → 2^(n²−n). Equivalence relation COUNT (not size) = Bell number B(n) — GATE rarely expects you to compute Bell numbers directly for large n, usually asks for small n or asks about LARGEST/SMALLEST equivalence relation SIZE instead (which has simple closed forms). 1. Identify n = |A|, and compute |A×A| = n². 2. If NO constraint: answer = 2^(n²). 3. If reflexivity required: subtract the n forced diagonal pairs from the exponent → 2^(n²−n). 4. If symmetry required: pairs come in (a,b)/(b,a) mirror groups except diagonal — count = 2^(n(n+1)/2). 5. If asked for LARGEST/SMALLEST equivalence relation size (not count): largest = n² (one class = whole set), smallest = n (identity relation, each element its own class). Confusing 'number of equivalence RELATIONS' (Bell number, hard) with 'size of the LARGEST equivalence relation' (n², easy) — read the question very carefully. Off-by-one in the exponent for reflexive-relation counting. Probability variant (2020): pick a random relation from all 2^(n²), find probability it's reflexive = 2^(n²−n) / 2^(n²) = 2^(−n). Comparing relation-count formula to function-count formula (n^n) for the same set — asked which grows faster.

title: Equivalence Relation Combination (does R∪S / R∩S stay an equivalence relation?)
text: Do (ya zyada) equivalence relations R aur S diye hain, aur poocha hai R∪S ya R∩S bhi equivalence relation hoga ya nahi — ye combination-pattern hai, chhota but recurring cluster. INTERSECTION of equivalence relations is ALWAYS an equivalence relation — safe to answer TRUE without much checking. UNION of equivalence relations is USUALLY NOT an equivalence relation — transitivity is the property that typically breaks. To disprove union-is-equivalence: construct a tiny 3-element counterexample where R and S individually partition differently. 1. Recall the safe defaults: intersection preserves all three properties (reflexive/symmetric/transitive independently hold under intersection); union preserves reflexive and symmetric but usually breaks transitive. 2. If a specific TRUE/FALSE claim about union is made, construct a 3-element counterexample: pick A={1,2,3}, R = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)}, S = {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(2,3),(3,2)} — R∪S contains (1,2) and (2,3) but not (1,3), breaking transitivity. Assuming union behaves the same as intersection (it doesn't). Poset/lattice framing (least-upper-bound, greatest-lower-bound existing) combined with combination-of-relations reasoning.

title: Transitive Closure Computation
text: 'Transitive closure of R', 'reflexive-transitive closure', ya digraph diya hai aur smallest m,n poocha hai jahan path exist kare — ye closure-computation pattern hai. Transitive closure = keep adding (a,c) whenever (a,b) and (b,c) are present, until no more can be added. Equivalent to: is there a PATH from a to c in the relation's directed graph? — transitive closure = reachability. Standard algorithm: Warshall's algorithm, O(n³) — this is also the source of the time-complexity PYQ in this cluster. 1. Draw the relation as a directed graph (nodes = elements, edges = related pairs). 2. Transitive closure = add an edge (a,c) for every pair of nodes a,c connected by ANY path (of length ≥1). 3. For small explicit relations, do this by direct path-tracing rather than running full Warshall's by hand. 4. For 'reflexive transitive closure', additionally add all self-loops (a,a). Stopping after only ONE pass of adding transitive pairs instead of iterating until no changes occur (closure needs to reach a fixed point). Digraph given, asked for smallest exponents m,n such that R^m = R^n (relation power / cycle-detection framing).

title: Equivalence Classes / Partition Construction
text: 'Find the equivalence classes', ya 'how many equivalence classes' poocha hai for a specific relation (jaise mod-n congruence) — ye partition-construction pattern hai. Every equivalence relation partitions the domain into disjoint equivalence classes. For mod-n congruence, the equivalence classes are exactly the n residue classes {0,1,...,n-1}. Pick one representative element, find everything related to it — that's one class; repeat with an unpicked element until domain exhausted. 1. Verify (or accept as given) that the relation is an equivalence relation. 2. Start with any unvisited element x, collect all y such that xRy — that's one equivalence class. 3. Repeat with the next unvisited element until all elements are classified. 4. Count classes / describe them as asked. Double-counting an element into two different classes — classes must be disjoint by definition. Equivalence classes defined via function-equality (f~g iff f(0)=g(0)) rather than numeric congruence.

title: Proof-Style Reasoning About Relations (flawed-proof spotting, existence claims)
text: Descriptive/older-style question jisme ek 'proof' diya gaya hai (jaise 'symmetric+transitive implies reflexive') aur poocha hai flaw kahan hai, ya general existence-style claim prove/disprove karna hai — ye abstract-reasoning pattern hai, mostly pre-2005. The classic flawed proof 'symmetric+transitive ⟹ reflexive': it assumes for every x there EXISTS some y with xRy — but if x has NO related element at all, the proof never gets to apply symmetry/transitivity for that x. Isolated elements are the counterexample. For general existence claims, try to construct a small explicit example before attempting a general proof. 1. Identify exactly which universal claim ('for all x...') the flawed proof implicitly relies on. 2. Find an element for which that assumption fails (e.g., an element with NO outgoing related pairs at all). 3. Construct the smallest possible counterexample relation to make the flaw concrete. Accepting the flawed proof at face value without checking the 'for all x' assumption.

title: Group Theory
text: Discrete Mathematics: Set Theory & Algebra group-theory

title: Group Theory — concept notes
text: Group Theory me GATE do cheezein baar-baar test karta hai: (1) diya gaya (Set, Operation) pair Semigroup/Monoid/Group/Abelian-Group hai ya nahi — ek fixed 4-point checklist se, (2) Lagrange's theorem based subgroup-order questions. Algebraic structure = (Set, Binary Operation). GATE 4 levels test karta hai: Semigroup (closure+associative) → Monoid (+identity) → Group (+inverse for every element) → Abelian Group (+commutative). Har level pichle level ka superset hai. Socho ek 'club' hai (the set) aur ek 'rule' hai do members ko combine karne ka (the operation). Closure = combine karne se result bhi club ke andar hi rahe (bahar na chala jaaye). Associative = grouping matter na kare ((a*b)*c = a*(b*c)). Identity = ek 'neutral' member ho jo kisi ko change na kare. Inverse = har member ka ek 'undo partner' ho jo combine karne par neutral de de. Commutative = order matter na kare (a*b = b*a). Semigroup = closure + associative only. Monoid = Semigroup + identity element. Group = Monoid + every element has an inverse. Abelian Group = Group + commutative. Lagrange's Theorem: order of any SUBGROUP divides the order of the GROUP. This is the single most-tested fact in this topic. Every group of prime order p is cyclic and has ONLY two subgroups: {e} and itself (no proper nontrivial subgroups) — direct Lagrange consequence. A cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup for each divisor of n. Identity element and inverses in a group are always UNIQUE. |H| divides |G| for any subgroup H of group G. Left cosets of H in G all have size |H| and partition G — hence |G| = |H| × (number of cosets, i.e. the index [G:H]). A cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of order d, for every divisor d of n. Checking closure/associativity but forgetting to verify EVERY element has an inverse WITHIN the set (not just that an inverse formula exists in general). Assuming commutativity is required for a 'Group' — it's only required for ABELIAN group, plain groups need not be commutative. Assuming a subset that is 'closed' under the operation is automatically a subgroup — it also needs identity and inverses within that subset. For 'largest proper subgroup' questions, forgetting that the answer must be the LARGEST divisor of |G| that is STRICTLY less than |G|. For structure-identification: run the 4-point checklist in order (closure → associative → identity → inverse → commutative) and stop as soon as one fails, naming the highest level reached. For subgroup-order questions: list ALL divisors of |G|, that's your set of POSSIBLE subgroup orders (Lagrange gives necessary, not sufficient, condition — but GATE mostly tests the necessary-condition direction). For 'largest proper subgroup': find the largest divisor of |G| that is strictly less than |G| itself — for |G|=prime, this is always 1 (only trivial subgroup).

title: Structure Identification (Semigroup / Monoid / Group / Abelian Group / Ring)
text: Ek (Set, Operation) pair diya hai (jaise matrices under multiplication, integers mod n, strings under concatenation) aur poocha hai ye Semigroup/Monoid/Group/Abelian Group hai ya nahi, ya kaunsa statement TRUE hai — ye is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (33 me se 14 PYQs). Run the checklist IN ORDER: Closure? → Associative? → Identity exists? → Every element has inverse? → Commutative (for Abelian)? Stop at the first failure and name the highest level reached (e.g., 'closure+associative but no identity → Semigroup only'). For matrix/modular-arithmetic sets, the most common failure point is INVERSE (e.g., 0 has no multiplicative inverse, singular matrices aren't invertible). 1. Write down the set and the operation precisely. 2. Closure: does combining two elements of the set always stay in the set? 3. Associativity: almost always holds for standard operations (+, ×, matrix mult, concatenation) — usually safe to assume true unless the operation is custom-defined. 4. Identity: does a neutral element exist WITHIN the set? 5. Inverse: does EVERY element (not just some) have an inverse within the set? 6. If all four hold, check commutativity for Abelian classification. Custom operators: NOT assuming associativity holds without checking — this is the #1 trap in recent (2023-2024) MSQ questions. 0 under multiplication, or singular matrices — always fail the inverse check. Non-empty string concatenation set WITHOUT the empty string — fails identity (no neutral element) unless empty string is included. Custom-defined operator (not standard +/×) — must verify associativity explicitly rather than assuming it, since custom operators can fail associativity. Incomplete operation table given, asked to complete it consistent with group axioms. 'Which statement is FALSE' framing — test each option against the checklist rather than assuming.

title: Lagrange's Theorem / Subgroup Order Questions
text: |G| ka order diya hai aur subgroup ka possible/largest/exact order poocha hai, ya coset-based proof poocha hai — ye Lagrange's Theorem application pattern hai. |H| must divide |G| — first list all divisors of |G|. 'Largest PROPER subgroup' = largest divisor of |G| that is strictly less than |G|. For |G| = prime number, the ONLY possible subgroup orders are 1 and |G| itself (no proper nontrivial subgroup). 1. Factorize |G| to list all its divisors — these are ALL the theoretically possible subgroup orders. 2. If 'largest proper subgroup' is asked: pick the largest divisor strictly less than |G|. 3. If a constraint is given (e.g., 'size of H is at least k'), filter the divisor list by that constraint and pick accordingly. 4. For proof-style coset questions: remember cosets of H partition G into equal-size blocks of size |H|, hence |G|=|H|×(number of cosets). Forgetting 'PROPER' means excluding G itself. Assuming every divisor of |G| is GUARANTEED to have an actual subgroup of that order — Lagrange only gives a NECESSARY condition, not sufficient (though GATE questions are usually built so the necessary-condition answer is correct). NAT-style direct numeric answer (2018, 2020, 2014 papers) instead of MCQ. Combined with cyclic-group reasoning (is H necessarily cyclic given |G| and |H|).

title: Group Property Proofs (abelian conditions, even-order element, equivalence relations on groups)
text: Descriptive/proof-style question: 'show that G is abelian if...', 'show that a group of even order has an element of order 2', ya ek relation define hoti hai on group elements aur poocha hai equivalence relation hai ya nahi — ye proof-reasoning pattern hai. 'a*a=e for all a ⟹ abelian' — standard proof: expand (a*b)*(a*b)=e, manipulate using inverses to get a*b=b*a. Even-order group has an element of order 2: pair up elements with their inverses (a and a⁻¹); elements NOT self-paired come in pairs, so an odd leftover count forces at least one self-inverse non-identity element. For 'is this relation an equivalence relation on G' questions, run the standard Reflexive/Symmetric/Transitive check (reuse the Relations topic's pattern). 1. Identify exactly what needs to be shown (abelian? subgroup? equivalence relation?). 2. Use group axioms (existence of inverse, associativity, identity) as your only allowed tools — don't assume commutativity unless proving/given. 3. For 'does there exist an element with property X' questions, use counting/pairing arguments (like the even-order pairing trick) rather than brute-force search. Assuming a property (like commutativity) that hasn't been proven or given. Missing the pairing/counting trick for even-order existence proofs and trying exhaustive case analysis instead. Multi-part descriptive proofs (pre-2005) building up a bigger result step by step (e.g., leading to Lagrange's theorem itself).

title: Cyclic Groups, Generators & Operation Tables
text: 'Generators of a cyclic group', 'complete the operation table', ya 'number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order n' poocha hai — ye cyclic-group-structure pattern hai. An element g generates the whole cyclic group of order n iff gcd(g's index, n) = 1 — count of generators = φ(n) (Euler's totient). Number of non-isomorphic abelian groups of order n = number of ways to write n's prime factorization exponents as partitions (fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups). Operation tables must be LATIN SQUARES (each row/column is a permutation of the group elements) — use this to fill missing entries. 1. For generator-counting: find n = |G|, compute φ(n), that's the count of generators (for a cyclic group). 2. For incomplete table completion: use the Latin-square constraint — each row and column must contain every group element exactly once. 3. For 'how many self-inverse elements' (a=a⁻¹): solve a*a=e directly within the given group structure. Forgetting operation tables must be Latin squares — missing entries can often be deduced by elimination alone. Confusing 'order of an element' (smallest k with a^k=e) with 'order of the group'.

title: Misc (matching-type / non-standard formats)
text: Old-style 'match the following' or other non-standard descriptive format — rare, low-value, just read carefully. No fixed method — read carefully, apply relevant definitions directly.

title: Functions
text: Discrete Mathematics: Set Theory & Algebra functions

title: Functions — concept notes
text: Functions topic me do cheezein dominate karti hain: (1) COUNTING — kitne functions/one-one/onto possible hain, (2) PROPERTY REASONING — given ek function, one-one/onto/bijective hai ya nahi, aur composition/image-preimage identities. Function f: A→B ek special relation hai jisme HAR element of A ka EXACTLY ONE image B me hota hai. One-one (injective) = alag inputs → alag outputs. Onto (surjective) = har output kisi na kisi input se aata hai. Bijective = dono (one-one aur onto). Function ko ek 'assignment machine' socho — har A ke element ko EK aur SIRF EK B ka element assign karta hai (do options nahi, aur khali bhi nahi chhod sakta). One-one = koi do alag inputs same output share nahi karte (no clash). Onto = B ka HAR element kisi na kisi input se cover hota hai (koi B-element chhoot na jaaye). Total functions from an m-element set to an n-element set = n^m. One-one (injective) functions from m-element to n-element set (m≤n) = n·(n-1)·...·(n-m+1) = P(n,m) = n!/(n-m)!. If m>n, NO injective function can exist (Pigeonhole Principle). Onto (surjective) functions from m-element to n-element set (m≥n) = n! × S(m,n), where S(m,n) is the Stirling number of the 2nd kind — for GATE, usually computed via inclusion-exclusion instead: Σ (-1)^k C(n,k) (n-k)^m for k=0 to n. Bijective functions exist only when |A|=|B|=n, and there are exactly n! of them. f(A1∩A2) ⊆ f(A1)∩f(A2) in general (NOT equal) — equality holds when f is injective. f(A1∪A2) = f(A1)∪f(A2) always (this one IS an equality, no injectivity needed). f⁻¹(B1∩B2) = f⁻¹(B1)∩f⁻¹(B2) and f⁻¹(B1∪B2) = f⁻¹(B1)∪f⁻¹(B2) — preimage always distributes cleanly over both ∩ and ∪, unlike forward image. n^m (m = |domain|, n = |codomain|) P(n,m) = n! / (n-m)! (requires m ≤ n) Σ_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k C(n,k) (n-k)^m n! (only when |A|=|B|=n) 2^(2^n) (n boolean variables → 2^n input rows → each row independently 0/1 in output) Applying the 'equal-size sets ⟹ one-one iff onto' shortcut to sets of DIFFERENT sizes — only valid when |A|=|B| and both finite. Assuming f(A∩B) = f(A)∩f(B) — this is false in general, a very common GATE trap option. Forgetting the inclusion-exclusion correction terms when counting onto functions — just using n^m − (something) without the full alternating sum. Confusing 'number of functions' (n^m) with 'number of one-one functions' (permutation, not power). For counting questions: identify domain size m and codomain size n FIRST, then match to the right formula (total/one-one/onto/bijective) based on what's asked and the m-vs-n relationship. For property-verification questions (image/preimage identities): test with a tiny concrete example (2-3 element sets) rather than abstract proof. For composition questions (g∘f onto ⟹ is g onto? is f onto?): remember g∘f onto ⟹ g MUST be onto (not necessarily f); g∘f one-one ⟹ f MUST be one-one (not necessarily g) — memorize this asymmetry.

title: Counting Functions (Total / One-One / Onto / Bijective / Boolean)
text: 'How many functions', 'number of one-to-one functions', 'number of onto functions' — seedha counting poocha gaya hai between two finite sets. Sabse bada cluster hai is topic ka (14/30 PYQs). First check: |domain|=m, |codomain|=n — and whether m<n, m=n, or m>n, since that decides WHICH formulas are even possible. Total functions = n^m. One-one needs m≤n = P(n,m). Onto needs m≥n = inclusion-exclusion sum. Bijective needs m=n = n!. If reverse-given (told the COUNT, asked for |A| or |B|) — set up the formula as an equation and solve. 1. Extract m=|domain|, n=|codomain|. 2. Match the question's keyword (any function / one-one / onto / bijective) to the corresponding formula. 3. For onto counting via inclusion-exclusion: Σ_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k C(n,k)(n-k)^m — compute term by term, don't skip the alternating signs. 4. For reverse-direction questions, set formula = given count, solve for the unknown. Using n^m formula when the question actually asks for ONE-ONE or ONTO specifically. Forgetting m≤n is required for one-one to be possible at all (else answer is 0). Codomain is itself a power set (functions INTO 2^B) — combine with power-set-size formula from Set Theory. Probability variant: randomly pick a function from all n^m, find probability it's one-one = P(n,m)/n^m. Constrained counting: bijections with a fixed point condition (f(x)≠x for some x, or f(1)=k) — adjust via direct casework on the constrained elements first.

title: Injective/Surjective/Bijective Verification & Composition Reasoning
text: Ek specific function di hai (formula se, jaise f(x)=x² ya piecewise) aur poocha hai one-one/onto hai ya nahi, ya f aur g compose karke banaye gaye g∘f ke baare me poocha hai — ye property-verification/composition pattern hai. For equal-size FINITE sets: one-one ⟺ onto ⟺ bijective — check just ONE of them if |A|=|B|. For composition g∘f: g∘f onto ⟹ g is onto (not necessarily f). g∘f one-one ⟹ f is one-one (not necessarily g). Memorize this direction — it's asymmetric and a favorite trap. For infinite sets (like ℝ→ℝ or ℕ→ℕ), the equal-size shortcut does NOT apply — must check both properties independently. 1. If domain and codomain are both finite and same size, just check ONE property (say, injectivity) and conclude bijective if it holds. 2. Otherwise, check injectivity directly: assume f(a)=f(b), derive whether a=b is forced. 3. Check surjectivity directly: for arbitrary y in codomain, can you always find x in domain with f(x)=y? 4. For composition questions, use the two memorized composition rules above rather than re-deriving from scratch each time. Applying the equal-finite-size shortcut to infinite sets. Getting the composition-implication direction backward (assuming g∘f onto implies BOTH f and g onto — false, only g is guaranteed). Descriptive/older-style explicit proof required (1988, 2001 papers) vs modern MCQ-style TRUE/FALSE. Inverse function computation for an explicit bijective formula.

title: Image/Preimage of Sets Under a Function (f(A∩B) vs f(A)∩f(B) style identities)
text: Question me f(A) ya f⁻¹(B) jaisi notation hai, aur A/B ke union/intersection ke saath combine karke ek identity TRUE hai ya nahi poocha hai — ye ek narrow but recurring GATE trap-pattern hai. Preimage (f⁻¹) is 'well-behaved': distributes over BOTH ∪ and ∩ perfectly, always. Forward image (f) is 'partially behaved': distributes over ∪ always, but only gives ⊆ (not =) over ∩ — equality needs f injective. 1. Identify whether the identity involves forward image f(·) or preimage f⁻¹(·). 2. If preimage: both ∪ and ∩ identities are TRUE, always. 3. If forward image with ∩: it's generally FALSE as an equality (only ⊆ holds) unless the question also states f is injective. 4. If forward image with ∪: it's TRUE as an equality, always. Assuming image behaves identically to preimage — it doesn't, intersection is the asymmetric case.

title: Equivalence-Classes-via-Function (kernel/quotient) & Advanced Combinatorial Counting
text: Function se induced equivalence relation (a~b iff f(a)=f(b)) define hoti hai, ya function ki jagah matrices/subsets ka function-jaisa counting hota hai — ye advanced/hybrid pattern hai, mostly recent (2021+) tough questions. Every function f:A→B induces an equivalence relation on A: a~b iff f(a)=f(b). The equivalence classes are exactly the 'fibers' (preimages of single points). If f is onto, the number of equivalence classes = |B|. 'Bijection between matrices/subsets and functions' framing — recognize the underlying set is secretly a function space in disguise. 1. Identify the 'disguised' function space (e.g., an m×n boolean matrix ≡ a function from {1..m}×{1..n} to {0,1}). 2. Translate the question into standard function-counting/property language. 3. Apply the relevant counting or property pattern from above. Not recognizing the disguised function-space framing and trying to solve from scratch.

title: Misc Concrete Function Puzzles (encoding schemes, functional-equation recursion, boolean identities)
text: Ek specific, self-contained function-based puzzle hai jo upar ke patterns me clean fit nahi hota — jaise ek prime-based encoding scheme, ya ek recursive functional equation (f(2n)=..., f(2n+1)=...), ya ek boolean-algebra identity check. Low-frequency but worth recognizing as 'read carefully, work from the given definition directly' rather than forcing a memorized formula. No single formula applies — read the custom definition very carefully and work forward from small concrete cases. 1. Work out the function's behavior on the first few small inputs by hand. 2. Look for a pattern before attempting the general case. Trying to force-fit a memorized counting formula onto a custom-defined function.

title: Set Theory
text: Discrete Mathematics: Set Theory & Algebra set-theory

title: Set Theory — concept notes
text: Set Theory Discrete Math ka sabse basic building block hai — GATE khud isse directly kam poochta hai (27 PYQs), lekin iske concepts (power set, inclusion-exclusion, set identities) baaki poore Discrete Math aur DBMS me baar-baar use hote hain. Isliye pehle isko solid karo. Set = well-defined collection of distinct objects. GATE me 3 cheezein baar-baar test hoti hain: (1) kitne elements/subsets hain — counting, (2) do sets ke operations (union/intersection/complement/symmetric difference) ki identities, (3) proof-style reasoning about finite/infinite sets. Set ko ek 'bag of distinct items' socho — order matter nahi karta, repetition allowed nahi. Power set = us bag ke SAARE possible sub-bags (empty bag se lekar poora bag tak) ka collection — agar bag me n items hain, to 2^n possible sub-bags. Inclusion-Exclusion ek 'double-counting avoid karo' trick hai jab teen groups overlap karte hain. |P(A)| = 2^n where n = |A|. Number of subsets of size k (from an n-element set) = C(n,k). Number of subsets with ODD cardinality = number with EVEN cardinality = 2^(n-1) (for n ≥ 1) — a very common trap/NAT answer. A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A ⟺ A = B. Symmetric difference A △ B = (A−B) ∪ (B−A) = (A∪B) − (A∩B). De Morgan's Laws: (A∪B)' = A'∩B' and (A∩B)' = A'∪B'. For infinite sets, a proper subset CAN have the same cardinality as the whole set (e.g., even numbers vs all integers) — finite-set intuition breaks here, classic trap. |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B| |A∪B∪C| = |A|+|B|+|C| − |A∩B| − |B∩C| − |A∩C| + |A∩B∩C| |P(A)| = 2^|A| Number of subsets of odd size = 2^(n-1) A △ B = (A ∪ B) − (A ∩ B) Confusing 'at least two' with 'exactly two' in inclusion-exclusion word problems — these need DIFFERENT formulas. Forgetting the +|A∩B∩C| correction term in the 3-set inclusion-exclusion formula (only subtracting pairwise, not adding back the triple). Applying finite-set cardinality intuition to infinite sets (e.g., assuming a proper subset must be 'smaller'). Mixing up ⊆ (subset) with ∈ (element of) when a set itself contains sets as elements (common in power-set property questions). For word problems: draw a 3-circle Venn diagram, label all 7 regions, and solve for the innermost region first (triple overlap), then work outward. For power-set/subset-counting: think 'each element has a binary choice — in or out' — this converts counting problems into 2^n or C(n,k) directly. For 'which statement is TRUE' set-identity questions: pick a small concrete example (3-4 element sets) and test each option rather than doing abstract algebra under time pressure.

title: Inclusion-Exclusion Word Problems (overlapping groups)
text: 'Out of N persons, X eat vegetables, Y eat fish, Z eat eggs... how many eat at least two/exactly two/all three' jaise word problems — 3 overlapping groups, counting poocha gaya hai. Ye pattern GA ke Venn Diagram topic me bhi repeat hota hai. Draw a 3-circle Venn diagram immediately, label all 7 regions. |A∪B∪C| = |A|+|B|+|C| − pairwise sums + triple overlap 'At least two' region = (all pairwise overlaps) − 2×(triple overlap). 'Exactly two' = (pairwise overlaps) − 3×(triple overlap). 1. List given: |A|, |B|, |C|, and whichever pairwise/triple intersections are given. 2. Draw the Venn diagram, solve for the CENTER region (all three) first if not given directly. 3. Fill outward: each pairwise-only region = (pairwise total) − (triple). 4. Answer 'at least two' = sum of all regions with 2+ overlap; 'exactly two' = sum of pairwise-only regions (excluding center); 'exactly one' = total in one circle minus its overlaps. 'At least two' vs 'exactly two' confusion — always re-read which one is asked before picking the formula variant. Forgetting the +|A∩B∩C| term. Number-theory flavored version: 'how many integers 1-1000 divisible by 2, 3, or 5' — same formula, sets defined by divisibility instead of people. Given total + individual group sizes + pairwise overlaps, asked to find the triple-overlap (reverse direction of the formula).

title: Power Set Cardinality & Properties
text: Agar 'power set', 'P(A)', ya 'number of subsets' shabd dikhe — chahe seedha count poocha ho ya property TRUE/FALSE poochi ho — ye power-set pattern hai. Isme kabhi seedha 2^n, kabhi constrained subset-counting (odd size, contains a fixed element) hota hai. |P(A)| = 2^|A| — the default starting formula. Each element independently 'in or out' of a subset → binary choice model for any constrained counting variant. Power-set element itself is a SET (of subsets) — questions about P(P(A)) or membership-vs-subset relations are common traps here. 1. Identify n = |A|. 2. If plain power-set size asked: answer = 2^n. 3. If a constraint is given (odd-size subsets, subsets containing a specific element, subsets NOT containing a specific element): model each element's inclusion as an independent binary choice and count directly, or use 2^(n-1) for the odd/even-size split. 4. If it's a property/TRUE-FALSE question about power sets, plug in a tiny concrete set (n=2 or 3) and check each option. Confusing 'element of A' with 'subset of A' — remember ∅ and A itself are always subsets, always counted. Off-by-one on odd/even split when n itself changes between sub-parts of a question. NAT-style direct computation (2015: cardinality of power set of a given set = 2048 etc.). Conceptual TRUE/FALSE about complement-within-power-set behavior — needs De Morgan's + power-set combined.

title: Set Algebra Identity Verification (De Morgan's, complements, symmetric difference)
text: Question me set operations (∪, ∩, complement, symmetric difference △) ki koi identity di hai aur poocha hai TRUE hai ya nahi — ye pure set-algebra proof/verification pattern hai, mostly conceptual MCQ. De Morgan's Laws are the most-tested identity: (A∪B)' = A'∩B', (A∩B)' = A'∪B'. When unsure of an identity abstractly, TEST with a concrete 3-4 element universal set and 2-3 subsets — fastest way to eliminate wrong options under time pressure. Symmetric difference is associative and commutative — useful for simplifying chained △ expressions. 1. Try to recognize a standard identity (De Morgan, distributive, associative) directly. 2. If the expression is unfamiliar/complex, pick a small concrete universal set U and 2-3 subsets with actual elements, evaluate both sides of the claimed identity numerically. 3. For 'which of the following is/are TRUE' with Venn-diagram-friendly claims, sketch the diagram rather than algebra-bash. Sign errors when expanding complements of unions/intersections. Assuming an identity that holds for numbers (like distributivity) also holds the same way for all set operations without checking. Given |A|, |B| and asking about relationships between |A∩B|, |A∪B|, |A−B| for finite sets (algebraic, not just identity-matching).

title: Finite vs Infinite Set Proof-Style Reasoning
text: Agar question 'infinite set', 'prove that', ya multi-part descriptive/induction-style hai, ya 'which statement about infinite sets is true' poochta hai — ye abstract proof-reasoning pattern hai, mostly pre-2010 papers me, calculation kam hai, logical reasoning zyada. Finite-set intuition (proper subset is always 'smaller') FAILS for infinite sets — this is the #1 trap source in this pattern. For induction-style proofs: base case + inductive step, standard template. For 'does there exist a set such that...' statements: try to construct a concrete example or counterexample rather than proving abstractly. 1. If the question asks 'does there exist...', try to CONSTRUCT an example first — often faster than proving impossibility. 2. If it's an induction proof, write base case explicitly, then assume true for k and prove for k+1. 3. Watch specifically for any claim that treats infinite sets like finite ones (subset ⟹ smaller cardinality) — that's usually the false option. Assuming finite-set cardinality rules apply to infinite sets. Graph-on-subsets construction (vertices = subsets, edges = symmetric-difference condition) — combines set theory with graph theory language.

title: Extremal Set-Family Cardinality (advanced/Sperner-style)
text: Agar question ek collection of subsets define karta hai with a CONSTRAINT (jaise 'no subset contains another', ya 'every pair reacts under some rule') aur poochta hai MAXIMUM possible size/cardinality of such a family — ye advanced extremal combinatorics pattern hai, GATE ka sabse tough set-theory type. This is often a disguised Sperner's-theorem-style question (max antichain in subset lattice = C(n, n/2)). Try small n by hand (n=2,3,4) to spot the pattern before generalizing. These are typically the hardest/lowest-attempt-rate questions in this topic — budget time accordingly, consider skipping first pass. 1. Restate the constraint precisely (no subset ⊆ another = antichain condition, is the most common). 2. Test small cases (n=2,3,4) by brute-force enumeration to find the pattern. 3. Recognize C(n, floor(n/2)) as the go-to answer shape for 'largest antichain' style constraints. Trying to solve abstractly without testing small cases first — wastes time in the exam. Framed as chemistry compounds/reactions or as vectors with an abstract binary relation — same underlying extremal-family math under different dressing.

title: Limits
text: Engineering Mathematics: Calculus limits

title: Limits — concept notes
text: Limit ka matlab: x kisi value ke paas jaaye to f(x) kis value ke paas jaata hai. GATE me indeterminate forms (0/0, inf/inf), standard limits (sin x / x, (1+1/x)^x), L'Hopital rule aur squeeze/bounded-function arguments aate hain. Pehle direct substitution try karo. Agar 0/0 ya inf/inf aaye to L'Hopital rule (numerator aur denominator ka alag alag derivative) ya standard limit use karo. Limit nikaalna = value ke 'kareeb jaana', value par pahunchna nahi. Substitute karke dekho: agar seedha number mil gaya to wahi answer. 0/0 ya inf/inf form indeterminate hai, tab derivative lagao. x -> infinity par bade powers jeetate hain; dono taraf se limit barabar ho tabhi exist karta hai. Standard: lim sin x / x = 1 (x->0), lim (1 - cos x)/x^2 = 1/2, lim (e^x - 1)/x = 1, lim ln(1+x)/x = 1. lim (1 + 1/x)^x = e (x->inf); lim (1 + x)^(1/x) = e (x->0). L'Hopital: 0/0 ya inf/inf par lim f/g = lim f'/g'. Bounded function x vanishing function = 0 (e.g., x sin(1/x) -> 0). Squeeze theorem: g <= f <= h aur lim g = lim h = L to lim f = L. x -> inf: polynomial ratio me highest power ka ratio. Limit exist karta hai <=> left = right. Rationalise karo jab square roots ka difference aaye (inf - inf). lim sin x / x = 1 lim (1-cos x)/x^2 = 1/2 lim (1+1/n)^n = e lim f/g = lim f'/g' lim (e^x - 1)/x = 1 Determinate form par bhi L'Hopital lagana. Left/right limit alag hone par exist maan lena. inf - inf ko 0 samajhna. Substitute -> classify form. Rationalise / factor / standard limit / L'Hopital. 1^inf form: exponent method.

title: Evaluate Limit via Indeterminate Form (0/0, inf/inf, L'Hopital, Standard Limits)
text: Trigonometric/exponential/rational expression ka limit nikaalna. Classify form; L'Hopital or standard limit. 1. Direct substitute. 2. Indeterminate ho to factor/rationalise. 3. L'Hopital ya standard limit. Non-indeterminate par L'Hopital. Without series expansion condition. Infinity limits of ratios.

title: Existence / Bounded-Function Arguments
text: Kya limit exist karta hai; bounded function ya inequality diya hai. Left/right limit; squeeze. 1. Left aur right limit alag se. 2. Bounds se squeeze lagao. One-sided limit ko full limit maan lena. x sin(1/x) type.

title: Maxima Minima — concept notes
text: Function ke local/global maxima-minima, critical points, monotonicity, roots count. Critical point: f'(x)=0. f''>0 => local min, f''<0 => local max. Closed interval par global extrema critical points aur endpoints par. Pehle derivative nikalo aur 0 karo. Second derivative sign se nature. Closed interval me endpoints bhi compare karo. Increasing everywhere <=> f' >= 0 sab jagah. f'(c)=0 critical point; f''(c)>0 min, <0 max. Closed interval: compare critical points aur endpoints. Increasing everywhere: f' >= 0. Rolle/IVT se roots ki existence. f'=0 aur f''=0 to test inconclusive. f''>0 min, f''<0 max Endpoints bhoolna. f'=0 ko hamesha extremum maan lena. f' ka sign chart banao.

title: Find Extrema / Max / Min Value
text: Function aur interval; max/min value ya location. Derivative test. 1. f'. 2. Critical points. 3. Compare. Endpoints.

text: Engineering Mathematics: Calculus differentiation

title: Differentiation — concept notes
text: Derivative rules, differentiability at a point, piecewise functions, polynomials degree, numerical derivative. Differentiable => continuous (converse false). Piecewise function me junction par left = right derivative chahiye. Piecewise function ke parameters ke liye continuity aur derivative dono equations lagao. |x| jaise corner par differentiable nahi. Product/quotient/chain rules. Differentiable => continuous. Piecewise junction: value aur derivative match. Degree of f' = n-1 (nonconstant polynomial). Second derivative approx: (f(x+h)-2f(x)+f(x-h))/h^2. Sum/product of differentiable functions differentiable. (f(x+h)-2f(x)+f(x-h))/h^2 Continuity aur differentiability confuse. Junction equations.

text: Engineering Mathematics: Linear Algebra eigen-value

title: Eigen Value — concept notes
text: Eigenvalue lambda wo scalar hai jiske liye Av = lambda v (v != 0). GATE me: eigenvalues nikaalna (characteristic polynomial), trace/determinant se shortcut, matrix functions (A^2, A+kI, A^-1) ke eigenvalues, aur special matrices (symmetric, projection, triangular) ki properties. det(A - lambda I) = 0 characteristic equation hai; uske roots eigenvalues hain. Sum of eigenvalues = trace, product = determinant. Eigenvector wo direction hai jo matrix lagne par sirf stretch/shrink hoti hai (ghumti nahi). Poori 2x2 ya 3x3 ka polynomial banane ke bajay pehle trace aur determinant shortcut socho: agar ek eigenvalue diya ho to baaki trace/det se mil jaate hain. Triangular/diagonal matrix me eigenvalues = diagonal entries. Sum of eigenvalues = trace(A); product of eigenvalues = det(A). Triangular/diagonal matrix ke eigenvalues = diagonal entries. A^k ke eigenvalues lambda^k; A + cI ke lambda + c; cA ke c*lambda; A^-1 ke 1/lambda (lambda != 0). A aur A^T ke eigenvalues same. Singular matrix <=> 0 eigenvalue hai <=> det = 0. Symmetric real matrix: eigenvalues real; alag eigenvalues ke eigenvectors orthogonal (dot product 0). Positive definite: sab eigenvalues > 0. Idempotent/projection matrix (A^2 = A): eigenvalues sirf 0 aur 1. Nilpotent (A^k = 0): sab eigenvalues 0. Rank-1 matrix uu^T: ek non-zero eigenvalue = u^T u, baaki 0. Cayley-Hamilton: matrix apni characteristic equation satisfy karta hai. Adjacency matrix of graph symmetric hoti hai, eigenvalues ka sum 0 (trace 0). sum(lambda_i) = trace(A) prod(lambda_i) = det(A) det(A - lambda I) = 0 eig(A + cI) = lambda + c eig(A^k) = lambda^k eig(u u^T) = {u^T u, 0, ..., 0} lambda^2 - trace*lambda + det = 0 A^-1 ke eigenvalue lena par 0 eigenvalue ke case me invertible hi nahi hota. Eigenvalues ka product determinant se sign galat. Eigenvector ko normalise karna bhoolna jab unit vector maanga ho. 2x2: lambda^2 - tr*lambda + det. 3x3 me trace + det + ek known eigenvalue. Function of matrix: eigenvalues par function lagao. Rank-1/projection jaise special structures pehchano.

title: Matrix — concept notes
text: Matrix algebra ke basic ideas: determinant, rank, inverse, singular/non-singular, symmetric counting, trace, null space, orthogonal/projection matrices, LU factorization. Square matrix A invertible <=> det(A) != 0 <=> full rank <=> rows/columns linearly independent <=> Ax=0 ka sirf trivial solution. Matrix ke bahut saare properties ek hi baat ke different chehre hain: singular = determinant 0 = rows dependent = null space non-trivial. Isliye statement check karte waqt in equivalences ko use karo. Counting questions me free entries gino: n x n symmetric 0/1 matrix ke liye 2^(n(n+1)/2). Singular <=> det = 0 <=> rows (columns) linearly dependent. det(AB) = det(A)det(B); det(A^T) = det(A); det(kA) = k^n det(A); det(A^-1) = 1/det(A). Row swap det ka sign badalta hai; row addition det nahi badalti; scaling det ko scale karti hai. rank(A) + nullity(A) = number of columns (rank-nullity theorem). (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1; (AB)^T = B^T A^T. trace(AB) = trace(BA); trace = sum of diagonal = sum of eigenvalues. Symmetric n x n matrices with 0/1 entries: 2^(n(n+1)/2). Orthogonal matrix: Q^T Q = I, norm-preserving, det = +/-1. Projection matrix: P^2 = P. Sum of two singular matrices non-singular ho sakti hai aur two non-singular ka sum singular ho sakta hai. AB = I (square) => BA = I, dono inverse hain. det(AB) = det A det B det(kA) = k^n det A rank + nullity = n A^-1 = adj(A)/det(A) 2^(n(n+1)/2) det(A+B) = det A + det B maan lena (galat). det(kA) = k det A (n dimension ka power bhoolna). AB = BA maan lena (matrices generally commute nahi karte). Null space vector ke saath det ke conclusion. Row operations se det/rank/inverse. Statement 'ALWAYS true' me chhota counter-example try karo. Trace/eigenvalue link use karo.

title: System of Equations — concept notes
text: Ax = b ka solution: unique, infinite ya none — rank of A aur augmented matrix [A|b] se decide hota hai. Homogeneous Ax = 0 ka non-trivial solution det(A) = 0 hone par. Rank test: rank(A) = rank([A|b]) = n => unique; rank(A) = rank([A|b]) < n => infinite; rank(A) < rank([A|b]) => no solution (n = number of unknowns). Row-reduce karke echelon form banao. Agar koi row 0 = non-zero jaisi aa jaye to inconsistent (no solution). Free variables jitne, utne parameters, yaani infinite solutions. Square system me unique solution tabhi jab det(A) != 0. Unique: rank(A)=rank([A|b])=n. Infinite: rank(A)=rank([A|b])<n. None: rank(A)<rank([A|b]). Homogeneous Ax=0 hamesha consistent; trivial solution x=0. Homogeneous me non-trivial solution <=> rank(A) < n <=> det = 0 (square). Homogeneous solution space ki dimension = n - rank(A). m < n (kam equations) wala consistent system infinite solutions deta hai. Ax=b ke do solutions ka difference Ax=0 ka solution hota hai. Gaussian elimination operations ~ n^3/3 multiplications. rank(A) vs rank([A|b]) vs n n - rank(A) approx (n^3)/3 multiplications Sirf det dekhkar 'no solution' bol dena (infinite bhi ho sakta hai). title: Probability — concept notes
text: Basic probability: sample space, events, counting-based probability, conditional probability, independence, Bayes rule, total probability, aur inclusion-exclusion. GATE me dice, coins, cards, balls-in-bag, divisibility aur multi-stage experiments aate hain. P(event) = favourable outcomes / total equally likely outcomes. Complex events ko AND (multiply, independent ho to), OR (add, mutually exclusive ho to), aur complement (1 - P) se todo. Pehle sample space socho: kitne equally likely outcomes hain. 'At least one' wale sawal me complement use karo: 1 - P(none). 'Given that' aaye to conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B), yaani sample space chhota ho jaata hai. Multi-step experiment ke liye tree diagram banao aur paths ko multiply/add karo. P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B). P(A^c) = 1 - P(A). Independent: P(A n B) = P(A)P(B). Mutually exclusive: P(A n B) = 0 (independent se alag concept). Total probability: P(B) = sum P(B|A_i)P(A_i). Bayes rule posterior nikalta hai. Without replacement: conditional probabilities badalte hain; with replacement: independent. Two dice: 36 outcomes; n dice: 6^n. Sum of dice type: coefficient/generating function ya enumeration. Birthday-type: P(all distinct) = n!/(n^k) style. Symmetry: kisi bhi do positions par aces hone ki probability same. Repeated trial until success: geometric series (e.g., 'roll again on tie'). P(A u B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A n B) P(A|B) = P(A n B)/P(B) P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B) P(B) = sum P(B|Ai)P(Ai) 1 - P(none) P(A n B) = P(A)P(B) Mutually exclusive ko independent samajhna. Ordered vs unordered outcomes mix karna. Conditional me denominator galat (original space use karna). Divisibility problems me overlap (inclusion-exclusion) miss karna. Sample space likho. title: Most Appropriate Word — concept notes
text: Sentence completion, analogy, word intensity order, prepositions/pronouns, aur idiom/phrasal usage. Yeh vocabulary + context ka test hai. Sentence ka tone (positive/negative), contrast words (despite, but) aur grammar (subject-verb, preposition) se sahi word chuno. Pehle blank ke aage-peeche ke clues padho: kya sentence contrast dikha raha hai (despite, although) ya reason (because)? Phir options me se grammar aur meaning dono match karo. Analogy me pehle dono words ka relation batao (synonym, intensity, part-whole). Contrast markers: despite, although, but, however -> blank opposite meaning maangta hai. Cause markers: because, since, therefore -> same direction meaning. Analogy relation pehle likho: synonym, antonym, degree, tool-user, place-person. Intensity order: low -> medium -> high (e.g., walk, jog, sprint). Commonly confused words: fair/fare, beside/besides, nearly/utterly. Subject-verb agreement aur phrasal verbs (break down, revolve around) dekho. Elimination: pehle grammar galat options hatao. Sirf familiar word chun lena bina context. Grammar (preposition/verb form) ignore karna. Analogy me relation ulta lena. Blank ka part of speech socho. Context clue underline karo. Elimination + sentence me daalkar padho.

title: Sentence Completion by Context (Word/Phrase)
text: Blank ke liye sabse suitable word/phrase chunna. Context clue aur grammar. 1. Sentence ka tone/relation. 2. Part of speech. 3. Elimination. Familiar word par bharosa. Multiple blanks ek saath.

title: Grammar-Based Usage (Pronoun, Preposition, Phrasal Verb, Homophone)
text: Correct form: that/which, besides, break down, fair/fare. Grammar rule. 1. Grammatical role. 2. Rule apply karo. Similar sounding words. Homophone pairs.

title: Analogy and Intensity-Order Questions
text: A : B :: C : ?, ya intensity ordering me missing word. Relation batao aur apply karo. 1. Relation pehchano. 2. Wahi relation second pair par lagao. Relation ulta. Degree/intensity analogies (2024).
