text: Operating System process-synchronization

title: Process Synchronization — concept notes
text: Process Synchronization OS ka sabse bada topic hai (52 PYQs). 6 skills: critical-section solution VERIFY karna (Peterson's-jaise flag/turn algorithms), semaphore-based classic problems (producer-consumer, reader-writer), semaphore-code TRACE karke possible outputs/counts nikaalna, test-and-set/atomic-instruction based mutex, precedence-graph/fork-join concurrent programming, aur conceptual definitions. Semaphore = ek integer counter jisme sirf 2 atomic operations hote hain: P()/wait() (decrement, agar 0 se neeche jaaye to BLOCK/wait), V()/signal() (increment, agar koi wait kar raha hai to usse WAKE UP karo). MUTUAL EXCLUSION ke liye binary semaphore (0/1) use hota hai — critical section ko P()...V() se ghero. RESOURCE-COUNTING ke liye counting semaphore use hota hai (jaise buffer slots). Semaphore ko ek 'token counter' socho — P() ek token LETA hai (agar available hai; nahi to wait karta hai jab tak koi token na de de), V() ek token WAPIS karta hai. Mutual exclusion ke liye 1 token wala semaphore (mutex) use karo — sirf EK process critical section me ja sakta hai kyunki sirf 1 token hai. Producer-Consumer me DO semaphores chahiye: 'empty slots count' aur 'full slots count' — producer empty slot LETA hai aur full slot BADHATA hai, consumer ulta. A VALID critical-section solution must satisfy all THREE: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, Bounded Waiting. Testing a given solution means checking EACH of these three properties. Peterson's Algorithm (2 processes, flag[] + turn variable) is a CORRECT software-only solution satisfying all three properties — the canonical example to compare against. Producer-Consumer (bounded buffer, size N): needs 3 semaphores — mutex (binary, =1, for mutual exclusion on buffer access), empty (counting, =N initially, tracks empty slots), full (counting, =0 initially, tracks filled slots). Producer: wait(empty), wait(mutex), add, signal(mutex), signal(full). Consumer: wait(full), wait(mutex), remove, signal(mutex), signal(empty). Reader-Writer Problem: multiple readers can read SIMULTANEOUSLY, but a writer needs EXCLUSIVE access (no readers or other writers). Standard solution uses a read-count variable + mutex (protecting read-count) + a 'wrt' semaphore (writer exclusion, also held by the FIRST reader and released by the LAST reader). Test-and-Set based mutex: while(TestAndSet(lock)); — BUSY-WAITING (spinlock) solution, simple but WASTES CPU cycles while waiting (no blocking/sleeping). Dining Philosophers deadlock avoidance: classic fix = have at least one philosopher pick up forks in the OPPOSITE order (breaks the circular-wait condition) — or limit the number of philosophers allowed to sit simultaneously to N-1. wait(S)/P(S): S--; if(S<0) block. signal(S)/V(S): S++; if(S≤0) wakeup a blocked process Mutual Exclusion + Progress + Bounded Waiting — ALL THREE required for a correct CS solution mutex=1 (binary), empty=N (counting), full=0 (counting) for a size-N bounded buffer readcount (int, protected by mutex) + wrt (semaphore, held during any write OR by the span from first-reader-in to last-reader-out) Assuming any flag/turn-based solution is automatically correct like Peterson's — many similar-looking proposed solutions actually FAIL one of the three properties (often progress or bounded waiting) — always verify all three explicitly. Mixing up which semaphore protects WHAT in producer-consumer (empty vs full vs mutex) — a swapped or misplaced wait/signal breaks the whole solution. For reader-writer, forgetting that only the FIRST reader needs to wait(wrt) and only the LAST reader needs to signal(wrt) — middle readers skip this. Assuming semaphore-based code has a SINGLE deterministic output — concurrent execution usually has MULTIPLE possible valid interleavings/outputs unless proven otherwise. For critical-section-solution verification: check Mutual Exclusion (can two processes be in CS simultaneously under any execution order?), Progress (can the CS sit empty while a waiting process is blocked from entering despite CS being free?), Bounded Waiting (can a process wait indefinitely while others repeatedly cut in?) — test with concrete small interleavings for each. For producer-consumer/reader-writer: match the given code against the STANDARD template, identify which semaphore serves which role, spot deviations from the correct pattern. For semaphore-trace/output-count questions: enumerate the POSSIBLE valid interleavings (respecting each process's own instruction order and semaphore wait/signal constraints), compute the resulting value/count for each, report the range or count of distinct possibilities. For test-and-set/atomic-instruction questions: recall these provide BUSY-WAITING mutual exclusion — correct but CPU-wasteful, contrast with semaphore's blocking (sleep-based) approach.

title: Critical Section Solution Verification (flag/turn-based, Peterson's-style)
text: Ek proposed critical-section solution di hai (flag[]/turn variables use karke, jaise Peterson's algorithm ka variant) aur poocha hai ye Mutual Exclusion/Progress/Bounded-Waiting satisfy karta hai ya nahi — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (52 me se 10 PYQs). Check all THREE properties explicitly: Mutual Exclusion (two processes in CS together?), Progress (CS empty but a waiting process still blocked unnecessarily?), Bounded Waiting (indefinite postponement possible?). Try concrete interleavings (process A runs a bit, then B, then A again) to find a counterexample if the solution is flawed. 1. Trace through a SPECIFIC interleaving of the two (or more) processes' code. 2. Check if mutual exclusion is ever violated (both in CS simultaneously). 3. Check if progress fails (CS free, but no waiting process allowed to enter due to a logic flaw). 4. Check if bounded waiting fails (one process can be perpetually skipped). 5. If all three hold under EVERY possible interleaving, the solution is correct. Verifying mutual exclusion but forgetting to separately check progress and bounded waiting — a solution can satisfy ME while failing the other two. 3-process generalizations of 2-process algorithms (like Peterson's extended to 3) — verify the SAME three properties, often harder to satisfy with more processes. N-process solutions using a 'max' function or ticket-number scheme (bakery-algorithm-style) — trace the ticket-assignment and ordering logic specifically.

title: Semaphore-Based Classic Problems (Producer-Consumer, Reader-Writer)
text: Producer-Consumer (bounded buffer) ya Reader-Writer problem ka semaphore-based solution diya hai aur poocha hai ye CORRECT hai ya nahi, ya blanks fill karne hain — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (52 me se 10 PYQs). Producer-Consumer needs 3 semaphores: mutex(1), empty(N), full(0) — match given code against this template. Reader-Writer: readcount+mutex (protects readcount) + wrt (writer exclusion, held by first-reader-in/last-reader-out only). 1. Identify which semaphores are present and their initial values. 2. Match against the STANDARD template (mutex/empty/full for producer-consumer; readcount/mutex/wrt for reader-writer). 3. Spot any deviation (missing wait/signal, wrong initial value, wrong ordering) that would break correctness. 4. For fill-in-the-blank questions, insert the operation that matches the standard template's role at that point. Swapping the roles of 'empty' and 'full' semaphores (producer should wait on empty/signal full; consumer waits on full/signals empty) — a very common exact-reversal trap. Single binary semaphore reader-writer variant (busy-waiting, simplified) — different from the full readcount+mutex+wrt version, verify against ITS specific simpler correctness requirements.

title: Semaphore Code Trace / Possible Output Values
text: Concurrent processes given semaphores ke saath, aur poocha hai shared variable ki FINAL possible values kya hain, ya ek statement KITNI BAAR print hoga — is topic ka teesra bada pattern hai (52 me se 10 PYQs). Enumerate the POSSIBLE valid interleavings (respecting each process's own instruction order and any semaphore constraints) — there's usually a RANGE of possible outcomes, not just one. Look specifically for RACE CONDITIONS (unprotected shared-variable read-modify-write) that allow multiple different final values. 1. Identify the shared variable(s) and each process's operations on them. 2. Determine which operations are PROTECTED (inside a semaphore-guarded critical section) vs UNPROTECTED (can interleave freely). 3. Enumerate the distinct interleavings of unprotected operations, compute the resulting value for each. 4. Report the count/range of DISTINCT possible final values, or the exact count as asked. Assuming a single deterministic outcome when the code actually allows multiple valid interleavings — always check for genuine race conditions before concluding a unique answer. Multi-threaded lock-based (not pure semaphore) synchronization with non-reentrant locks — reason about deadlock potential if a thread tries to re-acquire its own held lock. Fetch-and-Add / atomic read-modify-write instructions used directly (no separate lock) — these ARE atomic by definition, so no race condition on that specific operation alone.

title: Test-and-Set / Atomic Instruction Based Mutual Exclusion
text: TEST-AND-SET (ya Fetch-and-Add, ya similar atomic read-modify-write) instruction use karke mutual exclusion implement kiya gaya hai — poocha hai ye CORRECT hai ya nahi, ya kis TYPE ka waiting hai (busy vs blocking). Test-and-Set busy-waits (spinlock) — CPU keeps checking in a loop, doesn't sleep/block. TAS-based mutex is simple and CORRECT for mutual exclusion, but wastes CPU cycles while waiting — contrast with semaphore's sleep-based blocking. 1. Recall TAS atomically reads old value AND sets to 1 in one indivisible step — this guarantees only ONE process can successfully 'acquire' at a time. 2. Verify the enter_CS/leave_CS pseudocode correctly loops on TAS until success (enter) and resets the flag (leave). Assuming TAS-based spinlocks provide FAIRNESS/bounded-waiting automatically — basic TAS loops don't guarantee this without additional mechanism (like a ticket system).

title: Precedence Graph / Fork-Join Concurrent Programming
text: Sequential code diya hai aur poocha hai iska PRECEDENCE GRAPH banao, ya fork/join constructs use karke concurrent program likho jo diye gaye precedence constraints satisfy kare. Precedence graph: nodes=statements, edges=must-happen-before dependencies (based on shared variable read/write dependencies). Convert to concurrent code using semaphores: one semaphore per edge in the precedence graph, signal() after the source statement, wait() before the destination statement. 1. Analyze each statement's variable reads/writes, identify true dependencies (a statement reading a variable another writes, must come after). 2. Draw the precedence graph connecting dependent statements. 3. For concurrent-code generation: assign one semaphore per graph edge (initialized to 0), have the SOURCE statement signal() it and the DESTINATION statement wait() on it before executing. Missing an implicit dependency (two statements both writing the SAME variable, or one reading what another writes) when constructing the graph.

title: Conceptual Definitions (critical section, race condition, classic named problems)
text: Poocha hai 'critical section kya hai', 'race condition kise kehte hain', ya Dining Philosophers jaise classic problems ke deadlock-avoidance techniques — ye definitional/classic-problem pattern hai (52 me se 14 PYQs, sabse bada single cluster). Critical section = code segment accessing SHARED resources, needing mutual exclusion. Race condition = outcome depends on the RELATIVE TIMING/SPEED of concurrent processes. Dining Philosophers deadlock avoidance: break circular wait (one philosopher picks up forks in opposite order, or limit concurrent diners to N-1). 1. Recall the precise definition directly for terminology questions. 2. For Dining-Philosophers-style questions, recall the standard deadlock-avoidance fixes (asymmetric fork order, or resource limiting). Confusing 'race condition' with 'deadlock' — race condition is about OUTCOME depending on timing; deadlock is about processes permanently BLOCKED waiting on each other. Barrier synchronization construct definition and analysis (all processes wait until ALL arrive, then all proceed together). Fork/join process-creation semantics combined with synchronization variable counting.

title: Process Scheduling
text: Operating System process-scheduling

title: Process Scheduling — concept notes
text: Process Scheduling GATE ka sabse bada OS topic hai (49 PYQs). Core skill EK hi hai baar-baar: given processes (arrival time + burst time), ek SPECIFIC algorithm (FCFS/SJF/SRTF/RR/Priority) simulate karo, aur average WAITING/TURNAROUND time compute karo. Baaki skills: algorithm PROPERTY comparison, process STATE TRANSITIONS, aur performance-metric definitions. Turnaround Time = Completion Time − Arrival Time. Waiting Time = Turnaround Time − Burst Time (kitna time process READY queue me wait karta raha, execute hue bina). Algorithms differ SIRF is baat me ki 'ready queue se AGLA kaunsa process choose karein': FCFS=jo pehle aaya, SJF=sabse chhota burst, SRTF=SJF ka preemptive version (naya chhota process aaye to switch), Round Robin=fixed time-quantum ke rounds me, Priority=highest priority pehle. Scheduling simulation ko ek 'Gantt chart banao' socho — ek timeline draw karo, har time-unit pe decide karo kaunsa process CPU pe chal raha hai (algorithm ke rule ke hisaab se), jab process khatam ho jaaye uska completion time note karo. Fir formula se turnaround aur waiting time nikaal lo. Preemptive algorithms (SRTF, preemptive priority) me HAR naye process arrival pe check karna padta hai ki kya CURRENT running process ko ROKO aur naya shuru karo. FCFS (First Come First Serve): non-preemptive, simple, but suffers from CONVOY EFFECT (short processes stuck behind one long process). SJF (Shortest Job First, non-preemptive): minimizes AVERAGE waiting time among non-preemptive algorithms — theoretically optimal for non-preemptive, but needs to KNOW burst times in advance (often unrealistic) and can cause starvation of long jobs. SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First, preemptive SJF): minimizes average waiting time among ALL algorithms (preemptive included) — the theoretical optimum, but has scheduling overhead (frequent context switches) and can still starve long jobs. Round Robin: FAIR (no starvation), good RESPONSE time for interactive/time-shared systems, but average waiting time is usually worse than SJF/SRTF; performance depends heavily on the TIME QUANTUM choice (too small → too much context-switch overhead ≈ processor sharing; too large → degenerates toward FCFS). If Round Robin's time quantum EXCEEDS the maximum burst time of any process, RR DEGENERATES to FCFS (never actually gets preempted). Priority Scheduling can cause STARVATION for low-priority processes — solved via AGING (gradually increase waiting processes' priority over time). FCFS, SJF (non-preemptive), and completed-Priority-non-preemptive do NOT cause starvation issue the same way — actually SJF and Priority (without aging) CAN starve low-priority/long jobs; only FCFS and Round Robin are starvation-free by design. TAT = Completion Time − Arrival Time WT = TAT − Burst Time Average = Σ(metric for each process) / number of processes If time quantum ≥ max burst time among all processes, Round Robin behaves identically to FCFS Forgetting to RE-EVALUATE the scheduling decision at every new arrival for PREEMPTIVE algorithms (SRTF, preemptive priority) — a shorter/higher-priority process arriving mid-execution should trigger a context switch. Confusing Turnaround Time with Waiting Time (WT = TAT − Burst, easy to drop the burst-time subtraction). Applying non-preemptive SJF logic when the question specifies SRTF (preemptive) or vice versa — these give DIFFERENT schedules and different answers. Missing tie-breaking rules when multiple processes have equal burst/priority at the same decision point — always check what tie-breaking rule the question specifies (often arrival order or process ID). For ANY scheduling numerical: (1) list all processes with arrival+burst times, (2) draw a Gantt chart timeline applying the SPECIFIC algorithm's selection rule at each decision point (process completion OR new arrival for preemptive algorithms), (3) compute each process's completion time from the chart, (4) apply TAT=Completion−Arrival and WT=TAT−Burst, (5) average as asked. For algorithm-comparison/best-fit-for-scenario questions: match the scenario's stated goal (interactive/fair→RR, minimize avg wait→SJF/SRTF, simplicity→FCFS, importance-based→Priority) to the algorithm's known strength. For state-transition-diagram questions: recall the standard 5-state model (New→Ready→Running→{Waiting,Terminated}, Waiting→Ready) and check which direct transitions are VALID (e.g., Waiting→Running directly is INVALID, must go through Ready first).

title: Numerical Scheduling Simulation (compute avg waiting/turnaround time)
text: Processes ki arrival+burst times di hain, ek SPECIFIC algorithm (FCFS/SJF/SRTF/RR/Priority) naam se poocha hai, aur average waiting/turnaround time (ya total context switches) nikaalna hai — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (49 me se 30 PYQs), almost pura topic isi ke around hai. Draw a Gantt chart timeline, apply the SPECIFIC named algorithm's selection rule at every decision point. For PREEMPTIVE algorithms (SRTF, preemptive priority): re-check the decision at EVERY new arrival, not just at completions. TAT = Completion−Arrival; WT = TAT−Burst. 1. Tabulate all processes with arrival time and burst time (and priority, if relevant). 2. Build the Gantt chart: at each decision point (process completes, OR — for preemptive algorithms — a new process arrives), apply the named algorithm's rule to pick the next process to run. 3. Read off each process's completion time from the finished chart. 4. Compute TAT and WT per process using the formulas. 5. Average as asked, being careful with rounding if the question wants decimals. Forgetting to re-evaluate at new arrivals for preemptive algorithms — silently running non-preemptively when SRTF/preemptive-priority was specified. Mixing up which algorithm variant (preemptive vs non-preemptive) is actually being asked. Multiprocessor scheduling (2+ CPUs available) — track each CPU's timeline SEPARATELY, apply the algorithm's rule per-CPU when choosing among ready processes. Processes with I/O bursts interleaved with CPU bursts (not pure CPU-bound) — track when each process becomes READY again after I/O completes, feed back into the scheduling decision. Weighted mean completion time (jobs have associated weights) — apply the weighted-average formula instead of a plain average. Multilevel/aging-priority schemes (priority increases with waiting time) — recompute priority dynamically at each re-evaluation point per the given rule.

title: Algorithm Property/Comparison (best-fit scenario, preemptive vs non-preemptive, starvation)
text: Poocha hai kaunsa algorithm best hai for a scenario (interactive system, minimize avg wait), ya kaunsa PREEMPTIVE/non-preemptive hai, ya kaunse STARVATION cause kar sakte hain — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (49 me se 13 PYQs). Interactive/time-shared system → Round Robin (fair response time). Minimize average waiting time → SRTF (preemptive, theoretically optimal) or SJF (non-preemptive optimal). Can cause starvation: SJF, SRTF, Priority (without aging). Cannot: FCFS, Round Robin. Non-preemptive: FCFS, SJF (plain), non-preemptive Priority. Preemptive: SRTF, RR, preemptive Priority. 1. Identify the scenario's stated goal or constraint (fairness? minimize wait? simplicity? avoid starvation?). 2. Match to the algorithm known for that strength. 3. For classification questions (preemptive/non-preemptive, starvation-prone), recall the direct fact list. Assuming SJF is always achievable in practice — it needs FUTURE burst-time KNOWLEDGE, which is often the exact point being tested (SJF is theoretically optimal but practically requires prediction). Time-quantum sizing question for RR (balance context-switch overhead vs response time) — reason about the trade-off directly. 'RR degenerates to X when quantum is very large/very small' — very large → FCFS-like; very small → fair-share/processor-sharing-like with high overhead.

title: Process State Transition Diagram
text: Ek process state-transition diagram diya hai (New/Ready/Running/Waiting/Terminated) aur poocha hai kaunsi transitions VALID/INVALID hain. Standard model: New→Ready, Ready→Running (dispatch), Running→Ready (preemption/time-slice-expiry), Running→Waiting (I/O/event wait), Waiting→Ready (I/O/event complete), Running→Terminated. INVALID direct transitions: Waiting→Running (must go through Ready first), New→Running (must go through Ready). 1. Recall the standard state diagram directly. 2. Check each candidate transition against the standard model's allowed edges — anything not directly connected is invalid. Assuming Waiting→Running is valid — a waiting process must always re-enter Ready first, even if the CPU happens to be free. Multi-CPU system state-count questions (max processes simultaneously in 'running' state = number of CPUs).

title: Performance Metric Definitions & Criteria
text: Poocha hai turnaround-time/waiting-time jaisी performance criteria ki UNDESIRABLE characteristics kya hain — definitional/critique pattern, mostly old descriptive papers. Turnaround time can be misleading for LONG jobs (a long job's turnaround time is dominated by its own burst time, not scheduling quality) — doesn't fairly reflect scheduling efficiency for jobs of very different lengths. Waiting time alone doesn't account for a job's inherent size — a fair comparison sometimes needs a NORMALIZED metric (like turnaround/burst ratio). 1. Consider how the named metric behaves for edge-case jobs (very short vs very long) to identify its 'undesirable' bias.

title: Virtual Memory
text: Operating System virtual-memory

title: Virtual Memory — concept notes
text: Virtual Memory me 4 skills: (1) page table SIZE aur multilevel page table ka address split, (2) Effective Access Time (EAT) with TLB/page faults, (3) TLB structure (tag bits, size), (4) conceptual/definition questions. Virtual address = [page number | offset]. Page table page number ko frame number me map karta hai. Virtual space > physical memory ho sakta hai kyunki sirf zaroori pages RAM me rakhe jaate hain (demand paging); baaki disk (swap space) pe. Virtual memory ek 'bada naksha' hai jo har process ko lagta hai ki poori memory uski hai. Asli RAM chhoti hai, isliye OS pages ko disk se laata hai jab zarurat ho. Page table ek 'address book' hai: virtual page se physical frame. Isi address book ki SIZE aur access-time hi zyadatar numericals ka core hai. Offset bits = log2(page size). Page number bits = VA bits - offset bits. Frame number bits = PA bits - offset bits; PTE mein frame bits + valid/dirty/permission bits hote hain. Multilevel page table: sirf use hone wale hisse allocate hote hain, isliye memory bachti hai; lekin memory accesses badh jaate hain (TLB miss pe levels+1). Ideal multilevel design me har level ka table exactly ek page me fit hona chahiye: entries per table = page size / PTE size. Page table entry ka essential content = page frame number (virtual page number index se implicit hota hai). Swap space disk pe hoti hai. CPU address lines se virtual address space decide hota hai: physical memory se bada, secondary storage se chhota ya barabar. 2^(VA bits - offset bits) x PTE size page size / PTE size = entries in one page-sized table bits per level = log2(entries per page); levels = ceil(page-number bits / bits per level) EAT = (1-p)*memAccess + p*faultServiceTime EAT = h*(t_tlb + t_mem) + (1-h)*(t_tlb + (levels+1)*t_mem) [+ fault terms] tag = VA bits - offset bits - log2(#sets) KB/MB/GB ko 2^10/2^20/2^30 lena; ms aur ns/us ka unit mismatch. PTE size mein extra bits (valid/dirty/permission) bhoolna. Multilevel me levels ki bits sum = page number bits hona chahiye, top level ko remainder mil sakta hai. TLB miss time me sirf 1 memory access add karna jab k-level table ho (k+1 accesses lagte hain). Hamesha pehle offset bits nikaalo, phir page-number bits, phir PTE/level split. EAT questions me probability tree: hit/miss/fault teeno paths likho aur weighted sum lo. Multilevel: ek page me kitni PTE fit hoti hain woh nikaalo, wahi bits per level hain.

title: Page Table Size / Multilevel Address Split
text: VA bits, PA bits, page size, PTE size di hain aur page table ka size, levels, ya kisi level ki bits poochi hain — sabse bada pattern (43 me se 18). Offset = log2(page size); page number bits = VA - offset. Ek page me PTE count = page size / PTE size, yahi bits per level hain. 1. Offset, page number, frame bits nikaalo. 2. Single level: entries x PTE size. 3. Multilevel: bits per level = log2(page size/PTE size); levels = ceil(page-number bits / bits per level). 4. Asked quantity (table size, #levels, memory for a process) compute karo. PTE me extra bits bhoolna. Unit conversion mistakes. Segmented paging (segment table + page tables). Maximum page-table size ke andar page count back-solve karna.

title: Effective Access Time (TLB, page faults)
text: Hit ratio, TLB time, memory time, page fault service time diye hain aur EAT poocha hai. Probability tree banao: TLB hit / TLB miss / page fault. Fault rate p ka weightage service time se hota hai. 1. Har path ka time likho. 2. Har path ki probability se multiply karke sum lo. 3. Units consistent rakho. TLB lookup time ko miss path me add karna bhool jaana. ms vs ns. Multilevel table + TLB combined (miss pe levels+1 accesses). Dirty page ka extra write-back time.

title: TLB Organization (tag bits / size)
text: TLB entries, associativity, VA bits di hain aur TLB tag ya size poochi hai. Sets = entries / ways. Tag = page number bits - set-index bits. 1. Page number bits nikaalo. 2. Set-index bits = log2(sets). 3. Tag bits = page number - index; entry size me tag + frame + control bits. Fully associative me index bits 0.

title: Conceptual / Definitions
text: True/false ya match-the-following: virtual memory ke advantages, page table content, swap space, MMU responsibilities, hardware support. Virtual memory protected address spaces deti hai, program ko RAM se bada hone deti hai. Multilevel page table memory bachata hai, access time nahi. 1. Direct definition recall karo. 2. Har option ko definition se check karo. 'Multilevel table access time kam karta hai' galat hai — memory footprint kam karta hai. Demand paging + LRU list simulation. Segmented paging me segment table ka page table.

title: Page Replacement
text: Operating System page-replacement

title: Page Replacement — concept notes
text: Page Replacement me do main skills: reference string pe FIFO/LRU/Optimal simulate karke page faults count karna, aur algorithm properties (Belady's anomaly, stack algorithms). Baaki: thrashing, dirty bit, locality. Page fault pe agar saare frames bhare hain to OS ek victim page choose karta hai. FIFO: sabse purana load hua page. LRU: sabse der se use hua page. Optimal (OPT): jo page future me sabse der baad use hoga. OPT practically implement nahi ho sakta (future pata nahi) — sirf benchmark hai. Socho RAM ek chhoti almari hai. Nayi cheez rakhni ho aur jagah nahi, to purani cheez hatani padegi. FIFO 'sabse pehle aayi cheez hatao', LRU 'jo kaafi der se haath nahi lagayi wo hatao', OPT 'jo aage sabse der baad kaam aayegi wo hatao' (crystal ball chahiye). Belady's anomaly (frames badhane par faults badh sakte hain) sirf FIFO me possible hai (in standard algorithms). LRU aur OPT stack algorithms hain, unme anomaly nahi hoti. OPT faults ka minimum deta hai; koi bhi algorithm OPT se kam faults nahi kar sakta. Dirty bit: page memory me modify hua ya nahi; sirf dirty page ko evict karte waqt disk pe likhna padta hai (unnecessary writes bachte hain). Thrashing: process ko itne kam frames ki paging me hi time lagta hai — excessive page I/O, CPU utilization girta hai; working-set model isse rokta hai. Locality of reference: haal hi me use hue pages ke dobara use hone ki sambhavna zyada hoti hai; isi wajah se LRU achha kaam karta hai. Ek process ko minimum frames instruction set architecture decide karta hai (ek instruction ke sabhi operands ko ek saath memory me hona chahiye). Zyada RAM = kam page faults, isliye performance behtar. faults = number of references that miss (hit = page already in a frame) Evict the page whose next use is farthest in the future Evict the page whose last use is farthest in the past Stack algorithms (LRU, OPT): pages in n frames subset of pages in n+1 frames, so no Belady's anomaly LRU me hit par bhi recency update karna bhoolna. FIFO me hit par order NAHI badalta (LRU se yehi fark hai). OPT me 'future me kabhi use nahi hoga' wale page ko sabse pehle evict karna bhoolna. Frame count ya initial state (empty vs pre-loaded) galat padhna. Table banao: har reference ke liye frames ki state aur hit/fault likho. LRU: recency list maintain karo; FIFO: queue; OPT: aage scan karke next-use dekho. Belady/property questions me yaad rakho: FIFO anomaly-prone, LRU/OPT nahi.

title: Page Fault Count Simulation (FIFO / LRU / OPT)
text: Reference string aur frames diye hain aur page faults ya final frame contents poochi hain — sabse bada pattern (31 me se 14). Table banao, har reference pe hit/fault mark karo. FIFO me hit pe order nahi badalta; LRU me hit pe recency badalti hai. 1. Frames khali se shuru (jab tak alag na bataya ho). 2. Har reference: page frames me hai to hit, nahi to fault. 3. Fault pe frames bhare hain to algorithm ke rule se victim choose karo. 4. Faults gino / frame contents padho. LRU me hit par recency update na karna. Address ko page number me convert karna bhool jaana. Address sequence di hai (page number khud nikaalna: address / page size). Modified OPT variant (custom rule) — rule ko sahi padhkar simulate karo. Do algorithms (FIFO vs LRU) ki comparison.

title: Belady's Anomaly & Algorithm Properties
text: Poocha hai kaunsa algorithm Belady's anomaly dikhata hai, ya frames badhane ka effect, ya OPT/LRU ki definition. Belady's anomaly = FIFO (standard algorithms me). LRU aur OPT stack algorithms hain, anomaly nahi. 1. Algorithm ka naam pehchano. 2. Stack-algorithm hai to anomaly nahi; FIFO hai to ho sakti hai. 3. Definition wale options me OPT = future me sabse der baad use, LRU = past me sabse der pehle use. 'Frames badhane par faults hamesha ghategi' — FIFO ke liye galat. Random replacement ke baare me statement (Belady possible/impossible) — random stack algorithm nahi hai.

title: Concepts: Dirty Bit, Locality, Thrashing, Minimum Frames
text: Definition/true-false: dirty bit ka kaam, locality of reference, thrashing, minimum frames, RAM badhane ka asar. Dirty bit unnecessary disk writes bachata hai. Thrashing = excessive page I/O. 1. Concept ki standard definition yaad karo. 2. Har option ko definition se test karo. Thrashing ko 'page I/O kam karta hai' likhna — ulta hai. Paging external fragmentation hatati hai par internal fragmentation laati hai (page size se prabhavit).

title: Misc (memory allocation, 3-level page table, EAT with dirty pages)
text: Topic tag Page Replacement hai par question allocation ya address translation ka hai. Question ka asli concept pehchano (heap allocation / multilevel table / EAT) aur us topic ki method lagao. 1. Concept identify karo. 2. Virtual Memory topic ke patterns (page table size, EAT) reuse karo. Sab paths ki probability add karna bhool jaana. EAT me dirty page ka extra replace time weighted karna.

title: Disk
text: Operating System disk

title: Disk — concept notes
text: Disk ki geometry (surfaces, tracks, sectors), capacity, access time = seek + rotational latency + transfer, aur file-system numerics (inode, FAT, block size trade-off). Disk access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time. Capacity = surfaces x tracks x sectors x sector size. Disk ek ghoomti hui plate hai. Head ko sahi track par le jaana (seek), plate ke ghoomne ka wait (rotation, average aadha chakkar) aur data padhna (transfer). Numerical me sab units (ms, bytes, RPM) ek jaise karo. Bade block size se throughput badhta hai par space waste (internal fragmentation) badhta hai. Capacity = surfaces x cylinders(tracks) x sectors/track x bytes/sector. Rotational latency (average) = half rotation time = 0.5 x 60/RPM. Transfer time for one sector = rotation time / sectors per track. Ek track padhne me ek full rotation lagta hai. Sector address (c,h,s) se linear sector number: ((c x heads) + h) x spt + s. RAID: fault tolerance aur/ya speed. Bade block size: better throughput, poorer space utilization. Free space: bit map ya free list. Swap space process data ke liye. surfaces x tracks x spt x sector bytes 0.5 x (60/RPM) s seek + rotational latency + transfer ((c*H)+h)*spt + s RPM se time nikalne me units (60/RPM seconds). Average latency me aadha rotation bhoolna. Cylinders ka count surfaces se confuse. Ek line me sab parameters likho. Total time = seeks + rotations + transfers step by step. Capacity/size questions me units ek karo.

title: Capacity / Geometry / Address Calculation
text: Tracks, surfaces, sectors, bytes diye; capacity ya cylinders ya sector address. Multiplication of geometry. 1. Parameters likho. 2. Multiply / divide. 3. Units check. Sectors overhead bhoolna. Unformatted vs formatted capacity.

title: Access / Read Time of a File or Records
text: Seek, RPM, sector size diye; file/records read karne ka total time. seek + latency + transfer. 1. Ek access ka time. 2. Kitni accesses (sequential vs random). 3. Total. Har record ke liye seek maan lena. Sequential file me sirf ek baar seek.

title: File-System Layout Numerics (inode, FAT, free list, block size)
text: Inode direct/indirect pointers se max file size, FAT overhead, free list bits, block-size choice. Pointers per block = block size / address size. 1. Pointers per block. 2. Direct + single + double + triple sum. 3. Multiply block size. Address size vs block size confuse. Max file size given address size.

title: Disk Concepts (RAID, device driver, formatting, root dir, swap)
text: Direct concept/definition wale sawal. Definitions. 1. Definition yaad. Options me subtle wording. Seek latency non-linear.

title: Resource Allocation
text: Operating System resource-allocation

title: Resource Allocation — concept notes
text: Resource Allocation = Deadlock. 4 skills: minimum resources jisse deadlock kabhi na ho (formula), Banker's algorithm se safe state check, allocation graph/scenario me deadlock detect karna, aur prevention/avoidance theory. Deadlock = processes ka ek group jahan har process us resource ka wait kar raha hai jo doosre ke paas hai. Chaar Coffman conditions ek saath hone chahiye: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait. Koi ek tod do to deadlock nahi (prevention). Do log darwaze pe: A ne left key li hai, B ne right key, dono ko doosri key chahiye. Koi peeche nahi hat sakta, koi aage nahi badh sakta — yehi deadlock. Banker's algorithm bank manager jaisa hai: loan tabhi deta hai jab guarantee ho ki sab clients ka kaam kabhi na kabhi poora ho sakta hai (safe state). Deadlock-free guarantee: n processes, har ek ko max k units chahiye, total R units: R >= n(k-1)+1 hone par deadlock kabhi nahi hoga. Isliye maximum n for deadlock-free = floor((R-1)/(k-1)). Different max demands (k1..kn): deadlock-free ke liye R >= sum(ki-1)+1. Banker's algorithm: Need = Max - Allocation; Work = Available; koi bhi process jiska Need <= Work ho, use finish karo aur Work += Allocation; sab finish ho gaye to safe. Resource allocation graph me har resource ka single instance ho to cycle = deadlock; multiple instances me cycle sirf necessary hai, sufficient nahi. Circular wait deadlock ke liye necessary hai. Resource ordering (numbered resources, sirf badhte order me request) circular wait tod deta hai — valid prevention. Deadlock prevention requests ko rok kar conditions todta hai; avoidance (Banker's) safe state ke basis par grant karta hai — safe state ki jaanch avoidance ka kaam hai, prevention ka nahi. Sab resources release karke hi nayi request karne wali policy me deadlock nahi hoga, par starvation ho sakta hai. R >= n*(k-1) + 1 (each process max k units) n_max = floor((R-1)/(k-1)) Need = Max - Allocation Pick process with Need <= Work; Work = Work + Allocation; repeat until all finish Mutual exclusion + Hold and wait + No preemption + Circular wait Formula me k ki jagah k-1 use karna bhool jaana (R >= n(k-1)+1). Unsafe state ko deadlock samajhna. Banker's me Need ki jagah Max compare kar dena. 'Deadlock hai' aur 'deadlock ho sakta hai' me farak na karna. Min-resources: worst-case allocation (k-1 each) socho aur +1 karo. Banker's: Need matrix banao, Work vector maintain karo, step-by-step processes finish karo. Graph/scenario: pehle single-instance ya multi-instance dekho, phir wait-for cycle dhundo.

title: Minimum Resources for Deadlock-Free / Max Processes
text: n processes, har ek ko max k units, total R units — minimum R ya maximum n poochha hai (27 me se 7). R >= n(k-1)+1. Worst case: har process ek unit kam par atka ho. 1. Har process ki max demand likho. 2. Worst-case: har ko (demand-1) units allocate karo. 3. Total worst-case + 1 = minimum resources. 4. Ulta: n_max = floor((R-1)/(k-1)). k-1 ki jagah k use karna. Floor/ceiling galat lena. Alag alag max demands: sum(ki-1)+1. 'Could lead to deadlock' wale option ka ulta reasoning.

title: Banker's Algorithm / Safe State
text: Allocation, Max (ya Need) aur Available table diya hai; safe state, safe sequence, ya request grant hogi ya nahi poochha hai. Need = Max - Alloc. Work >= Need wala process finish karo, Work me uska Alloc jodo. 1. Need matrix banao. 2. Work=Available se shuru karo. 3. Koi bhi process jiska Need <= Work ho use finish karo, Work += Alloc. 4. Sab finish to safe, warna unsafe. 5. Request ho to pehle tentative grant karke safety check karo. Need ki jagah Max compare karna. Work update me Alloc add karna bhool jaana. Kaunsa request (ya kaunsa process pehle) safe sequence deta hai — options ko ek ek test karo. Non-preemptive allocation policy ke saath multiple resource types.

title: Deadlock Detection: RAG, Lock Scenarios, Wait-for
text: Resource allocation graph ya processes ke request/release sequences diye hain aur deadlock possible hai ya nahi, ya kaunse process deadlock me hain. Single instance: RAG cycle = deadlock. Lock/semaphore code me interleaving se circular wait bana kar dekho. 1. Har process kya hold karta hai aur kya maang raha hai likho. 2. Wait-for graph banao, cycle dhundo. 3. Multi-instance me cycle ke baad bhi check karo ki koi process finish ho sakta hai ya nahi. Multi-instance me cycle ko hamesha deadlock maan lena. Priority/timestamp based request logic me deadlock ya starvation. Semaphores ke saath 3 processes ka code segment.

title: Prevention / Avoidance Theory & Coffman Conditions
text: Kaunsi scheme valid prevention hai, kaunsa statement galat hai, necessary conditions kaun si hain. Prevention = ek Coffman condition todna; avoidance = safe state check. Resource ordering circular wait todta hai. 1. Har option ko dekho ki kaunsi condition tod raha hai. 2. Prevention vs avoidance ki definition se mismatch pakdo. Prevention aur avoidance ko ek doosre ki jagah likhna. Sab release karke hi nayi request: deadlock nahi par starvation possible.

title: Disk Scheduling
text: Operating System disk-scheduling

title: Disk Scheduling — concept notes
text: Disk Scheduling me head ki movement (total seek distance/time) compute karni hoti hai FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK ke liye; plus algorithm properties aur disk access time formula. Disk head ek cylinder se doosre tak jaata hai; seek time = cylinders cross kiye x time per cylinder. Algorithm decide karta hai pending requests me se agla kaunsa service ho. Lift (elevator) socho: FCFS = jo pehle bola usi order me jao. SSTF = sabse paas wali manzil pehle. SCAN/LOOK = ek direction me chalte hue raaste ki saari requests nipatao, phir ulta ghoomo. C-SCAN/C-LOOK = ek hi direction me service, end par wapas shuru (circular). FCFS: fair, par zyada seek. SSTF: seek kam, par starvation possible. SCAN: end tak jaata hai; LOOK: last request tak hi jaata hai (end tak nahi). C-SCAN/C-LOOK: sirf ek direction me serve karta hai, wapasi ka jump alag count hota hai (question padho ki count karna hai ya nahi). SSTF me head ek direction me chalta reh sakta hai; direction change tabhi hota hai jab ek side ki requests khatam ho. Disk access time = seek time + rotational latency (average = half rotation) + transfer time. Best throughput ke liye nearest-cylinder-next (SSTF) achha hai. sum of absolute differences between consecutive serviced cylinders average = (1/2) x (60/RPM) seconds (1/sectors per track) x rotation time per sector read seek + rotational latency + transfer SCAN me disk ke end (0 ya max) tak jaana bhool jaana. C-LOOK ka return jump count karna ya na karna — question ke hisaab se. Initial direction ignore karna. Time = distance x per-cylinder time, unit conversion. Requests ko sorted list me rakho, head position mark karo. Servicing order likho, phir consecutive differences jodo. SSTF: har step par current position se nearest unserviced request.

title: Head Movement / Seek Time Computation
text: Request queue, head position aur algorithm (FCFS/SSTF/SCAN/LOOK/C-LOOK) diya hai; total seek distance ya time poochha hai (16 me se 9). Pehle servicing order nikaalo, phir distances jodo. Direction aur initial head position dhyaan se. 1. Requests aur head position note karo. 2. Algorithm ke rule se servicing order likho. 3. Consecutive |differences| jodo (SCAN me disk end ka detour bhi). 4. Time = distance x per-cylinder seek time. SCAN me end tak jaana bhool jaana. Circular jump count karna ya na karna galat lena. Do algorithms ka comparison ('additional distance' by SSTF vs FCFS). Request ids ke saath (id, cylinder) format.

title: Algorithm Properties (SSTF direction change, throughput)
text: Poocha hai kaunsi strategy best throughput degi, ya SSTF me direction kab badalta hai, ya FCFS ko SSTF se badalne ka asar. SSTF throughput achha, starvation possible. SSTF me head direction tab badalta hai jab ek side ki requests khatam ho jaayein. 1. Algorithm ka rule yaad karo. 2. Chhota concrete example banao aur trace karo. SSTF ko fair samajhna. Maximum request-set cardinality jahan direction ek baar hi badle.

title: Disk Access Time (RPM, sectors, transfer)
text: RPM, sectors per track, tracks aur seek time diye hain; access ya transfer time poochha hai. Access = seek + rotational latency + transfer. Average rotational latency = half rotation. 1. Rotation time = 60/RPM. 2. Latency = half rotation. 3. Transfer = (sectors to read / sectors per track) x rotation time. 4. Jodo. Rotational latency me poori rotation lena. Platters/cylinders/sectors se address calculation.

title: Matching / Definitions
text: Match the following: scheduling algorithm aur uski property. Direct definition recall. 1. Har algorithm ki definition se match karo.

title: Semaphore
text: Operating System semaphore

title: Semaphore — concept notes
text: Semaphore = shared integer with atomic wait (P) and signal (V). Counting vs binary. GATE me: final semaphore value, mutual exclusion / ordering with semaphores, output of concurrent code, monitor with semaphores. wait(s): s--, block if negative (or wait till s>0). signal(s): s++, wake a waiting process. Semaphore ek counter hai. wait matlab 'ek resource lo', signal matlab 'ek resource wapas do'. Final value = initial - (#wait) + (#signal), jab tak koi block na ho.
