text: Theory of Computation finite-automata

title: Finite Automata — concept notes
text: Finite Automata TOC ka sabse bada topic hai (43 PYQs). 4 skills: diya gaya automaton (state diagram) se LANGUAGE identify karna, ek language ke liye automaton CONSTRUCT karna, NFA/DFA equivalence aur closure-operations-on-automata (complement/product/union machine), aur ek specific string pe automaton ko TRACE karna. DFA = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) — states, alphabet, transition function (EXACTLY one transition per state-symbol pair), start state, final states. NFA relaxes δ to allow MULTIPLE (or zero) transitions per state-symbol pair, plus ε-transitions. DFA aur NFA EXACTLY same power rakhte hain (recognize same class: regular languages) — NFA sirf DESIGN me easier hota hai, DFA EXECUTION me deterministic/simpler hota hai. DFA ko ek 'strict robot' socho — har state pe, har input symbol ke liye EXACTLY ek hi agla step hota hai, koi confusion nahi. NFA ek 'confused robot' hai jo ek hi state-symbol pe MULTIPLE options try kar sakta hai (parallel universes me), aur agar KOI BHI path accept state pe pahunche to NFA accept karta hai. Subset construction NFA ko DFA me convert karta hai — har DFA state NFA ke 'possible current states ka SET' represent karta hai. Subset Construction (NFA→DFA): each DFA state = a SET of NFA states (the 'possible current states'). Start state = ε-closure of NFA's start. DFA accepting states = any subset containing at least one NFA accepting state. Product Automaton construction: for L(M1)∩L(M2) or L(M1)∪L(M2), build states as PAIRS (q1,q2) from M1×M2, running both machines in parallel; accepting condition differs (AND for intersection, OR for union). Complement of a DFA's language: SWAP accepting and non-accepting states (works ONLY for a COMPLETE DFA — one with a transition defined for every state-symbol pair, including a 'dead/trap' state if needed). To trace an automaton on a string: start at q0, follow transitions symbol by symbol, check if final state is accepting at the end (DFA); for NFA, track the SET of all possible current states (or check if ANY path reaches acceptance). Number of strings of length n accepted by a DFA can be computed via the ADJACENCY-MATRIX-POWER technique: (transition matrix)^n gives path counts between states, sum over (start,accepting) pairs. NFA with n states → DFA with AT MOST 2^n states (via subset construction); minimal DFA may need fewer |Q1| × |Q2| states for the product automaton (used for intersection/union of two DFAs) Complement = swap final/non-final states, ONLY valid on a COMPLETE DFA (add a trap state first if the given DFA is partial) Number of length-n strings accepted = sum over accepting states f of (TransitionMatrix^n)[start][f] Forgetting to complete a partial DFA (add trap/dead state) before complementing it — leads to an incorrect complement language. Confusing NFA's 'accept if SOME path accepts' semantics with DFA's single deterministic path — when tracing NFAs, must consider ALL possible paths, not just one. Assuming NFA needs fewer states 'because it's more powerful' — NFA and DFA recognize the exact SAME class of languages (regular), NFA is just more CONCISE in representation for some languages, not more powerful. For string-counting questions, forgetting to use matrix exponentiation and instead trying to enumerate all strings by hand for large n. For 'identify the language' questions: trace a few SHORT example strings through the automaton, observe what property gets accepted vs rejected, then generalize to a language description or regex. For 'construct an automaton' questions: identify the KEY STATE VARIABLE the automaton needs to track (e.g., 'have I seen two consecutive 1s yet?', 'is the count of a's even?') — design states around that state variable directly. For NFA-DFA conversion: apply subset construction mechanically — start from ε-closure(start), and for each new subset-state, compute transitions to other subsets. For product-automaton (intersection/union) questions: build the (q1,q2) pair-state table directly, transitioning both components together. For string-tracing questions on a SPECIFIC input: just walk through the automaton step by step, don't try to shortcut.

title: Identify the Language Accepted by a Given Automaton
text: Ek DFA/NFA ka state diagram diya hai aur poocha hai ye kaunsi LANGUAGE accept karta hai (ya equivalent regular expression kya hai) — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (43 me se 13 PYQs). Trace a handful of short strings (empty, single symbol, 2-3 symbols) through the automaton and note accept/reject — look for the PATTERN in what's accepted. Check what each state seems to 'remember' (e.g., 'last symbol was 0', 'seen odd number of 1s so far') — state MEANING reveals the language. 1. Trace 4-5 short example strings, noting accept/reject for each. 2. Hypothesize what property distinguishes accepted from rejected strings. 3. Assign a MEANING to each state ('this state = last char was X', 'this state = count is even', etc.) to confirm the hypothesis structurally, not just from examples. 4. Express the final answer as a language description or equivalent regex. Testing too few example strings and generalizing prematurely — always verify the hypothesis against at least one string NOT obviously covered by the first few tests. Automaton given as a REGULAR GRAMMAR instead of a state diagram — translate production rules into states/transitions first. 'If final and non-final states are swapped, what language results' — apply the complement logic (only valid if DFA is complete).

title: Construct a DFA/NFA for a Given Language
text: Ek language description di hai (English ya set-builder notation me) aur poocha hai DFA/NFA construct karo — ye design pattern hai. Identify the MINIMAL state variable the automaton needs to track to decide accept/reject at any point. Design states as 'snapshots' of that tracked variable (e.g., for 'ends in 01': track 'last 2 chars seen'). 1. Determine exactly what INFORMATION the automaton needs to remember to correctly decide membership (this becomes your state space). 2. Create one state per distinct 'value' of that tracked information. 3. Define transitions based on how each input symbol updates the tracked information. 4. Mark accepting states as those where the tracked information indicates the string SHOULD be accepted. Forgetting to handle ALL input symbols from every state (leaving an incomplete DFA transition table) — for DFA, EVERY state needs a defined transition for EVERY alphabet symbol. Construct FROM a given regular expression (Thompson's construction: build NFA piece by piece matching the regex's structure — concatenation, union, star each have standard NFA-combination templates).

title: NFA↔DFA Equivalence & Closure Operations on Automata
text: Poocha hai do automata equivalent hain ya nahi, ya ek automaton se COMPLEMENT/PRODUCT/UNION machine banana hai, ya NFA-DFA power comparison ke baare me conceptual TRUE/FALSE — ye is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (43 me se 13 PYQs). Complement: swap accept/non-accept states, but ONLY on a COMPLETE DFA (add a trap state first if needed). Product automaton for L1∩L2 or L1∪L2: build (q1,q2) pair-states, run both machines together. NFA and DFA are equally POWERFUL (recognize the same class) — never conclude one can express something the other can't. 1. For complement questions, FIRST check/make the DFA complete (add a trap state for any missing transitions), THEN swap accept/reject. 2. For product-automaton questions, build the paired-state table explicitly, transition both components on each input symbol together. 3. For NFA-vs-DFA power questions, default to 'equally powerful, NFA just more concise for SOME languages' as the correct framing. Complementing an incomplete DFA by naive accept/reject swap without adding a trap state first — produces a WRONG complement. Assuming 'all states accepting' automatically means the language is Σ* — doesn't account for missing transitions or stuck paths in an NFA. 'If all NFA states are accepting, is the language Σ*' — check carefully: FALSE in general if some states are UNREACHABLE from the start on certain inputs, or if the NFA can 'get stuck' with no valid transition (unlike a complete DFA).

title: Trace/Simulate Automaton on a Specific String or Count Accepted Strings
text: Ek specific string diya hai aur poocha hai automaton ise ACCEPT karega ya nahi, ya reachable states kya honge, ya length-n ke kitne strings accept honge — ye direct simulation/counting pattern hai. For DFA: follow the UNIQUE path symbol by symbol. For NFA: track the SET of all currently-possible states (or check every branching path). For 'count strings of length n accepted': use transition-matrix exponentiation (Matrix^n), sum entries from start to all accepting states. 1. For a specific string: trace step by step, symbol by symbol, from the start state. 2. For NFA: maintain a SET of possible current states after each symbol (subset-construction-style tracking), check if any is accepting at the end. 3. For counting length-n accepted strings: build the transition matrix, raise it to the n-th power, sum the (start, accepting-state) entries. For NFA tracing, forgetting to track ALL possible current states (just following one arbitrary path can miss a valid accepting path). Mealy/Moore machine output-sequence tracing (state machines that PRODUCE output, not just accept/reject) — track both state AND output at each step. Extended transition function δ* notation questions — apply the recursive definition (δ*(q,ε)=q, δ*(q,xa)=δ(δ*(q,x),a)) directly.

title: Context Free Language
text: Theory of Computation context-free-language

title: Context Free Language — concept notes
text: CFL, Regular Language se ek level upar hai — ab 'ek level ki matching' (jaise a^n b^n) possible hai, lekin do-level (a^n b^n c^n) abhi bhi nahi. 4 skills: grammar diya hai to uski LANGUAGE identify karna, ek language CFL hai ya nahi classify karna, CFL closure properties, aur grammar-property questions (ambiguity, determinism). CFG = (V, Σ, R, S) — non-terminals, terminals, production rules (LHS single non-terminal → RHS string of terminals/non-terminals), start symbol. CFL = koi bhi language jo CFG se generate ho sake, equivalently koi PDA (stack-based automaton) se accept ho sake. KEY INTUITION: PDA ke paas EK stack hai — isliye ek 'matching pair' (jaise a's push karo, b's pe pop karo) track kar sakta hai, lekin DO independent matching pairs SIMULTANEOUSLY nahi (stack sirf ek hi cheez top pe rakh sakta hai). CFG ko ek 'recipe book' socho jisme rules hain 'is symbol ko in symbols se replace karo'. Grammar se language derive karne ke liye start symbol se shuru karo, rules apply karte jao jab tak sab terminals na reh jayein. PDA (jo CFL accept karta hai) ek DFA/NFA + STACK hai — stack ek 'unbounded memory' deta hai, lekin sirf LIFO (last-in-first-out) discipline me — isliye ek matching-pair track kar sakta hai (a's push, b's pop, match ho gaya to stack khali), do independent pairs nahi. CFL closed under: union, concatenation, Kleene star, REVERSAL, and intersection/union with a REGULAR language (CFL∩Regular = CFL, CFL∪Regular = CFL). CFL NOT closed under: intersection (of two CFLs), complement — this is the single most tested closure fact in this topic. Grammar reading trick: if a rule looks like S→aSb|ε, this generates a^n b^n (matched nesting) — the classic CFL-not-regular example. If a rule looks like S→aS|bS|ε (or similar 'append anything, any order'), this is often just a REGULAR language in CFG clothing — always check if the grammar ACTUALLY needs the stack's matching power or if it's secretly regular. Deterministic CFL (DCFL, accepted by a DPDA) is a STRICT SUBSET of CFL — some CFLs are inherently NON-deterministic (need to 'guess' when to switch from pushing to popping, like palindromes without a center marker). a^n b^n c^n (n≥0) is the classic example of a language that is NOT context-free (needs matching THREE things, beyond a single stack's power) — provable via the CFL Pumping Lemma. Closed under: ∪, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, ∩ with Regular, ∪ with Regular NOT closed under: intersection of two CFLs, complement S→aSb|ε generates {a^n b^n : n≥0} — classic single-matching-pair CFL DCFL ⊊ CFL (some CFLs are inherently non-deterministic) Confusing 'CFL closed under intersection with Regular' (TRUE) with 'CFL closed under intersection with another CFL' (FALSE, no guarantee). Assuming every grammar with recursive rules generates a non-regular language — many recursive-looking grammars (like S→aS|bS|ε) are secretly regular. Forgetting DCFL is a STRICT subset of CFL — not every CFL has a deterministic PDA. Trying to prove a language IS context-free by giving a PDA/grammar attempt that doesn't actually work for ALL cases — verify the construction handles the general case, not just small examples. For 'what language does this grammar generate' questions: derive a few short strings by hand (apply rules starting from S), look for the emerging pattern. For 'is L context-free' classification: try to construct a PDA/grammar directly (single stack, single matching relationship) — if it needs only ONE matching pair, it's likely CFL; if it needs to match/compare MULTIPLE independent counts simultaneously, suspect NOT CFL (use CFL Pumping Lemma to confirm). For closure-property questions: recall the CFL closure list — closed under ∪/concat/star/reversal/∩-with-regular; NOT closed under ∩-with-CFL or complement. For grammar-ambiguity questions: try to find TWO DIFFERENT parse trees (or leftmost derivations) for the SAME string — if found, the grammar is ambiguous.

title: Given a Grammar, Identify the Generated Language
text: Ek CFG (production rules) di hai aur poocha hai L(G) kya hai — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (35 me se 14 PYQs). Derive a few short strings by hand from S, applying rules repeatedly — the pattern usually becomes clear within 2-3 derivations. Look for the STRUCTURAL shape: nested matching (aSb style) = a^n b^n family; sequential append (aS|bS style) = often just regular; symmetric/palindrome-style rules = palindrome family. 1. Start from S, apply rules to derive 2-3 short strings. 2. Identify the emerging pattern (matched counts? specific substring structure? palindrome?). 3. Express as a language description or compare against the given MCQ options directly by testing whether each option's strings ARE/AREN'T derivable. Deriving too few strings and generalizing prematurely — verify the hypothesized pattern against at least one 'edge' string (very short or with an unusual structure). Multiple grammars given, asked which PAIR of languages they respectively generate — derive each independently. 'Which string is NOT generated' — test each candidate string against the grammar directly rather than deriving the full language.

title: Classify a Language as CFL or Not
text: Ek language description di hai aur poocha hai ye CONTEXT-FREE hai ya nahi — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (35 me se 12 PYQs). Needs only ONE 'matching pair' relationship (like equal counts of two symbols, or nested structure)? → likely CFL, try constructing a grammar/PDA. Needs THREE or more independent counts matched simultaneously (like a^n b^n c^n), or TWO unrelated matching pairs in one string? → likely NOT CFL, suspect CFL Pumping Lemma applies. 1. Try to construct a grammar or PDA directly (one stack, one matching relationship) — if straightforward, it's CFL (constructive proof). 2. If the language seems to need matching MORE than one independent thing at once, suspect non-CFL. 3. Confirm non-CFL via the CFL Pumping Lemma (assume CFL, derive contradiction) or by reducing from a known non-CFL language. 4. For languages built via intersection/union of other languages, use closure facts (CFL∩Regular=CFL is always safe; CFL∩CFL has NO guarantee). Assuming any language with 'equal counts of two things' is automatically CFL WITHOUT checking if a THIRD independent count is also required (which would push it out of CFL). Language involving string REVERSAL or a marker symbol (#) separating two halves — CFL closure under reversal and concatenation often makes these CFL even when they look complex. Deterministic vs non-deterministic CFL distinction (is there a DPDA, not just a PDA) — a stricter/harder classification than plain CFL membership.

title: CFL Closure Property Verification
text: Poocha hai CFL kis OPERATION ke under closed hai (union? intersection? complement? intersection with regular?) — ye closure-fact-recall pattern hai. CLOSED: union, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, intersection/union WITH a regular language. NOT CLOSED: intersection of two CFLs, complement — memorize this exception list specifically. 1. Identify the specific operation asked about. 2. Check against the memorized closed/not-closed list. 3. For 'intersection with a regular language' specifically, remember this IS closed (special case), unlike general CFL-CFL intersection. Forgetting that intersection with a REGULAR (not another CFL) language IS safe — the exception matters. 'Which of these combined operations is NOT necessarily CFL' — check each option against the closure list, the intersection-of-two-CFLs case is the usual culprit.

title: Grammar Properties (ambiguity, determinism, DPDA existence)
text: Poocha hai ek grammar AMBIGUOUS hai ya nahi, ya language ke liye DETERMINISTIC PDA exist karta hai ya nahi — ye grammar/machine-property pattern hai. Ambiguous grammar: find TWO distinct parse trees (or leftmost derivations) for the SAME string. DCFL (has a DPDA) is a STRICT subset of CFL — some CFLs are inherently non-deterministic (classic example: even-length palindromes without a center marker, since the PDA can't know where the 'middle' is without guessing). 1. For ambiguity: try deriving a specific string via TWO different rule-application orders/structures — if both succeed differently, ambiguous. 2. For DPDA-existence questions: check if the language requires 'guessing' a transition point (like the middle of a palindrome) — if so, likely NOT deterministic even though it IS context-free. Assuming every CFL has an equivalent DPDA — false, DCFL is strictly smaller than CFL.

title: Misc Construction (FA+grammar combined design task)
text: Descriptive-style question jisme dono FA aur grammar construct karna hai ek combined task ke through — mostly older, pre-2005 style. Break the combined task into its FA-construction part (reuse Finite Automata topic technique) and grammar-construction part (reuse standard CFG design) separately. 1. Handle each sub-task (FA design, grammar design) independently using the respective topic's standard technique.

title: Regular Language
text: Theory of Computation regular-language

title: Regular Language — concept notes
text: Regular Language poore TOC ka foundation hai. 4 skills: ek specific language REGULAR hai ya nahi classify karna, closure properties verify karna (kaunse operations regularity preserve karte hain), minimal DFA ka state-count reason karna, aur pumping-lemma-style proof technique. Regular Language = wo language jo koi FINITE AUTOMATON accept kar sake (equivalently: regular expression se describe ho sake). Key INTUITION: agar language ko recognize karne ke liye 'UNBOUNDED MEMORY/COUNTING' chahiye (jaise a^n b^n — n ko yaad rakhna padega, jo FINITE states se nahi ho sakta for ALL n), to wo language regular NAHI hai. Socho DFA ek 'bahut limited memory wala robot' hai — usके paas sirf FINITE states hain, wo kisi cheez ko 'count karke yaad' nahi rakh sakta agar count UNBOUNDED ho sakta hai. a^n b^n check karne ke liye robot ko 'kitne a the' yaad rakhna padega taaki utne hi b match kar sake — lekin n kuch bhi ho sakta hai (infinite possibilities), aur robot ke paas sirf FINITE states hain to distinguish karne ke liye. Isliye a^n b^n regular NAHI hai. Lekin a*b* (koi bhi count a's phir koi bhi count b's, bina match kiye) regular HAI — kyunki count MATCH karne ki zaroorat nahi. Regular languages are CLOSED under: union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, and (for a regular L) any FIXED prefix/suffix/substring extraction that doesn't require unbounded counting. Regular languages are NOT necessarily closed under: arbitrary quotient by a NON-regular language, 'half' construction combined with unbounded matching, or operations requiring counting/comparison of unboundedly many positions. EVERY FINITE language is regular (trivially — a DFA can just have one state-chain per string, or use the disjunction of all string-matching automata). Every SUBSET of a FINITE set is regular (finite sets are always regular) — but NOT every subset of a regular (infinite) set is regular (e.g., a^n b^n is a subset of a*b*, which is regular, but a^n b^n itself is not). Intersection of a regular language and a context-free language is ALWAYS context-free (this fact often resolves 'is L1∩L2 regular/CFL' questions when one side is regular). Myhill-Nerode theorem: the number of states in the MINIMAL DFA for L equals the number of distinct equivalence classes of the relation 'x~y iff for all z, xz∈L ⟺ yz∈L' — this is the formal tool behind 'is this regular' and 'how many states minimum' questions. Regular languages closed under: ∪, ∩, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal Regular ∩ Context-Free = always Context-Free (useful reduction trick) Minimal DFA state count = number of distinct Myhill-Nerode equivalence classes of L Assuming ALL subsets of a regular (infinite) language are regular — false; only subsets of FINITE sets are guaranteed regular. Assuming intersection/union of two NON-regular languages is always non-regular — not guaranteed either way, check case by case. Confusing 'every finite language is regular' (TRUE, always) with 'every regular language is finite' (FALSE — most regular languages, like a*, are infinite). Missing the useful shortcut: Regular ∩ CFL = CFL — this resolves many 'classify this intersection' questions instantly without needing Pumping Lemma. For 'is L regular' classification: first try to construct a DFA/regex directly (if it looks finite-state-representable, it likely is). If it seems to need unbounded counting/comparison (like matching counts, palindromes, primes), suspect NON-regular and try Pumping Lemma or Myhill-Nerode distinguishability. For closure-property questions: recall the standard closure list (∪,∩,complement,concat,star,reversal all closed) — anything requiring UNBOUNDED matching/counting across the construction is suspect. For minimal-DFA-state-count questions: use Myhill-Nerode — find the maximum number of pairwise distinguishable strings (strings x,y are distinguishable if some suffix z makes exactly one of xz,yz in L). For Pumping-Lemma proofs: pick a string of length ≥ the pumping length that's clearly IN the language, split it per the lemma's constraints, then show pumping produces a string OUTSIDE the language — deriving the contradiction.

title: Regular vs Non-Regular Classification
text: Ek specific language define ki gayi hai (set-builder notation ya description se) aur poocha hai ye REGULAR hai ya nahi — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (35 me se 14 PYQs). Does recognizing this language need UNBOUNDED counting/matching (like a^n b^n, equal count of two symbols, palindromes)? → likely NOT regular. Can you construct a DFA/regex directly without needing to 'remember' an unbounded count? → likely regular. Regular ∩ CFL = always CFL — useful shortcut for intersection-classification questions. 1. Try to directly construct a DFA or regex — if straightforward, it's regular (constructive proof). 2. If it seems to require unbounded memory (counting, matching, comparing), suspect non-regular. 3. Confirm non-regularity via Pumping Lemma (find a string that can't be pumped without leaving the language) or Myhill-Nerode (exhibit infinitely many pairwise-distinguishable strings). 4. For SET-OPERATION-derived languages (L1∩L2, L1∪L2 where one/both might be non-regular), use known closure facts (e.g., Regular∩CFL=CFL) rather than re-deriving from scratch. Assuming any language with a 'count' condition is automatically non-regular — BOUNDED/modular counting (like 'number of a's is even', or 'exactly 3 more a's than b's') IS regular; only UNBOUNDED exact matching is not. Language defined via occurrence-COUNT comparisons between symbols (n_a(w) vs n_b(w) relationships) — classic pumping-lemma-non-regular territory unless the comparison is BOUNDED (like 'exactly 2 more a's than b's' which IS regular, vs 'MORE a's than b's' unboundedly which is NOT). Multiple candidate languages given, asked which subset is regular — classify each independently.

title: Closure Property Verification
text: Poocha hai ek OPERATION (union, intersection, complement, reversal, subset, prefix/suffix/half construction) regularity PRESERVE karta hai ya nahi — ye is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (35 me se 13 PYQs). Standard closures (always preserve regularity): union, intersection, complement, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal. NOT guaranteed: arbitrary subset of an infinite regular language, some 'half'/'square-root'-style length-based constructions can break regularity in edge cases. 1. Check if the operation is one of the STANDARD closed operations (∪,∩,complement,concat,star,reversal) — if so, answer preserved/TRUE directly. 2. If it's a less-standard construction (half, quotient, some custom transform), try to construct a counterexample: take a known regular L, apply the operation, check if the result requires unbounded memory. 3. For 'is every SUBSET of a regular set regular' — FALSE (counterexample: a*b* is regular, a^n b^n is a non-regular subset). Confusing 'every finite subset is regular' (always TRUE) with 'every subset is regular' (FALSE in general). Assuming infinite union of regular languages stays regular — only finite unions are guaranteed. 'Every FINITE subset of a non-regular set is regular' — TRUE (finite sets are always regular, regardless of the superset's regularity). Infinite union of regular/finite languages — NOT guaranteed regular (only FINITE unions are guaranteed closed).

title: Minimal DFA State-Count Reasoning
text: Poocha hai ek language ke minimal DFA me KITNE STATES chahiye, ya diya hai ki minimal DFA me k states hain aur poocha hai language ke baare me kya conclude kar sakte hain — ye Myhill-Nerode application pattern hai. Minimal states = number of Myhill-Nerode equivalence classes = maximum set of PAIRWISE DISTINGUISHABLE strings you can find. Two strings x,y are distinguishable if some suffix z exists such that exactly ONE of xz, yz is in L. 1. Try to find the maximum set of strings that are PAIRWISE distinguishable (for each pair, find a suffix that puts exactly one into L). 2. That count is the minimum DFA state count. 3. For 'given k states, what can be said about L' (reverse direction): reason about what k equivalence classes could represent structurally (e.g., k=2 often means a simple parity/membership-in-Σ check). Assuming NFA states directly equal minimal DFA states — the subset construction gives an UPPER bound (2^n), not the exact minimal count. NFA-to-DFA state-count relationship questions (an NFA with n states corresponds to a DFA with AT MOST 2^n states via subset construction, but the MINIMAL DFA could need fewer). 'Order of a language' defined via a custom function — translate the custom definition into the standard minimal-state framework.

title: Pumping Lemma / Algorithmic Decision-Procedure Reasoning
text: Poocha hai ek finite/regular language ke baare me strongest TRUE classification (decidable? Turing-recognizable? context-sensitive?), ya do automata ka LANGUAGE-SUBSET check karne ka algorithm design karna hai — ye meta/algorithmic pattern hai. Every FINITE language is trivially regular (hence also context-free, context-sensitive, decidable, Turing-recognizable) — pick the STRONGEST/most specific TRUE classification when asked. L1⊆L2 for two DFAs is DECIDABLE — check if L1∩complement(L2) is empty (constructible and testable via automata operations). 1. For 'strongest TRUE statement about a finite language': identify the MOST RESTRICTIVE class it belongs to (regular, being the strongest common claim for ALL finite languages). 2. For algorithmic subset-checking: construct the automaton for L1∩complement(L2), check emptiness (a decidable procedure via reachability of an accepting state) — L1⊆L2 iff this intersection is empty. Picking a weaker-but-still-true statement instead of the STRONGEST true one when the question specifically asks for the strongest.

title: Identify Class Language
text: Theory of Computation identify-class-language

title: Identify Class Language — concept notes
text: Ye TOC ka CAPSTONE topic hai — ek language di gayi hai, poocha hai wo Chomsky hierarchy me KAHAN fit hoti hai: Regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ Recursive ⊂ Recursively Enumerable ⊂ (everything). 4 skills: direct single-language classification, set-operation-combined languages ki classification, cross-class closure properties, aur machine-model equivalence proofs. Chomsky Hierarchy (strict containment, each level STRICTLY bigger): REGULAR ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ CONTEXT-SENSITIVE ⊂ RECURSIVE ⊂ RECURSIVELY ENUMERABLE ⊂ (all languages). Classification ka general approach: PEHLE check karo regular hai ya nahi (finite-state test), phir CFL hai ya nahi (single-stack matching test), phir agar dono nahi to RECURSIVE/RE/undecidable ki taraf jao (Decidability topic ke tools use karke). Socho ye ek 'power ladder' hai — Regular sabse KAM powerful (bas finite memory), phir CFL (ek stack), phir Recursive (Turing machine jo HAMESHA rukta hai — decidable), phir Recursively Enumerable (Turing machine jo accept pe rukta hai, reject pe shayad kabhi na ruke). Language classify karne ka tareeka: neeche se upar test karo — pehle regular try karo (sabse simple), phir CFL, phir upar. Canonical boundary-witness languages (memorize these): a*b* (Regular) ⊊ palindromes without marker (needs NPDA, DCFL fails, still CFL) ⊊ a^n b^n c^n (needs CSL/context-sensitive, not CFL) ⊊ Halting-Problem-related languages (Recursively Enumerable but not Recursive) ⊊ complement of Halting Problem (not even RE). A language and its COMPLEMENT: if L is Recursive, complement is ALSO Recursive (Recursive is closed under complement). If L is RE but NOT Recursive, complement is NOT RE (this is the exact non-closure boundary). FORTRAN/most programming languages are technically CONTEXT-SENSITIVE (not context-free) due to features like 'declare before use' type-checking requirements — a classic GATE trivia fact. Turing machine with a READ-ONLY input tape and CONSTANT-SIZE work tape = exactly as powerful as a FINITE AUTOMATON (the bounded work tape can only hold finitely many distinct configurations, collapsing to finite-state power). Intersection/union across DIFFERENT hierarchy levels: result belongs to the HIGHER (more powerful) of the two classes, in general (e.g., Regular∩CFL=CFL; Regular∪RE=RE) — EXCEPT for CFL∩CFL which can escape CFL entirely (not simply 'higher class', genuinely breaks out). Regular ⊊ DCFL ⊊ CFL ⊊ Context-Sensitive ⊊ Recursive ⊊ RE ⊊ all languages L Recursive ⟹ complement(L) Recursive (closed) L is RE but not Recursive ⟹ complement(L) is NOT RE (the classic non-closure boundary) Turing machine with read-only input + O(1) work tape ≡ Finite Automaton in power Assuming set operations always move UP the hierarchy predictably — CFL∩CFL can jump OUT of CFL entirely (into context-sensitive or beyond), not just 'stay CFL or become the next level up'. Confusing 'Recursive' (always halts, decidable) with 'Recursively Enumerable' (halts on YES, may loop forever on NO) — these are genuinely different classes with different closure properties. Forgetting that Recursive is closed under complement, but RE (without also being Recursive) is NOT closed under complement — this asymmetry is heavily tested. Applying CFL/Regular classification tests to a language that's actually built from a DECIDABILITY-flavored construction (should be tested with Decidability topic tools instead, likely lands in Recursive/RE). Work BOTTOM-UP through the hierarchy: is it Regular? (quick pumping-lemma/Myhill-Nerode check) → is it CFL? (single-stack-matching test, CFL pumping lemma) → is it Context-Sensitive/Recursive/RE? (usually needs a Decidability-topic-style reduction argument). For set-operation-combined languages, apply known closure facts level by level (Regular closed under everything standard; CFL closed under most things except CFL∩CFL and complement; Recursive closed under complement, union, intersection; RE closed under union, intersection, but NOT complement in general). For machine-model equivalence questions (like bounded-tape TM = FA), think about what INFORMATION the restricted resource can actually distinguish — if it's finite, the power collapses to finite-state.

title: Direct Classification of a Single Given Language
text: Ek specific language di hai (formula/description se) aur poocha hai ye Regular/CFL/CSL/Recursive/RE me se kahan fit hoti hai — direct single-language classification pattern. Test bottom-up: Regular? → CFL? → higher. Recognize canonical boundary examples (a*b*=Regular, a^nb^n=CFL-not-Regular, a^nb^nc^n=CSL-not-CFL, Halting-Problem-style=RE-not-Recursive). 1. Check if it's Regular (finite-state constructible, or matches known regular patterns). 2. If not, check if it's CFL (single matching-pair constructible via PDA/grammar). 3. If not, reason about Recursive/RE — is there an algorithm that always halts and decides membership (Recursive)? Or only an algorithm that halts on YES (RE)? 4. Compare against canonical boundary-witness languages if the construction looks similar to a known example. Missing that a BOUNDED stack (fixed max size) collapses PDA to finite-automaton power — a classic 'looks like CFL but is actually Regular' trap. PDA with a STACK-SIZE LIMIT (bounded to k items) — this collapses PDA power down to FINITE AUTOMATON power (bounded stack = only finitely many distinguishable configurations), so the language is REGULAR, not CFL. Real-world programming language classification (FORTRAN, etc.) — typically CONTEXT-SENSITIVE due to semantic checks like declare-before-use.

title: Classify Languages Built via Set Operations on Known Classes
text: Do ya zyada languages di hain (kuch Regular, kuch CFL, kuch RE), aur unke UNION/INTERSECTION/COMPLEMENT se banaye gaye language ka class poocha hai — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (31 me se 14 PYQs). Regular combined with anything via ∪/∩ usually stays at the OTHER language's level (Regular∩CFL=CFL, Regular∩Recursive=Recursive, etc.). CFL∩CFL is the DANGEROUS combination — no guarantee, can jump to CSL or beyond. Recursive is closed under complement; RE (non-Recursive) is NOT. 1. Identify each component language's class first. 2. Apply the relevant closure rule: Regular+X (∪/∩) → stays at X's level; CFL+CFL (∩ specifically) → NO guarantee, could escape CFL; Recursive+Recursive → stays Recursive; RE+RE (∪/∩) → stays RE. 3. For complement specifically: Regular/Recursive closed under complement; CFL and RE(non-recursive) are NOT closed under complement in general. Treating CFL∩CFL the same as Regular∩CFL — CFL∩CFL has NO safety guarantee, while Regular combined with anything is much safer. DCFL vs CFL distinction within the combination (is the RESULT deterministic-CFL or just general CFL) — a finer-grained classification than plain CFL/not-CFL.

title: Cross-Hierarchy Closure Property Claims
text: General TRUE/FALSE claims about closure properties ACROSS the whole hierarchy (jaise 'intersection of two recursive languages is recursive', 'subset of RE is recursive') — ye is topic ka meta-theory pattern hai. Recursive is closed under ∪, ∩, complement — the 'best-behaved' class below RE. RE is closed under ∪, ∩ — but NOT complement in general. 'Every subset of an RE language is recursive' — FALSE (an RE language can have RE, non-recursive subsets). 1. Identify which level(s) the claim is about. 2. Check against the closure-property table: Regular (closed under everything standard), CFL (closed under most, NOT ∩-with-CFL or complement), Recursive (closed under everything standard including complement), RE (closed under ∪,∩, NOT complement). 3. For 'subset' claims, be skeptical by default — subset relationships rarely preserve decidability/recursiveness automatically. Assuming RE is closed under complement like Recursive is — it's specifically NOT, this asymmetry is the crux of the Recursive-vs-RE distinction.

title: Machine-Model Equivalence Proofs (restricted-resource collapse)
text: Poocha hai ek RESTRICTED machine model (jaise bounded-tape Turing machine, ya limited-stack PDA) kis language class ke EXACTLY equivalent hai — ye proof/equivalence pattern hai, mostly older descriptive papers. A resource that's BOUNDED to a CONSTANT size (independent of input length) only gives finitely many distinguishable configurations — this ALWAYS collapses the model down to finite-automaton (Regular) power, regardless of what the unrestricted version could do. 1. Identify what resource is being restricted (tape size, stack size) and whether the restriction is CONSTANT (independent of n) or GROWING (some function of n). 2. If constant: argue the number of distinct configurations is FINITE, hence the model collapses to Regular (Finite-Automaton) power — construct the equivalence direction both ways (restricted-model→FA and FA→restricted-model) if a formal proof is required. Assuming ANY tape/stack restriction (even a growing but sub-linear one) collapses to Regular — only TRULY CONSTANT (O(1), independent of input) restrictions do this cleanly.

title: Decidability
text: Theory of Computation decidability

title: Decidability — concept notes
text: Decidability TOC ka final topic hai — 'kaunse problems ALGORITHM se solve ho sakte hain (always halting, correct answer), aur kaunse NAHI'. 4 skills: ek problem DECIDABLE hai ya nahi classify karna (memorized decidable/undecidable list), reduction-based proof likhna, Recursive-vs-RE theory, aur basic Turing Machine definitions. DECIDABLE (Recursive) = algorithm exists jo HAMESHA halt karta hai, correct YES/NO deta hai. UNDECIDABLE = koi bhi aisa algorithm EXIST nahi karta (Halting Problem is the FOUNDATIONAL undecidable problem — sab kuch usी se REDUCE hota hai). Golden RULE OF THUMB: agar problem 'Turing machine ke BEHAVIOR ke baare me KUCH BHI non-trivial poochta hai' (jaise 'does it halt', 'does it accept empty language', 'is its language regular'), Rice's Theorem ke through ye UNDECIDABLE hai. Decidability ko ek 'kya iska pakka jawab pata karne ka tareeka hai' test socho. Halting Problem ('kya ye program kabhi rukega') PROVEN undecidable hai — ye foundational fact hai. Baaki saare undecidability proofs isi se REDUCE karte hain: 'agar mai iss NAYE problem ko solve kar saku, to mai Halting Problem bhi solve kar sakta hoon — lekin Halting Problem solve NAHI ho sakta, isliye ye naya problem bhi solve nahi ho sakta.' RICE'S THEOREM (the single most powerful tool here): ANY non-trivial property of the LANGUAGE a Turing machine recognizes (not about the machine's structure/code, but about L(M) itself) is UNDECIDABLE. Examples of undecidable-by-Rice's: 'is L(M) empty?', 'is L(M) regular?', 'is L(M) finite?', 'does L(M) contain a specific string?', 'is L(M)=Σ*?'. DECIDABLE problems about FINITE AUTOMATA / regular languages / CFGs (structural, not about arbitrary TMs): membership (given DFA/CFG and string, is it accepted?), emptiness (is L(M) empty for a DFA/PDA?), finiteness (is L(M) finite for a DFA/PDA?), equivalence of two DFAs (are they the same language?). UNDECIDABLE problems specifically about CFGs: ambiguity of a CFG, equivalence of two CFGs, whether a CFG generates Σ* (universality), whether the intersection of two CFLs is empty, whether a CFG is regular/ambiguous/inherently-ambiguous. UNDECIDABLE problems about Turing machines (via Rice's Theorem or direct Halting-Problem reduction): does TM halt on input w? Does TM halt on ALL inputs? Is L(TM) empty/finite/regular/=Σ*? Do two TMs accept the same language? L is Recursive IFF both L and complement(L) are Recursively Enumerable (a foundational theorem, useful for PROVING recursiveness by showing both directions RE). Any non-trivial semantic property of L(M) (for TM M) is undecidable L is Recursive ⟺ both L and complement(L) are Recursively Enumerable Membership, emptiness, finiteness DECIDABLE for DFA/PDA/CFG (structural questions about the machine/grammar, not about arbitrary TM behavior) Ambiguity, equivalence, universality (=Σ*), intersection-emptiness UNDECIDABLE for CFGs Applying Rice's Theorem to a question about the machine's STRUCTURE/CODE rather than its LANGUAGE — Rice's Theorem specifically applies to semantic (language) properties, not syntactic ones (like 'does the TM have exactly 5 states', which IS trivially decidable by just counting). Confusing decidability questions about DFAs/regular languages (usually decidable) with the SAME question about CFGs or TMs (usually undecidable) — the machine model matters enormously. Forgetting that 'undecidable' doesn't mean 'no algorithm at all' — many undecidable problems ARE Recursively Enumerable (a semi-algorithm exists that says YES correctly but may loop on NO). Assuming reduction direction — to prove problem X undecidable, reduce FROM a known undecidable problem TO X (show 'if X were decidable, I could decide the known-undecidable problem too'). For classification questions: first check if it's about a DFA/regular-language (likely decidable) or a CFG/TM (check against the memorized undecidable list, or apply Rice's Theorem if it's a semantic property of a TM's language). For reduction-based proofs: assume (for contradiction) the target problem IS decidable, show how you could use that decider to build a decider for the KNOWN undecidable Halting Problem (or another known-undecidable problem), deriving a contradiction. For Recursive-vs-RE questions: use the 'L is Recursive iff both L and complement(L) are RE' theorem as the key tool. When in doubt on an unfamiliar-looking problem: ask 'is this asking something about a TM's LANGUAGE (semantic)?' — if yes, strongly suspect undecidable via Rice's Theorem.

title: Classify a Problem as Decidable/Undecidable
text: Ek decision problem diya hai (ek ya multiple, list ke roop me) aur poocha hai kaunse DECIDABLE hain aur kaunse UNDECIDABLE — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (30 me se 17 PYQs). Is it about a DFA/regular language (structural)? → usually DECIDABLE. Is it about a CFG's semantic property (ambiguity, equivalence, universality)? → usually UNDECIDABLE. Is it about an arbitrary TM's LANGUAGE (semantic property)? → Rice's Theorem says UNDECIDABLE. 1. Identify the machine model the question is about (DFA, PDA/CFG, or TM). 2. For DFA questions: almost always decidable (membership, emptiness, finiteness, equivalence all decidable). 3. For CFG questions: check against the specific undecidable list (ambiguity, equivalence, universality, intersection-emptiness are undecidable; membership and plain emptiness/finiteness ARE decidable). 4. For TM questions about its LANGUAGE: apply Rice's Theorem — any non-trivial semantic property is undecidable. 5. For TM questions about its STRUCTURE/behavior-on-a-specific-input (not the full language): reason via direct Halting Problem reduction. Applying Rice's Theorem incorrectly to a STRUCTURAL question (like 'does this TM have ≤10 states', which is trivially decidable by direct inspection, NOT a language property). Assuming a CFG question is decidable just because 'CFGs are simpler than TMs' — many CFG semantic questions (ambiguity, equivalence) are still undecidable. List of 3-4 problems given, asked which SUBSET is decidable/undecidable — classify each independently, then match to the combined answer option. Problem framed as 'given TWO CFGs, is L(G1)⊆L(G2)' or similar comparative CFG question — almost always undecidable (equivalence-adjacent).

title: Reduction-Based Undecidability Proof
text: Poocha hai ek problem UNDECIDABLE hai, ye PROVE karo by REDUCING from Halting Problem (ya kisi aur known undecidable problem) — ye proof-construction pattern hai, mostly descriptive/older papers. Standard proof template: ASSUME the target problem X is decidable (has decider D_X). CONSTRUCT a decider for the Halting Problem using D_X as a subroutine. Since Halting Problem is undecidable, CONTRADICTION — so X must be undecidable too. The construction usually involves building a NEW Turing machine that 'wraps' the original halting-problem instance in a way that connects to X. 1. State the assumption: 'suppose X were decidable, via decider D_X'. 2. Design a transformation: given an arbitrary (TM, input) pair for the Halting Problem, construct a NEW instance of X such that 'X's answer' tells you 'does the TM halt on the input'. 3. Argue this construction, combined with D_X, would decide the Halting Problem — contradiction, since Halting Problem is undecidable. 4. Conclude X is undecidable. Reducing in the WRONG direction — must reduce FROM the known-undecidable problem TO the target (show target's decidability would imply Halting Problem's decidability), not the reverse. Reducing from a DIFFERENT known-undecidable problem (not directly Halting Problem) — same template, just a different 'known undecidable' starting point.

title: Recursive vs Recursively Enumerable Theory
text: Poocha hai Recursive vs RE ke beech relationship (closure under complement, NP-vs-decidable connection, 'L Recursive iff L and complement both RE') — ye theory/meta pattern hai. L is Recursive ⟺ both L and complement(L) are RE — the key theorem connecting the two classes. NP ⊆ Decidable (Recursive) — every NP language IS decidable (just maybe not efficiently, but an algorithm that always halts DOES exist, even if exponential). 1. For complement-related claims, apply the Recursive⟺both-RE theorem directly. 2. For NP-related claims, remember NP problems ARE decidable (NP⊆Decidable, this is NOT the P vs NP question, that's about EFFICIENCY not decidability at all). 3. Test claims against the CANONICAL counterexample: Halting Problem is RE but NOT Recursive, and its complement is NOT RE. Confusing 'NP' (efficiency class) with 'decidable' (a much weaker, definitely-implied property) — every NP language is trivially decidable via brute force, even if not efficiently. Polynomial-time reducibility CHAIN questions (L1≤L2≤L3, what can be concluded) — reason about transitivity of reducibility and what it implies about relative 'hardness'.

title: Turing Machine Basic Definitions & Structure
text: Poocha hai Halting Problem ki definition kya hai, ya ek specific TM ke states/transitions/tape-alphabet ke baare me basic structural question — ye definitional/structural pattern hai. Halting Problem: given a TM M and input w, does M halt on w? — state this precisely as the canonical undecidable problem. For structural TM questions (states, transitions, alphabet), these are usually DIRECT read-off/trace questions, not decidability judgments. 1. For definitional questions, state the precise formal definition. 2. For structural TM questions, trace the given transition function directly on the given input.

title: Regular Expression
text: Theory of Computation regular-expression

title: Regular Expression — concept notes
text: Regular Expression, Finite Automata ka ALGEBRAIC twin hai — same power (regular languages), different notation. 4 skills: English/language-description ko REGEX me translate karna, RE↔FA conversion, do regexes EQUIVALENT hain ya nahi verify karna, aur membership/counting questions. Regex building blocks: concatenation (ab = a followed by b), union/alternation (a|b = a OR b), Kleene star (a* = zero or more a's), Kleene plus (a+ = one or more a's, = aa*). Har regex ek regular language describe karta hai, aur har regular language kisi regex se describe ho sakta hai (Kleene's theorem). Regex ko ek 'pattern-building language' socho, jaise algebra ki tarah RULES follow karta hai. * (star) ka matlab 'is cheez ko 0 ya zyada baar repeat karo'. | (ya +) ka matlab 'in mein se koi ek choose karo'. Concatenation ka matlab 'ek ke baad doosra'. In teeno operations se KOI BHI regular language build ho sakti hai. KEY IDENTITIES (memorize): (r*)* = r* (star of star is just star). r*r* = r* (concatenation of two stars is just star). εr = rε = r (epsilon is concatenation identity). ∅r = r∅ = ∅ (empty-set kills concatenation). ∅* = ε (star of empty set is just epsilon, the empty string). ε* = ε. (a|b)* = a*(ba*)* = (a*b*)* — MULTIPLE regex forms can represent the SAME language; don't assume syntactic difference means different languages. r+ = rr* = r*r (one-or-more is NOT the same as r*, which allows ZERO occurrences too — r+ requires at least one). (a|b)* generates ALL strings over {a,b} (Σ*) — the 'anything goes' pattern. To find a regex for 'strings NOT containing substring X': often easier to think in terms of the COMPLEMENT structure — describe what CAN appear between/around avoiding X, rather than trying to negate the regex algebraically (regex has no native negation operator). (r*)* = r* r*r* = r* εr = rε = r ∅r = r∅ = ∅ ∅* = ε r+ = rr* = r*r (requires ≥1 occurrence, unlike r* which allows 0) Confusing r+ (one or more) with r* (zero or more) — a very common off-by-one-occurrence trap. Trying to directly 'negate' a regex algebraically — there's no native complement operator; must go through the automaton. Assuming syntactically different regexes must represent different languages — many equivalent forms exist for the same language, always verify via example strings or automaton equivalence if unsure. Missing that ∅* = ε (NOT ∅) — the star of the empty language is the language containing just the empty string (zero repetitions of nothing is still a valid 'zero occurrences'). For translating a language description to regex: break the description into independent SUB-PATTERNS first, then combine with concatenation/union/star as appropriate. For RE↔FA conversion: use Thompson's construction (regex→NFA, piece by piece) or state elimination method (FA→regex, removing states one at a time while updating edge labels with regex expressions). For equivalence-checking between two regexes: test several concrete strings against both (does each string match both regexes identically?), or convert both to minimal DFAs and check if the DFAs are structurally identical. For membership/counting questions: expand small cases explicitly, or convert to automaton and use direct enumeration/matrix-power counting for larger cases.

title: Translate Language Description → Regular Expression
text: English/set-builder me language description di hai (jaise 'strings with two consecutive 0s and two consecutive 1s', 'binary numbers divisible by 3') aur regex likhna hai — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (29 me se 11 PYQs). Break the description into independent sub-conditions, build sub-patterns for each, combine with concatenation/union/star. For 'divisible by k' in binary — this needs a specific per-digit-processing DFA-style regex construction (via state-elimination from the mod-k DFA), not a simple direct pattern. 1. Identify distinct required SUB-PATTERNS in the description (e.g., 'contains 00' AND 'contains 11', in any order/position). 2. Build a regex for each sub-pattern separately. 3. Combine using union (for 'either/or' requirements), concatenation (for 'followed by'), with Σ* wildcards filling in 'anything else can appear here'. 4. Test the assembled regex against a few example strings (both matching and non-matching) to verify. Forgetting Σ* 'wildcard' segments needed to allow arbitrary content around a required substring pattern. Missing edge cases like the empty string or single-character strings when the pattern requires 'two consecutive' something. Programming-language identifier lexical token definition (letter followed by letters/digits) — direct concatenation of character-class union and star. Divisibility-by-3-in-binary — requires understanding the underlying mod-3 DFA structure first, then converting to regex.

title: Regex ↔ Finite Automaton Conversion
text: Ek automaton (state diagram) diya hai aur poocha hai equivalent regex kya hai, ya regex diya hai aur automaton banana hai — ye two-way conversion pattern hai. FA→Regex: state elimination method — remove states one at a time, updating remaining edges with regex expressions capturing the eliminated paths. Regex→FA: Thompson's construction — build small NFA fragments for each regex piece (single symbol, union, concatenation, star), combine via ε-transitions. 1. For FA→Regex: pick a non-start/non-accept state to eliminate, redirect its incoming/outgoing edges through a combined regex expression (incoming · self-loop* · outgoing), repeat until only start/accept states remain, read off the final regex. 2. For Regex→FA: parse the regex's structure (identify the outermost operation — union, concat, or star), build sub-automata recursively for each piece, combine via the standard Thompson's templates. Losing self-loop terms during state elimination — a state's self-loop must be captured as a Kleene-star factor in the combined path expression. Multiple candidate regexes given, asked which ones ALL correctly represent a given automaton (multi-correct verification, not single conversion).

title: Regex Identity/Equivalence Verification
text: Do (ya zyada) regexes diye hain aur poocha hai ye EQUIVALENT hain ya nahi (same language represent karte hain) — is topic ka doosra bada pattern hai (29 me se 8 PYQs). Apply standard identities directly: (r*)*=r*, r*r*=r*, εr=r, ∅r=∅, ∅*=ε. If identities don't immediately resolve it, TEST concrete strings against both regexes — if any string matches one but not the other, they're NOT equivalent. 1. Try to simplify both regexes using known identities first. 2. If still unclear, test several concrete strings (including edge cases: empty string, single character, strings with repeated patterns) against both — a single mismatch disproves equivalence. 3. For a definitive proof (not just testing), consider converting both to minimal DFAs and checking structural equality. Assuming visually similar regexes (like (a|b)* vs a*b*) are equivalent without checking — a*b* is much more restrictive (only a's then b's) compared to (a|b)* (any order). Comparing regex-defined language relationships (L1⊆L2? L1∩L2=∅?) rather than pure equivalence — test membership of specific strings in both.

title: Membership / Counting Questions
text: Poocha hai ek specific string regex ke language me hai ya nahi, ya length ≤n ke kitne strings match karte hain, ya SHORTEST string jo language me NAHI hai — ye direct evaluation pattern hai. For membership: try to construct/derive the given string from the regex structure directly (does it match the pattern piece by piece?). For 'shortest string not in language': start checking from length 0 upward (empty string, then length 1, then 2...) until finding one that doesn't match. 1. For membership questions, break the target string into pieces matching the regex's structure (concatenation boundaries, which star-repetitions account for which substrings). 2. For counting-up-to-length-n questions, enumerate systematically by length or convert to automaton and use matrix-power counting. 3. For shortest-non-member questions, check strings in increasing length order starting from ε. Missing the empty string as a candidate when searching for 'shortest string not in language' — always check ε first. Comparing TWO regex-defined languages, counting strings in neither (set-difference-style counting) — enumerate all strings up to the length bound, classify each against both regexes.

title: Minimal State Automata
text: Theory of Computation minimal-state-automata

title: Minimal State Automata — concept notes
text: Ye topic almost ENTIRELY ek hi question-type ke around ghoomta hai: 'given language X, minimum kitne DFA states chahiye?'. 3 variants: seedha compute karna (Myhill-Nerode se), table-filling minimization algorithm apply karna (existing DFA ko minimize karna), aur NFA-vs-minimal-DFA state-count theoretical bounds. Minimum DFA states = number of DISTINCT 'residual behaviors' the automaton needs to remember. For modular-counting languages (jaise 'divisible by k'), states = k (track remainder). For MULTIPLE independent conditions combined (jaise 'a-count div by 2 AND b-count div by 3'), states = product of individual counts (2×3=6), since automaton needs to track BOTH conditions SIMULTANEOUSLY. Socho automaton ko ek 'remainder tracker' — agar language 'number of a's divisible by 5' check karti hai, to automaton ko sirf itna yaad rakhna hai 'abhi tak kitne a's the, mod 5' — yani 5 possible remainders = 5 states. Agar DO independent cheezein track karni hain (a's mod 2 AND b's mod 3), to automaton ko DONO simultaneously yaad rakhna hoga — jaise ek (x,y) pair state, x∈{0,1}, y∈{0,1,2} — total 2×3=6 combinations = 6 states. 'Divisible by k' (count of some symbol mod k) needs EXACTLY k states. Combining TWO independent modular conditions (mod p AND mod q) needs p×q states (product construction) — UNLESS the conditions aren't truly independent, in which case fewer states might suffice (always verify via distinguishability, don't just multiply blindly). 'Last k symbols are/have property X' (a sliding-window condition) typically needs 2^k or similar exponential-in-k states, since the automaton must remember the last k symbols exactly. Table-filling/partition-refinement minimization algorithm: start with 2 groups (accepting, non-accepting); repeatedly SPLIT any group where two states behave differently on some input symbol (go to different groups); repeat until no more splits — remaining groups = minimal states. Minimal DFA for a language is UNIQUE (up to renaming states) — there's only ONE minimal DFA for any given regular language. NFA with n states → minimal DFA has AT MOST 2^n states (subset construction upper bound), but could need as few as... there's no simple general LOWER bound guarantee; the relationship is NOT tight in general. 'divisible by k' needs exactly k states 'mod p AND mod q' (independent) needs p×q states (product construction) 'property of last k symbols' typically needs O(2^k) states (must remember exact last-k-symbol window) NFA with n states → minimal DFA has at most 2^n states; no simple universal lower bound Forgetting to verify the product-construction state count is actually MINIMAL (not just an upper bound) — always sanity check for unreachable/equivalent states in the combined automaton. Confusing NFA state count with minimal DFA state count — NFA states give an UPPER BOUND via subset construction (2^n), not the exact answer. For sliding-window languages, miscounting the exponent — carefully define exactly what 'window' needs to be remembered. For pure modular-counting languages: state count = the modulus (or product of moduli for combined independent conditions). For minimization of an EXISTING automaton (table-filling method): start with accepting/non-accepting partition, iteratively refine by checking if any two same-group states transition to DIFFERENT groups on some symbol — split if so, repeat to a fixed point. For NFA→minimal-DFA bound questions: recall that 2^n is only an UPPER bound; the actual minimal count requires either doing the subset construction and then minimizing, or direct Myhill-Nerode analysis of the underlying language. For sliding-window/last-k-symbols languages: enumerate the possible 'window states' explicitly for small k to verify the state count.

title: Compute Minimum DFA States for a Given Language
text: Ek language description ya regular expression di hai aur poocha hai MINIMUM kitne DFA states chahiye — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (25 me se 18 PYQs), almost pura topic isi ke around hai. Modular condition ('divisible by k') → k states. Multiple independent modular conditions → product of the moduli. Sliding-window/last-k-symbols condition → count distinct possible windows explicitly. For a regex, convert to NFA first (Thompson's), then think about what DISTINCT 'progress states' through the regex are needed. 1. Identify what TYPE of condition the language encodes: modular count, sliding window, structural pattern (like a specific substring), or combination. 2. Apply the matching formula (k for modular, product for combined, explicit enumeration for windows). 3. VERIFY by checking for unreachable or equivalent states in your constructed answer — don't just trust the formula blindly, especially for combined conditions. 4. For regex-given languages, build the automaton via standard construction first (or reason about the regex structure directly: e.g., (ab)* needs states tracking 'position within the ab pattern'). Assuming complement language needs a DIFFERENT state count than the original — it needs the SAME count (just different accepting states). Complement-of-a-language state count (usually SAME as the original language's minimal DFA, since complementing just swaps accept/reject, not the state structure). Divisibility-by-5-in-binary style number-theoretic languages — needs a specific per-digit-processing DFA design (track remainder mod 5 as you read bits MSB-first, updating via remainder = (remainder*2 + bit) mod 5).

title: DFA Minimization Procedure (table-filling / equivalence partitioning)
text: Ek EXISTING automaton/state-table diya hai (already built, possibly non-minimal) aur poocha hai minimize karo, ya equivalence partition find karo — ye is topic ka algorithmic-procedure pattern hai. Start with 2 groups: accepting states, non-accepting states. Repeatedly check: within a group, do any two states transition to DIFFERENT groups on the SAME input symbol? If so, split them apart. Repeat until no more splits happen — remaining groups are the minimal states. 1. Partition states into {accepting} and {non-accepting} initially. 2. For each partition, check each pair of states within it: do they transition to the SAME partition on every input symbol? If not, split the partition. 3. Repeat the refinement until stable (no more splits occur). 4. Merge equivalent states into single minimal-DFA states, redraw transitions using the merged states. Stopping the refinement too early (before reaching a stable partition) — must iterate until NO further splits occur in a full pass.

title: NFA-to-Minimal-DFA State Bound Theory
text: Poocha hai ek NFA with n states equivalent minimal DFA me KITNE states 'necessarily' honge (general theoretical bound, specific automaton nahi) — ye is topic ka theoretical/meta pattern hai. Subset construction gives UPPER bound 2^n — but there's no simple universal LOWER bound (could be as few as 1 state in trivial cases). 'Necessarily true' claims usually need to hold for EVERY possible NFA with n states — test against extreme/trivial examples to disprove overly strong claims. 1. Recall 2^n is the UPPER bound, not a guarantee of exact size. 2. For 'which statement is NECESSARILY true' questions, test the claim against a simple/trivial NFA (like one accepting Σ*, which needs just 1 DFA state) to see if the claim still holds — if not, it's not 'necessary'. 3. Be suspicious of any claim asserting a SPECIFIC minimal DFA size purely from n — the actual minimal size depends on the LANGUAGE, not just the NFA's state count. Assuming a tight relationship between n and minimal DFA size exists in general — only the LOOSE upper bound 2^n is guaranteed; actual minimal size varies widely by language.

title: Pushdown Automata — concept notes
text: PDA = FA + ek STACK. 3 skills: given language ke liye PDA construct karna, given PDA se language identify/trace karna, aur PDA theory (acceptance modes, determinism vs non-determinism power). PDA transitions: δ(state, input_symbol, stack_top) → (new_state, stack_push_string). Har move PEHLE stack ke top ko POP karta hai (implicitly, ya explicitly consume karta hai), phir NAYI string PUSH karta hai. Do acceptance modes: FINAL STATE (accept if input consumed aur ek accepting state pe ho) aur EMPTY STACK (accept if input consumed aur stack khaali ho gaya) — dono modes EQUALLY POWERFUL hain (same language class: CFL), koi bhi PDA ek mode se doosre me convert ho sakta hai. PDA ko FA socho jisके paas ek 'notepad' (stack) bhi hai — jab kuch yaad rakhna ho (jaise 'kitne a's dekhe'), wo notepad pe likh (push) sakta hai, aur jab match karna ho (jaise ek b dekha, ek a cancel karo), notepad se mita (pop) sakta hai. Stack LIFO hai — sirf UPAR wali cheez dekh/badal sakte ho, isliye sirf ONE matching relationship track kar sakte ho achhe se. Acceptance by final state and acceptance by empty stack are EQUIVALENT in power — any PDA of one type can be converted to the other type accepting the SAME language. DETERMINISTIC PDA (DPDA) is STRICTLY WEAKER than general (non-deterministic) PDA — some CFLs (like even-length palindromes without a center marker) can ONLY be accepted by a non-deterministic PDA, no DPDA exists for them. Every regular language's NFA can be trivially converted to a PDA that just never uses its stack — this confirms Regular ⊆ CFL structurally, not just as a closure fact. The complement of a CFL is NOT necessarily CFL (from the CFL topic), but the complement of a context-free language IS always recursive (decidable) — a weaker but still useful guarantee (since PDAs/Turing machines can always simulate 'try all derivations up to length n' for decidability, even without closure). L(PDA, final state) = L(PDA, empty stack) — for the SAME language class, conversion always possible between the two modes DCFL (accepted by DPDA) ⊊ CFL (accepted by general PDA) — strict subset Assuming DPDA and NPDA (general PDA) have the same power — DPDA is strictly weaker, some CFLs need non-determinism. Confusing 'complement of CFL is recursive' (TRUE, weaker guarantee) with 'complement of CFL is CFL' (FALSE, from the closure properties). Getting the push/pop ORDER backward when tracing — always process pop of current top FIRST (per the transition), then push the new string (which appears on stack in REVERSE order of writing, since the leftmost pushed symbol ends up on TOP). For PDA construction: identify the ONE matching relationship needed (e.g., match a's against b's), design push-on-a/pop-on-b transitions directly. For 'identify language from PDA' questions: trace a few short strings through the PDA, tracking BOTH the state AND the stack contents at each step. For acceptance-mode conversion questions: recall the standard technique (add a new start state that pushes a special bottom marker, and for final-state→empty-stack conversion, add transitions from all final states that pop everything down to the marker then to a new accepting state).

title: Construct a PDA for a Given Language
text: Language description di hai (jaise palindromes, a^n b^n) aur PDA construct karna hai — design pattern. Identify the ONE matching relationship the language needs (equal counts, palindrome structure) — design push/pop transitions directly around it. 1. Identify what needs to be 'remembered' via the stack (e.g., count of a's seen so far). 2. Design push transitions for the 'building up' phase, pop transitions for the 'matching down' phase. 3. For palindromes, need a way to 'guess' the middle (non-deterministic PDA) since there's no marker. 4. Specify the acceptance condition (final state or empty stack) explicitly. Designing a construction that only works for even-length or specific-length strings, missing the general case. Specifically requiring a DETERMINISTIC PDA — verify the construction doesn't require any 'guessing' step (like guessing the palindrome's center without a marker).

title: Identify the Language Accepted by a Given PDA / Trace Execution
text: Ek PDA (transition diagram/table) diya hai aur poocha hai ye kaunsi language accept karta hai, ya ek specific string pe trace karke accept/reject batana hai — is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (15 me se 9 PYQs). Trace a few short strings, tracking BOTH state and full stack contents at each step. Look for what the stack seems to be COUNTING/MATCHING to infer the general language pattern. 1. For a specific string: trace step by step, maintaining an explicit stack-contents list alongside the current state. 2. For general 'what language' questions: trace several short strings, infer the pattern from what gets accepted (stack empty + accepting state, or per the acceptance mode specified). 3. Pay attention to whether acceptance is by FINAL STATE or EMPTY STACK — check the problem statement for which mode applies. Losing track of the exact stack contents (not just the height) partway through a trace — always write out the full stack, symbol by symbol. Minimal PDA (1 state, 1 stack symbol) — reduces to a pure stack-height/counter interpretation. Transition notation using extended forms — carefully parse what's popped and pushed on each labeled edge before tracing.

title: PDA Theory (acceptance modes, determinism, PDA-CFL-FA relationships)
text: Poocha hai final-state vs empty-stack acceptance equivalent hain ya nahi, ya DPDA vs NPDA power comparison, ya PDA-FA-CFL ke beech general TRUE/FALSE claims — ye theory pattern hai. Final-state and empty-stack acceptance are EQUIVALENT in power (conversion always possible). DPDA ⊊ PDA (strict subset) — non-determinism genuinely adds power for PDAs (unlike for finite automata, where NFA=DFA in power). 1. For acceptance-mode questions, recall the equivalence directly. 2. For determinism-power questions, recall DPDA is strictly weaker — some CFLs need non-determinism. 3. For general TRUE/FALSE claims linking PDA to FA/CFL/regular concepts, verify each against the known hierarchy (Regular ⊆ CFL, DCFL ⊊ CFL, NFA→PDA trivial conversion exists). Assuming DPDA=NPDA in power (like NFA=DFA for finite automata) — this key difference between FA and PDA is a favorite conceptual trap.
